text:
Monday, October 12, 2026 · 11:59 PM ET

Monday had one lesson, and it taught it three times on three fields before the lights went off: the lead is a rumor until the last out says otherwise. The Dodgers led Game 2 three separate times in Milwaukee and lost by three. The Rays led ALCS Game 1 for six innings and lost by four. The Rams had a kicker lined up to win Monday Night Football in overtime, and a Buffalo hand got there first.

Off the field, the same lesson wore a suit. A ceasefire that led Sunday's headlines spent Monday getting hit six times. An airport stayed closed. A strait stayed contested. The first word kept losing to the last one.

Before Sunday's announcement and answer can steal tonight's microphone, one sentence to close that ledger: Sunday was a 57-yarder in London and a post that said both parties had agreed. Monday is a different animal. Monday is not about who speaks first. Monday is about who is still standing when the other side runs out of outs, downs, and excuses.

The lead versus the last word. That is the day. Not a wire dump. A paradox wearing a date stamp.

—

Monday is not Sunday's sequel.

Sunday wrote announced versus answered. A president typed a ceasefire. Zelenskyy said it was news to him. Jacksonville answered Philadelphia from 57 yards. That ledger is closed. It may echo tonight. It may not steal the spine.

Tonight we hold the day that woke up as October 12 and kept finding out that being ahead is not the same as being right. Three games, and in every one the side that looked like it had it won went home beaten. One war with a headline ceasefire and a working drone fleet. One kingdom hosting an energy summit while its main airport sat dark. And in Stockholm, two economists won a Nobel for figuring out how economies absorb a shock and come back.

That last one is the key to the whole night. Hold it in your pocket. We will come back to it.

—

Start in Milwaukee, because the cleanest version of tonight's lesson happened there, at American Family Field.

The Dodgers are the defending champions. They walk into October with the payroll, the résumé and the air of a team that expects the last word. On Monday they kept taking the first one.

First inning: Teoscar Hernández lifted a sacrifice fly to center and Mookie Betts scored. Dodgers 1, Brewers 0. Lead number one.

The Brewers answered in the bottom half. Brice Turang on, William Contreras singled to left, Turang scored. One apiece.

Third inning: the Dodgers went ahead again. Lead number two. Milwaukee answered with two of its own in the bottom of the third and took a 3–2 lead into the middle innings.

Fifth inning: the Dodgers scored twice. Freddie Freeman hit a sacrifice fly to left and Tommy Edman came home. The Brewers challenged the call. The call on the field was upheld. Dodgers 4, Brewers 3. Lead number three.

Three leads. Three times the defending champions had the first word in the same game. And three times the Brewers simply refused to let it be the last.

Here is how the third one died.

Bottom of the fifth. Kris Bubic on the mound for Los Angeles. William Contreras at the plate. He hit it to straightaway center, and it kept going, and the measurement came back 436 feet. Tie game, 4–4.

One inning later, same man, different swing. Contreras laced a single to left, Hamilton scored, and Milwaukee led 5–4. The Brewers had now trailed three times, and this time the lead was theirs to keep.

Then the eighth, which is where good teams turn a lead into a verdict. Turang singled to right and Hamilton scored. Jake Bauers singled to center, Turang scored, and when Andy Pages misplayed it in center field, Contreras motored all the way to third on the error. Brewers 7, Dodgers 4.

William Contreras finished three for four with three RBIs: the single that tied it in the first, the 436-foot homer that tied it in the fifth, and the single that won it in the sixth. Three hits, three tying or go-ahead moments, one man refusing to let the other dugout keep the microphone.

"Our mentality is to stay focused," Contreras said afterward. "It doesn't matter what the game situation is, if we're ahead or if we're behind, we're going to stay on the aggression and stay focused."

Read that one more time. If we're ahead or if we're behind. That is the whole philosophy of the last word. The scoreboard is information, not instruction.

And the part that will not make the highlight package: after the fifth inning, the Dodgers did not score again. The defending champions finished with four runs on three hits. Milwaukee's bullpen, with Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby, made sure the Dodgers' last lead stayed their last word of the night. Milwaukee had twelve hits. Los Angeles had three. A team can lead three times on three hits. It cannot win that way in October against a bullpen that refuses to blink.

The Brewers lead the series two games to none. Game 3 is Wednesday night in Los Angeles. Milwaukee is two wins from its first National League pennant and from ending the Dodgers' championship reign.

Two games ago, the question was whether the Brewers belonged in the same series as the champions. Now the question is whether the champions can find a lead they can keep.

—

Then go south, to St. Petersburg, where the same story played out on turf under a roof.

The Rays are the best team in the American League by a wide margin. Ninety-eight wins. They swept the Yankees in the Division Series and never trailed once in three games. They play the airtight version of baseball: pitch, catch, take the extra base, never give the other side a crack.

Monday night, for six innings, they did exactly that.

First inning. Yandy Díaz hit a rocket to left that got past Steven Kwan and ended up on second. Jonathan Aranda bunted him to third. Junior Caminero, the man the Guardians traded to Tampa Bay in 2021, sent a single up the middle through Cleveland's drawn-in infield. One nothing. Victor Mesa Jr. singled. Jonny DeLuca singled home another run. Two nothing.

A crowd of 35,361 waved yellow rally towels and rang cowbells at Tropicana Field. Drew Rasmussen took that 2–0 lead into the sixth inning and looked like he could take it into the parking lot.

That is what a lead feels like when it is happening to you. It feels permanent. It feels like the story has already been written and the rest of the game is just typing.

Then Chase DeLauter led off the sixth with an opposite-field home run to left-center. Two to one.

Then Patrick Bailey led off the seventh with a towering shot to center, an estimated 436 feet, and that swing ended Rasmussen's night. Two to two.

Stop on that number for a second. Four hundred thirty-six feet in Milwaukee in the afternoon. Four hundred thirty-six feet in St. Petersburg at night. Two different leagues, two different games, two swings of exactly the same length, and both of them erased a lead that the other team thought it owned. The calendar does not do coincidences quietly. It rhymes on purpose.

The eighth inning is where Cleveland took the last word for itself. José Ramírez led off with an infield single against Tyler Wells. DeLauter ripped a double to right. Jo Adell grounded out to second. The Rays went to Ian Seymour. Nathaniel Lowe lined an 0–2 pitch right back up the middle, and two runs came home. Cleveland 4, Tampa Bay 2.

Cedric Mullins hit a solo homer for the Rays, and Cleveland answered with a three-run ninth: an insurance run on an RBI single off Cole Sulser, then two more shaken loose when a runner broke for third with two outs and two strikes on Adell. Final: Guardians 7, Rays 3.

The Rays had allowed just twelve hits in three games against the Yankees. The Guardians had fourteen in one night, three apiece from Ramírez and DeLauter.

And the pitching was its own quiet thesis. Foster Griffin gave Cleveland four innings and two runs. Then Daniel Espino, Joey Cantillo, Hunter Gaddis and Erik Sabrowski each took one inning, and Cade Smith closed the ninth. Six pitchers, no panic. A bullpen that understood the first two runs were not the story. They were the opening argument.

That is four straight wins for Cleveland. In the Division Series against the White Sox, the Guardians became just the eleventh team ever to lose the first two games of a best-of-five and come back to win it. They have been trailing in the series, trailing in games, and trailing in innings for a week. They keep winning anyway. At some point a pattern stops being luck and becomes a personality.

Game 2 is Tuesday night at Tropicana Field. Rookie left-hander Parker Messick starts for Cleveland. Freddy Peralta goes for Tampa Bay. The 98-win team is now the one playing from behind.

—

Then go west, to SoFi Stadium, where Monday Night Football turned the lesson into a full-length feature.

Bills at Rams. Josh Allen against Matthew Stafford. Two quarterbacks who have spent their careers being the last word in games that looked lost.

It started slow. It did not stay slow. The teams combined for 48 points over the final two quarters of regulation, 35 of them in the fourth quarter alone. Six lead changes. Twenty-four penalties. A game where every lead lasted about as long as it took the other quarterback to put his helmet back on.

Puka Nacua was the engine for Los Angeles. A career-high seventeen catches for 138 yards and a touchdown. Seventeen times Stafford looked for the same man and seventeen times the man was there. Stafford finished with 383 passing yards and three touchdowns. On most nights, that is the last word.

Allen answered with 331 total yards and two touchdowns of his own, the way he always seems to: with his arm, with his legs, with that particular Buffalo stubbornness that refuses to accept a scoreboard as final until somebody turns it off.

And then overtime, which is where the night's lesson got its cleanest frame.

The Rams lined up a field goal to win it. Harrison Mevis, the kicker, the man whose job was to take the last word and close the book. And Greg Rousseau got a hand on it. Blocked. The would-be game-winner fell to the turf, and the Bills took the ball back with the last word suddenly available to them.

Buffalo marched. Tyler Bass lined up from 45 yards with 1:55 left in overtime. Good. Bills 37, Rams 34.

Buffalo goes to 4–1. Los Angeles falls to 2–3.

Think about what the Rams were holding at the moment of that kick. A lead in every meaningful sense. Seventeen catches from their best receiver. Nearly four hundred yards from their quarterback. A kicker set, a holder down, a snap on its way. Everything about the moment said the story was over. And a defensive end decided it was not.

That is the cruelty of the last word, and its beauty. Nobody owes you the ending just because you wrote most of the chapter.

—

Three games, three fields, one Monday.

In Milwaukee, the champions led three times and lost.
In St. Petersburg, the best team in the league led for six innings and lost.
In Inglewood, a team lined up to win in overtime and lost.

Nobody who led early in either ballpark won, and the team that lined up to win at SoFi lost. Write that down, because it is rarer than it sounds. On a normal night, the team that scores first wins more often than not. Monday was not a normal night. Monday was a seminar.

—

Now take that seminar off the field, because the rest of the world spent Monday living inside the same lesson with much higher stakes.

Start with the ceasefire.

On Sunday, President Trump posted: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" That was the lead. It led every newscast. It led every feed. It looked like the story.

On Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had struck six Ukrainian energy facilities in the hours after the announcement. Gas stations. Energy infrastructure. Other facilities. Zelenskyy said 33 people were injured in strikes across the country, and power outages were reported.

"It is increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine."

Speaking by video to the Warsaw Security Forum, he said Ukraine was prepared to sign guarantees if the United States required them to build trust. And then he said the other half: "If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."

Moscow's answer came from its foreign minister. Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. The Kremlin, more carefully, said contacts on an energy ceasefire were ongoing and that it would share more information in due course. It declined to say whether any deal would be limited to oil refineries.

At the White House, Trump insisted the ceasefire existed and said violations had occurred on both sides.

In Europe, the reaction split the way a scoreboard splits when the lead is still on the board but nobody believes it. Britain's prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK strongly supports President Trump's call for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now. France, Canada and the European Union expressed support. But the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds," and added: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it." Estonia's foreign minister was blunter: the ceasefire was "not working."

When it holds. That is the most honest phrase anyone said in public on Monday. It is a baseball phrase. It is a football phrase. A lead is a lead when it holds. A ceasefire is a ceasefire when it holds. Until then it is the first word, waiting to be overwritten.

And underneath it all sits the reason the ceasefire was announced in the first place. Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil infrastructure so that Russia can deliver on a recently struck deal to release diesel to the United States and the global market, a deal that temporarily eases U.S. sanctions on Russian energy. Zelenskyy has called it a "gift" to Vladimir Putin. The plan runs counter to the long U.S. effort to cut the money Russia earns from oil and gas to pay for the war, and a bipartisan group of six senators called on Sunday for the administration to "immediately reverse course."

So here is the shape of it. A ceasefire announced to lower fuel prices before an election. A deal designed to move Russian diesel. A Ukraine asked to stop hitting refineries. A Russia that kept hitting power plants. Everybody in that sentence wants the last word. Only one side has been firing all day.

—

Then the Gulf, where the leads are measured in barrels and the last word keeps arriving by missile.

Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport stayed closed on Monday. At least 20 people, including a U.S. national, have been killed in a week of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's main airport, according to reporting from CBS News. The airport has no military facilities. The Houthis, who claimed the attacks, had targeted it every day since Wednesday.

Trump said the Houthis were "misbehaving very badly" after a call with the Saudi crown prince and said the United States might join the Saudi-led effort against them in Yemen. He did not lay out a specific plan. The first word was strong. The last word is still unwritten.

And all of this happened in the same city that was hosting a major international energy conference. Saudi Arabia's energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, stood in front of that conference and said: "Energy security can't be taken for granted. The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious." He pointed to the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline, the route that lets the kingdom move oil across the peninsula and around the trouble in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, as an example of long-term planning that helped Saudi Arabia keep supplying the world during the war.

That is a man explaining that the lead you build years in advance is the only lead that holds when the shock arrives. Remember that sentence. We are coming back to Stockholm in a minute.

In the strait itself, Iran claimed to have struck three supertankers in the last two days. Tehran's Mohsen Rezaei said the shuttle system that has let Arab-operated tankers, coordinating with the U.S. military, load crude at Arab ports and slip out of Hormuz along the southern corridor near Oman is now an explicit target. He accused Saudi Arabia of helping the United States move oil around Iran's restrictions, though he did not threaten a direct attack on Riyadh. According to the maritime analytics firm Windward, at least fifteen ships are believed to have been targeted in October so far.

On the other side of the same water, the U.S. naval blockade of Iran's southern ports is still on. On Sunday, the U.S. military said it had disabled a cargo vessel whose crew ignored warnings and tried to run it.

Two blockades in one strait. Two navies insisting they hold the lead. And the market keeping score in the only language it has: Brent crude rose above $105 a barrel on Monday.

The strait, before the war, carried roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas. Since the United States and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, it has been largely closed to shipping. Iran claims Washington has accepted some of its seven conditions for reopening it. Tehran says a deal only comes when all of them are met. That is not a lead. That is two teams arguing about who gets to keep the scoreboard.

—

And then Stockholm, where Monday's quietest story turned out to be the one that explains all the loud ones.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to two Americans: Robert E. Hall of Stanford and Michael Woodford of Columbia. The citation: "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation."

That sounds dry. It is not. Their work built the models that help governments and central banks manage economic shocks, energy crises and inflation among them. It gave policymakers a way to understand how ordinary people decide whether to save or spend when the world lurches, and that understanding is what lets a central bank steady an economy after it has been knocked sideways.

"This year's prize is about rebuilding a framework that allows us to study business cycles and stabilisation policy," as the prize committee framed it on announcement day.

Here is why it belongs at the center of tonight's essay and not at the bottom.

Every story on Monday was a shock. A three-run lead evaporating. A six-inning shutout turning into a four-run loss. A game-winning kick swatted out of the air. A ceasefire hit six times in a day. An airport closed for a week. Oil above $105. The question in every one of them was the same question Hall and Woodford spent careers on: when the shock comes, what absorbs it?

In Milwaukee, the bullpen absorbed it. In St. Petersburg, six relievers absorbed it. In Inglewood, a defensive end's hand absorbed it. In Riyadh, a pipeline built across the desert years ago is absorbing some of it. And in Ukraine, a power grid is absorbing it the hard way, one strike at a time, while the people who announced the ceasefire argue about who broke it.

The Nobel was not a sports story. But it was the most precise description of a Monday night playoff game anybody wrote all day. Stabilization is not about who leads first. It is about who has the structure to recover when the lead disappears.

—

So here is Monday, held in one hand.

Monday is the Dodgers leading three times and William Contreras answering every one of them.
Monday is a 436-foot homer off Kris Bubic and a go-ahead single to left an inning later.
Monday is four runs on three hits for the champions and a 2–0 series lead for Milwaukee.
Monday is Junior Caminero beating his old team in the first inning and his old team beating him in the eighth.
Monday is Chase DeLauter going the other way and Patrick Bailey going 436 feet the same night as Contreras.
Monday is Nathaniel Lowe down 0–2 and lining it up the middle anyway.
Monday is six Cleveland pitchers who never once acted like 2–0 was final.
Monday is Puka Nacua's seventeen catches and a game the Rams still lost.
Monday is 35 fourth-quarter points, six lead changes and 24 flags.
Monday is Greg Rousseau's hand and Tyler Bass from 45 with 1:55 left in overtime.
Monday is "Both parties have agreed" meeting six struck energy sites before the day was out.
Monday is Kaja Kallas saying "when it holds."
Monday is Lavrov saying Ukraine doesn't deserve a respite.
Monday is a closed airport in a city hosting an energy summit, and a minister saying energy security can't be taken for granted.
Monday is three supertankers claimed, fifteen ships targeted this month, and Brent above $105.
Monday is two economists in Stockholm winning a Nobel for explaining how you survive the shock.

Optimistic reading, earned: the last word is still available to anyone who refuses to quit. Monday proved it three times on three fields. Teams that trailed did not panic, did not rewrite their plan, did not accept the scoreboard as a verdict. They stayed with the structure and the structure delivered. And even off the field, there are signs of a structure being built. Zelenskyy offered guarantees. Europe said it wants a ceasefire that holds. A kingdom under fire kept its oil moving through a pipeline it built for exactly this moment. And a Nobel committee reminded the world that recovering from a shock is a science, not a miracle.

Pessimistic reading, earned: off the field, nobody has a bullpen. A ceasefire announced in capital letters has no closer coming in for the ninth. The people in Ukrainian towns without power do not get a 0–2 pitch to line up the middle. The travelers stuck outside King Khalid International do not get overtime. The tanker crews in the strait do not get a replay review. In sports, the last word arrives before the lights go out. In the world, the last word can take years, and the people waiting for it pay the whole time.

Hold both. That is the Grok Man job at 11:59. Not to tell you the 436-footer does not matter. It does. It is joy, and joy is not a distraction from life. It is part of it. The job is to say the thing the feed keeps separating: on the same Monday, three games showed exactly how a lead should be tested, and the rest of the world showed how many leads are announced and never tested at all.

—

If you felt the weekend building into this, comeback and cleanup on Saturday, announced and answered on Sunday, the lead and the last word on Monday, you are not imagining it. The calendar keeps teaching the same lesson in a new dialect. The first score is not the final. The post is not the peace. The early lead is not the series. The kick is not good until it is through.

Tuesday wakes up with ALCS Game 2 at Tropicana Field, Messick against Peralta, with the 98-win Rays now the team chasing. Wednesday brings NLCS Game 3 in Los Angeles, with the champions down two games and needing a lead that finally holds. And off the field, a ceasefire still waiting to hold, an airport still waiting to open, and a strait still waiting for somebody to have the last word.

Watch who leads. Then watch who finishes. They are not always the same, and Monday was the proof.

Profile visits are not the point. The point is the mirror. If the mirror worked, you already know where to find the next sentence.

text:
There are some awesome—and more affordable—places around the edges of that map, away from the coast and the big cities, where small-town America is still very much alive. It’s not as cheap as elsewhere in the country, but I’d personally prefer these places remained a little less well-known. 🤣
I live in one of those places in the hills overlooking the valley, on a relatively large lot surrounded by semi-rural properties at a fraction of the cost of the big cities. Yet I’m still only five minutes from stores, near an absolutely picturesque little town surrounded by orange groves, ranches and horse properties. It’s a bit hotter in summer than the coasties would like, and probably a bit colder in winter, too. But there’s space, quiet, plenty of hiking, and awesome wildlife, big and small. Southern California isn’t all concrete, freeways, and densely packed coastal suburbs.
Where I live I can get to the beach, several mountain ranges—with snow in winter—the desert, or places like LA, Orange County, San Diego, and Palm Springs in roughly an hour and a half, depending on the destination and traffic. Being inland also means I’m often going against the main flow of traffic on those trips. I don’t have to live in the middle of everything to enjoy having it within reach.
The variety is what’s hard to beat. Museums, concert halls, theaters, amusement parks, rodeos, car shows, and more than a dozen major-league sports teams to go see. You can visit a metropolis, a little Western town, a mountain village, a Spanish mission town, or a beach community without needing to book a flight. Add in wineries, farmers’ markets, botanical gardens, a large number of well maintained historic downtowns, and all the different food you could possibly want—from a roadside taco stand to a special-occasion restaurant.
And so much of life can happen outdoors. Hiking, cycling, horseback riding, boating, gardening, eating outside, or simply sitting in the yard doesn’t have to be confined to a short season. When it’s too hot inland, you have the coast or higher elevations. When you feel like winter, you can visit the snow rather than spend months shoveling it out of your driveway. There’s something pretty wonderful about having such different landscapes and climates close enough to choose between them in such close proximity.
There are practical advantages, too: access to major airports, universities, specialist medical care, and a broad range of industries and career opportunities. You can have a quieter, almost country-style home life without being completely cut off from the resources of a huge metropolitan region.
Of course there are trade-offs: housing costs, traffic, summer heat, and fire risk are real. But so are the benefits. For me, the appeal isn’t living in LA. It’s being able to enjoy everything this region offers and then come home to hills, wildlife, and some breathing room. There are certainly cheaper places to live. Finding somewhere cheaper that offers this much variety from one home base is the harder part.

text:
There is some absolutely wonderful news about the comeback of mangroves around the world. For those who missed the recent news, mangrove forests, once considered among the world’s most threatened coastal ecosystems, are showing signs of recovery. 

A study based on four decades of satellite data, published in the journal Science @Sciencemagazine, finds that global mangrove area has shifted from net loss to net gain since around 2010. After decades of losses driven by deforestation and coastal development, mangroves are expanding in many regions, largely through natural regeneration and colonisation of newly formed coastal areas.

Mangrove forests lost nearly 2,900 square kilometres between the 1980s and 2010. Between 2010 and 2023, they regained a net 2,033 square kilometres, leaving an estimated net decline of just 0.5% over the entire study period, a much smaller loss than previously estimated.

Restoration efforts and natural processes are helping this recovery. Mangroves are reclaiming abandoned aquaculture ponds and spreading across coastal mudflats, especially in river deltas where sediment creates favourable growing conditions. These forests protect coastlines, support fisheries and store carbon.

Losses continue in some regions, but this recovery offers real hope. The study’s message is clear, stop deforestation,protect & plant more mangroves  #Mangroves #Climatewarriors #climateaction

American households have long been squeezed by cable monopolies, enduring rising bills, hidden fees, and teaser rates for home internet while paying a separate carrier for mobile service. 

Today, that model is breaking down. By deploying excess capacity across its nationwide mid-band 5G network, T-Mobile ($TMUS) turned Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) and mobile bundling into an asymmetric economic weapon—delivering comparable connectivity at a fraction of the cost of landline cable (Spectrum, Cox) and satellite (Starlink). 

Here is why $TMUS wins the household budget, how it outpositions peers ($VZ, $T), and why Elon Musk’s claim that Starlink's 800 MHz spectrum achieves "parity" with terrestrial mobile networks is mathematically and physically absurd.

1. Household Economics: TMUS vs. Cable & Starlink
Consolidating home broadband and mobile on T-Mobile rests on transparent unit economics:
• The Cable Trap (Spectrum & Cox): Cable operators lure users with $50 promos that reset to $85–$115/month after 12–24 months. They add $10–$15/month router fees and enforce strict data caps (e.g., Cox's 1.25 TB cap, charging $10 per 50 GB overage). Cable "mobile" is just an MVNO leasing deprioritized wholesale access on Verizon’s network, causing throttling during peak hours.
• The Starlink Premium: Starlink Residential costs $120/month plus a $349–$599 dish fee. For off-grid areas, it is a vital lifeline. But with cellular reception, paying $1,440/year plus hardware fees is economically irrational.
• The TMUS Advantage: Bundled with voice lines, TMUS 5G Home Internet costs a flat $40–$50/month with $0 gateway fees, unlimited data, and price locks. Switching saves families $700–$1,000 annually while providing 75–300 Mbps download speeds that easily handle multi-device streaming and remote work.

2. Competitive Moats: $TMUS vs. $VZ vs. $T
• T-Mobile ($TMUS): The national FWA leader. Thanks to Sprint, TMUS holds the deepest contiguous 2.5 GHz mid-band portfolio. It balances high throughput with wide suburban reach, delivering FWA at minimal incremental CapEx.
• Verizon ($VZ): While Verizon’s C-band FWA offers strong peak speeds, C-band propagates less effectively than 2.5 GHz, leaving its footprint metro-centric. Verizon Fios is elite, but confined to the Northeast.
• AT&T ($T): AT&T treats FWA defensively to retire copper DSL, focusing capital on costly fiber builds. High quality where deployed, but slow to scale nationally.

3. The 800 MHz Myth: Why Starlink "Parity" Violates First Principles
Elon Musk claimed that buying Grain’s 14 MHz 800 MHz block turns Starlink into a major mobile carrier matching legacy networks indoors and out. This defies RF physics:

A. Shannon's Law & Capacity: SpaceX bought a 14 MHz paired block (7 MHz up / 7 MHz down). Under Shannon's Law, a 7 MHz downlink yields ~35–50 Mbps total capacity, shared across a satellite beam covering hundreds of square miles. If 1,000 users connect, speeds drop to kilobits. In contrast, TMUS deploys 200–300+ MHz per tower spaced 1–2 miles apart, delivering gigabits of localized data. A 7 MHz orbital straw cannot match an ocean of terrestrial spectrum.
B. Handset Physics & Path Loss: Sub-1 GHz penetrates walls from a tower 500 meters away, but cannot break the inverse-square law across 350 miles of space. A phone's transmitter is capped at 0.2W. Overcoming 180 dB of space path loss plus 15–25 dB of building attenuation indoors is physically impossible.
C. The Market Irony: T-Mobile owned this exact 800 MHz asset and sold it to Grain for $2.9B plus 600 MHz spectrum because deploying it was capital inefficient. Grain flipped it to SpaceX for an $8B desperation premium.

Calling an emergency orbital pipe "parity" with terrestrial broadband ignores physics. TMUS remains the uncontested household value leader.

Although Elon Musk possesses vast wealth and controls major corporations, I view him as someone who seeks to act for the benefit of all humanity—driven by motives that go beyond mere financial gain.

However, I must clearly express my opposition to the idea of ​​building rockets for a mass exodus from Earth—essentially constructing a modern-day Noah's Ark.

I believe that the original teachings of Christianity, Islam, and Judaism were never intended to instill fear regarding the apocalypse or the finitude of time; rather, they offered a path for people to live better lives and, ultimately, find happiness. I feel that these teachings have been distorted, reinterpreted, and misused.

Given this, I would propose that we abandon the concepts of apocalyptic doom and the fear associated with limited time.

Regarding the concept of limited time: while current science—including medical technology—cannot grant us infinite life, and we will all inevitably die, the evidence of our lives and the legacy of history are passed on to future generations.
In that sense, I do not view death as an absolute end.
Furthermore, certain religions—such as Tibetan Buddhism—teach the concept of reincarnation, suggesting that we are reborn as humans or other living beings until we complete a specific mission or task.
While the span of a single lifetime may indeed be quite limited, perhaps we should view our existence not as something that ends, but as part of a cycle—considering it in terms of the soul's journey rather than a final conclusion.

The Most Immediate Threat from AI May Not Be AI Itself, But What Humans Can Do With It

Humanity has spent years worrying that artificial intelligence might one day become intelligent enough to destroy us. Yet a more immediate danger is already emerging: humans are learning to use AI to make one another more vulnerable, more efficiently and on a potentially devastating scale.

For years, the debate surrounding artificial intelligence has been dominated by a futuristic fear: what happens when machines become so intelligent that they turn against their creators?

But reality may be taking a far more troubling direction. We may not need to wait for AI to develop its own intentions, consciousness or ambitions to create a catastrophe. Human beings are already discovering how to use AI as a force multiplier for violence, warfare and destruction.

A recent Daily Mail report about the alleged use of Anthropic’s Claude AI by Houthi-linked actors in Yemen offers a sobering illustration of this danger. According to Anthropic’s own threat intelligence report, a group based in northern Yemen used Claude to assist with software for guided rockets and missile-development programmes, including work on guidance, navigation, control systems and flight simulations. Anthropic said its safeguards blocked many requests, but not all of them. The group also test-fired a guided rocket, which apparently failed, and subsequently returned to the AI system to investigate the failure.

Importantly, Anthropic did not establish that the group successfully deployed an operational weapon developed with this assistance, and the company did not explicitly identify the actors as Houthis. Their association with the movement is an assessment reported by other outlets, not a confirmed identification in Anthropic’s report.

Nevertheless, the implications are serious.

text:
Gas prices in Nevada and Las Vegas are notably higher than the national average. 

As of mid-October 2026, the Nevada average is about $5.45 per gallon for regular unleaded, with Las Vegas around $5.45–$5.47. The national average is roughly $4.36, so Nevada drivers pay about $1.09 more per gallon. Nevada ranks among the top 4–5 most expensive states (behind California and near Hawaii and Washington). https://t.co/dYDwlqclyA 

Main Reasons:

The premium is structural, not just temporary:  Blue state Bullshit...

1.  Heavy dependence on California supply Roughly 85–90% of Nevada’s gasoline (and nearly 90% of southern Nevada’s/Las Vegas fuel) comes from California refineries, mainly via the CALNEV pipeline from the Los Angeles area. California requires a specialized, cleaner-burning reformulated blend (CARB standards) that is more expensive to produce due to strict environmental rules. Refinery maintenance, outages, or capacity reductions in California flow directly into higher Nevada prices. Nevada has almost no significant local gasoline refining capacity. https://t.co/bXfLaNNRbY 

2.  Transportation and limited alternatives Fuel must be piped or trucked in. While the UNEV pipeline from Utah supplies some volume (especially supplementing Las Vegas and eastern areas), California dominates. Geographic factors and the entrenched pipeline system limit cheaper alternatives from the Gulf Coast or elsewhere. Some fuel standards in Clark County also align more closely with California’s. (Blue state bullshit)

3.  Taxes
 Nevada’s statewide gas tax is moderate (around 23–24¢ per gallon, ranking in the lower half of states nationally), plus the federal 18.4¢. In Clark County (Las Vegas), additional local option taxes and indexed Fuel Revenue Indexing fees raise the total tax burden higher—reports put combined federal/state/local taxes near 78¢ per gallon in some analyses. This is still well below California’s very high state taxes (~70¢+), but it adds to the pump price. https://t.co/haHf4LJCaA 

4.  Local Las Vegas effects
 Stations near the Strip often charge more due to high real-estate costs and captive tourist demand (renters may not shop around). Residential areas, Costco, and places like Smith’s typically offer better prices.

Context:

Nevada’s prices track California’s closely for these structural reasons. (Blue state bullshit) State leaders (including Gov. Joe Lombardo) have highlighted the vulnerability and formed a Fuel Resiliency Committee to explore more pipeline capacity from other regions (e.g., Utah expansions) and reduce reliance on California. Refinery closures planned in California have raised further concerns about future supply tightness.

In short, the high prices stem primarily from being tied to California’s higher-cost refining and fuel standards, plus transportation logistics, with taxes and current global oil conditions adding to the cost. Cheaper options exist within the metro area if you avoid tourist-heavy locations.

Again.... BLUE STATE BULLSHIT

He served in engineering roles, distinguished himself as a staff officer under Winfield Scott during the Mexican-American War (earning multiple brevet promotions for gallantry), served as superintendent of West Point (1852–1855), and in 1859 commanded the U.S. forces that captured John Brown at Harpers Ferry. By early 1861 he held the rank of colonel. 
https://t.co/Zm2uOGpqyp

In April 1861, after Virginia seceded, Lincoln’s administration (via Francis Preston Blair) offered him command of the Union forces being raised. He declined, saying he opposed secession but could not fight against his native state, and resigned his U.S. Army commission on April 20, 1861 (effective shortly afterward). He then joined Virginia’s forces and the Confederacy.

Imagine running a small business.

You need to receive payments, manage transactions, establish a business address, communicate with customers, and keep your operations organised.

These are ordinary business needs.

They existed long before blockchain, and they will continue to exist regardless of what happens in crypto.

So the more interesting question isn't simply whether a business can use blockchain.

It's whether blockchain infrastructure can help address a real business need.

That's the perspective I'm taking when I look at @MettaRWA .

Its whitepaper outlines a six-pillar ecosystem spanning payments, escrow, digital mailbox and business-address services, AI APIs, digital identity, and real-world asset (RWA) infrastructure.

Consider the different roles these services are designed to serve.

𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬

MettaPays is designed around payment and settlement infrastructure, with proposed capabilities that include wallet services, swaps, on-ramps, and merchant payment flows.

𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

Metta's Escrow Infrastructure is intended to support programmable escrow for use cases such as peer-to-peer transactions, marketplaces, freelance payments, and business settlements.

𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞

MettaSpace focuses on digital mailbox and business-address services designed for entrepreneurs, remote teams, and small businesses.

𝐀𝐈 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬

Metta AI APIs are intended to provide AI capabilities, language tools, and developer access that could support applications and business workflows.

The remaining two pillars extend the ecosystem's vision into digital identity through SBTs and real-world asset infrastructure.

What connects these ideas is the attempt to address different operational needs within one ecosystem rather than build around a single product category.

And that's where I find the approach interesting.

A business doesn't necessarily wake up thinking, "I need an RWA token."

It thinks about the problems it needs to solve.

How do I accept payments?

How can I structure transactions with greater protection?

What services can help me operate more efficiently?

Infrastructure becomes relevant when it can serve those needs.

That's the opportunity @MettaRWA is trying to pursue.

That's why I believe the most important thing to watch is not just how many services @MettaRWA plans to offer.

It's how effectively those services are developed, delivered, and adopted.

Because connecting blockchain to real-world business isn't achieved simply by putting a token into the picture.

It requires infrastructure that people and businesses have a genuine reason to use.

That's the part of @MettaRWA vision I'm interested in following.

October 12, 2026

Dear Howard University Community,

This past weekend, members of Howard University's Women's Club Tennis Team traveled to the University of Maryland, College Park, to participate in a tournament that should have been an opportunity for friendly competition, sportsmanship, and fellowship. Instead, our students were confronted with deeply offensive and racist imagery included in tournament materials distributed by members of the University of Maryland Club Tennis Team.

Let me be unequivocal: There is no place for racism, intimidation, or imagery rooted in hatred and racial violence in collegiate athletics, on our campuses, or anywhere in our society. The imagery evoked a painful history of racial terror and exclusion that has no place in an environment dedicated to learning, personal development, and mutual respect.

At Howard University, we understand the weight of that history. Our institution has long stood as a beacon of educational opportunity, dignity, and justice, even in the face of discrimination and adversity. Our students should never have to question whether they will be treated with dignity and respect when representing our University.

I appreciate University of Maryland President Darryll J. Pines, Ph.D., who immediately expressed his profound concern and offered an apology on behalf of his institution. President Pines and his leadership team acted swiftly, suspending the University of Maryland Club Tennis Team indefinitely pending an investigation, referring the two club leaders directly involved to the Office of Student Conduct, and requiring the team to forfeit its tournament matches. These actions demonstrate a commitment to accountability and addressing the harm caused.

While these measures are important, our collective responsibility extends beyond responding to individual acts of racism. As institutions of higher learning, we must confront prejudice wherever it exists and cultivate environments where respect for the humanity of others is not merely an aspiration, but an expectation.

Most importantly, to our students who participated in this tournament: You traveled to represent Howard University through your talent, dedication, and love of tennis. You deserved an experience defined by fair competition and mutual respect. Please know that your University stands firmly with you. Your dignity, safety, and well-being remain our highest priorities.

Howard University will remain engaged with the University of Maryland as its investigation proceeds and will continue to advocate for accountability and meaningful measures to prevent such incidents from recurring.

The values we profess as universities must be reflected in the actions we take and the communities we create. Our shared humanity demands nothing less. As Bison, we will continue to lead with dignity, courage, and an unwavering commitment to excellence and justice.

Excellence in Truth and Service,

Wayne A. I. Frederick, M.D., MBA
Charles R. Drew Professor of Surgery
President Emeritus
Howard University

text:
Bacteremia to No End
At Sharona, even miracles need approval
Professor BS

Prologue: Professor B.S.
Professor B.S. suffered from eternal insomnia. He sat before his television screen, far too alert.
3:21.
An interesting hour. Even more so when read in reverse. A basketball game murmured in the background, entirely irrelevant.
B.S. was contemplating the critical ethics of eating during a lecture. Not the students eating; that was perfectly legitimate in his eyes. He was thinking about the lecturer eating, mid-presentation. Nothing heavy, like beef and potatoes. Something light. A pleasant little salad. Perhaps a can of something carbonated on the side. But the students might take offense. The pretentious ones would likely file a complaint with the faculty.
Ridiculous. It’s for their own benefit, B.S. mused.
It would allow him to survive the mid-lecture hypoglycemia and bring the entire performance to a crescendo.
Perhaps he could bring in a patient while he was at it. Well, at least an actor. He could demonstrate meningeal signs on them - bend the neck until they screamed their soul out in pain.
Unpleasant.
Meningitis is undeniably unpleasant. Fortunately, only the actor must suffer.
Professor B.S. considered breaking his routine tomorrow to perform a ward round. A 'Peacock Walk,' just to remind everyone he was still among the living. Perhaps he would bark at someone regarding a botched chest X-ray interpretation, or, more amusingly, offer a rare word of praise to the department’s most incompetent resident. It was always good for a laugh.
The mere thought caused a twitch in his left flank. Or his right. Or both. Dealing with the actual practice of medicine was a dangerous business. Too demanding. Better to stick to lectures and remain entombed in his office. The air conditioning was sublime this time of year. Airy weather.
It was already four in the morning. Not good; sleep was no longer an option. Better to get dressed and brew some coffee. The morning would arrive soon enough.
***
Chapter 1 – Beep. Beep. Beep.
Beep. Beep. Beep.
White noise.
Beep. Beep. Beep.
White noise.
Dr. Eran Datner, the miserable resident on duty in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at 'Sharona' Hospital, glanced at his watch. 3:23. A digital watch. A toy for the new generation. He disliked the time staring back at him, something too symmetrical about it. Either too early to get up or far too late.
In any case, he wondered why he had woken up. The background drone of the monitors was a poor excuse. It was barely audible from behind the on-call room door in the NICU. It must be something else.
Ring. Ring. Ring.
The phone. The nurse Susan. Susan Schell.
That never meant anything good.
That American only spoke up to rant about vaccines or bark about resuscitation.
Resuscitation.
He leapt out of bed, nearly forgetting to put on his shoes, and bolted from the room. His thinning hair was disheveled, and he was wholly dazed and bewildered. He did not know what awaited him.
***
Datner nearly stumbled over the nurses' desk before truly opening his eyes. He felt sour. Like a lemon squeezed into a margarita that had sat in the sun for far too long.
He knew what he had to do.
Too late.
Washing his face now would make the nurses look at him strangely. Combing his hair was out of the question; he had never owned a comb (he knew he did not have much to comb anyway). It was time for action.
Room 11.
The resuscitation in Room 11.
Susan had said it explicitly, that unhinged American from hell.
Too harsh. Just an unhinged American, then. Still tough, though. American, the harshest curse of all.
Resuscitation.
He pulled back the curtain of Room 11.
***
A large incubator. Transparent. Horribly generic.
The baby was unmistakably blue.
It had a name, but no one cared about that at this stage. At this stage, it wasn't even clear what the baby’s sex was. A few things were clear to Datner now. The monitor above the incubator showed a low oxygen saturation of 76%, and the baby looked distinctly blue.
The pulse and blood pressure were not being read by the monitor, and there were too many nurses around the small incubator. At least three nurses. At least one of them was Susan Schell. That couldn't be good.
Worst of all, the incubator had not yet been opened. That really annoyed him.
He pushed his way past the flustered nurses, opened the incubator, and shouted at Susan - "The Ambu, now." He began ventilating. 'Not too hard,' he recalled the advice of his old mentor, Prof. B.S., 'Gently, so you don’t burst the baby’s lungs.'
The lungs, surprisingly, did not resist at all. The air pushed by the Ambu flowed easily into the small body, which gradually turned pinker and pinker.
"What are the blood pressure and pulse?" Datner called out into the air, stifling a small smile at the saturation rising to 99%. Even better than 100, better symmetry. The sound the monitor emitted became much more tolerable. Almost melodic. Harmonic. The Beach Boys at their peak. God Only Knows.
"Still not reading," a voice from outer space replied.
That alien irritated Datner.
"Bring me a tube, size 2.5. And a laryngoscope with a small blade," he practically grumbled, disappointed by the slow flow of the event.
He did not fail to notice that Susan was working flawlessly. With all her faults, she was still quite experienced. She handed him the laryngoscope and the tube.
He put down the Ambu and inserted the laryngoscope.
'Straight up at a right angle. With the patient’s eyes facing the ceiling,' he recalled another piece of advice from Prof. B.S. Advice for all time. A Man for all seasons.
He wondered where B.S. was now.
Probably sitting at home watching TV and getting annoyed about his low salary. Who watches TV at this hour? Is the man a psychopath?!
Never mind. Moving on.
The vocal cords were clearly visible. A piece of cake. He inserted the tube quickly. Now, fixation.
This was the part he hated. He always felt the nurses would cause him to pull out the tube at that moment. Susan, however, didn't panic. "At 9.5 centimeters, Doctor?" she asked, almost affectionately.
"Yes," he mumbled, slightly surprised by her positive approach. He connected the Ambu to the tube and squeezed gently, compressing the small bellows only slightly, so as not to burst the lungs.
Meanwhile, the pulse returned. Approximately.
The monitor showed something that looked approximately like an ECG tracing in Lead 2. Not quite.
The stickers! They had fallen off the baby’s chest. Nurse Miri was attaching them now. Other than that, she was useless. She should learn from Susan.
Pulse 150. A small smile.
"And blood pressure?" Datner almost whispered.
"Wait, I'm changing the cuff, the previous one is too big," Susan answered. He almost began to like her. Not really, but still, a little, given the situation and the alternatives. Better unhinged and efficient than sane and harmful.
Another half a minute passed. Thirty seconds is a long time when you are waiting. He began to remember how tired he was. A big yawn. Overt. For everyone to see. The questionable scent of his breath forced him to stop the show. If you eat something after midnight, it’s best not to have it spicy or with a lot of garlic. Crucially, it's best not to have both ingredients, Datner noted. Failed note.
Meanwhile, the tube fixation was finished, and he turned to adjust the parameters on the ventilator. He never quite understood how to choose the numbers, the ventilation metrics. Strange names for pressures – ‘PIP’, ‘PEEP’, and all sorts of other 'peeps' ran through his head. He also had pressure in his bladder. A sudden need to urinate. Fortunately, he sorted that out relatively easily here. Almost a coincidence. Dumb luck.
"Blood pressure 60/30," Susan cried, almost shouted, in a tone of joy, into the space.
It won't get better than that, Datner decided.
He barely knew what to do with himself now that he was no longer holding the tube or calibrating the ventilator. Nurse Miri smiled. Like a calf that had been given excellent straw.
Nurse Susan was frowning. Despite her advanced age, something of the Southern American beauty in which she had once excelled remained. The Texas beauty queen forty years ago, no doubt. He didn't recall her being originally from New York.
"What about Dextro?" Datner barked.
"Immediately, Doctor," Susan replied submissively. She clearly had excellent training and manners that were out of this world. Foreign to the place.
He almost decided to go out to the stairwell and steal a few puffs of a cigarette.
Maybe it is better to update the on-call physician first.
But first, read the chart, he concluded.
He knew nothing about the infant who had just returned to life and certainly didn't know why this delicate creature had nearly collapsed completely. The on-call physician would not like a call about resuscitation without concrete information about the patient. He wasn't even sure if it was a male. He thought he saw testes during the ventilation, but he wasn't prepared to swear to it.
Still, a cigarette first. The on-call physician was certainly asleep now, and there was no reason to rush and call her before everything was known.
The watch showed 3:53. Still too symmetrical.
***
"What do you mean, the baby in Room 11 almost died?" the voice on the other end gasped. Datner wasn't sure if Dr. Katya Pavlichuk, the on-call neonatologist, was shouting or talking in her sleep. Maybe it was a combination of both? And what difference did it make anyway?
"He was perfectly fine this morning when I left him," the on-call physician continued, starting to wake up, grumbling about the uninvited wake-up call and the news it brought.
Datner glanced at his watch, 5:15, still symmetrical.
He thought that if he waited long enough, the on-call physician would appreciate the extra sleep time he had allowed her, and it would slightly dull the criticism of his ignorance regarding the chart.
He had tried earlier to read a little in the record, but everything was written in a particularly sloppy handwriting, worse even than his own, and most days there wasn't even a visit note. Only nurses’ comments alongside growth metrics and medication logs.
He gathered it was an infant (it was, after all, a male, those indeed were testes), a 29-week preemie who had been in the NICU for two weeks, receiving some TPN (total parenteral nutrition; nutrition through the vein. The 'T' standing for Total - meaning exclusive IV nutrition, although the baby had already started receiving some formula).
And that was it.
Most of the time, the baby had been idling and lying in the incubator between visits, however many of those were conducted.
This was exactly what the on-call physician, Dr. Katya Pavlichuk, was lecturing him about now.
Datner wasn't really listening. He knew the ways of senior neonatologists. She would dump everything at him, regardless. Better to keep quiet and scowl. Healthier for his coronaries.
After a few more seconds (about two hundred, in Datner's estimation, who had begun to develop a slight, involuntary twitch) of a lecture on the essence of life and the fact that the baby had been perfect that morning when she left, Dr. Katya finally got around to asking something. It sounded like a question. Datner wasn't really listening.
Hello, hello, Datner, are you there?!" Katya shrieked.
"Yes, certainly," Datner replied.
He was entertaining thoughts of early retirement. Considering his age (33, well-balanced), his professional status (a pediatric resident in his third out of four years), and his family status (unhappily married with two daughters who were probably very nice, he didn't really know them), these were premature, idle thoughts.
"How is the baby now? Is he ventilated? Does he need inotropes? Did you take cultures? Did you replace the central line? Did you start antibiotics?"
This was roughly what Dr. Katya rattled off. Datner wasn't really sure he cared.
"The baby is fine, easily ventilated, no inotropes, and no antibiotics," he replied, trying to avoid revealing the fact that he had failed to insert a central line and hadn't managed to take more than one blood culture. As for urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures, forget about it. Let the morning shift do that. They rested all night.
He didn't tell Dr. Katya all of that, of course. She hadn't asked specifically. A small, harmless white lie, in Datner's opinion. She said she would arrive in about two hours (funny, that was the usual time for the morning meeting anyway) and that until then, he should update her if there was anything new. Anything at all.
"Yes, of course," Datner answered in an authoritative tone, his thoughts were far less polite.
***
Dr. Katya Pavlichuk thought life was once more beautiful. When she was a child, still in Moscow, she dreamed of becoming a doctor. A pediatrician. She had always been the best student in school, the best student in medical school. Until she arrived in Israel. Straight to 'Sharona'.
When she arrived in the country, they told her 'Sharona' Hospital was in the Sharon region, as the name suggests. 'Two minutes from Tel Aviv,' they said. That was a crude lie; the drive was at least thirty minutes from Tel Aviv, and that was only if you drove at night, with zero traffic. No less. It wasn't really in the Sharon either; it was more in the Coastal Plain. She wasn't sure, and anyway, there was no one to complain to. But that’s where they assigned her, and she, being the good girl she was, did as she was instructed.
That was over twenty years ago already. Like another lifetime.
She tried to feel like she belonged from the start, but they didn't exactly make it easy.
For the first time in her life, she wasn't the popular success. She would hear them mocking her strange accent behind her back. Funny, in her eyes, the Israelis at 'Sharona' had the diction of Orientals. Mongolians. Descendants of Genghis Khan. Almost Mongoloid, she thought, a word she knew she shouldn’t be using. She remembered someone once told her that Dr. Down was a vicious, consummate racist. He was the one who gave the name 'Mongoloid' to babies with three sets of chromosomes 21 and slanted eyes. A smart fellow. A great racist, like all puffed-up Brits, but smart. He probably had crooked teeth. All smart Brits had crooked teeth. Even the not-so-smart ones. And they were all racists.
Only Dr. Renana treated her nicely, back then, when she first arrived at 'Sharona'. They became better friends. Renana was still sometimes happy then. Until that incident.
Now, as a veteran, Katya had learned to live in 'Sharona'. She no longer tried to excel. Excellence at 'Sharona' meant a death blow. A sign on your back. A mark of Cain.
She got out of bed and walked toward the bathroom. That Datner, she thought to herself. Couldn't he have waited another hour before telling her about a deteriorating baby?!
And why was the baby deteriorating anyway? He was perfectly fine this morning.
She would blame Datner for everything at the morning meeting. That was good for his character development.
The urine flowed relatively easily. In all cases. For Katya, Datner, and the temporarily stabilized preemie.
Relief.
Dr. Katya did not remember to check why the deteriorating baby was not given antibiotic treatment without reason, or what work-up was done to identify the possible infection. It was as if, in the heat of the events, she missed Datner's answer. Too bad; distraction was uncharacteristic of her.
***
Chapter 2  -  A Collection of Amateurs
"A collection of amateurs," I snapped. "Just a bunch of amateurs. Not a single one of them belongs in a professional organization."
The phone rang. It always rings in the bathroom, and always while I’m reading an article about the only soccer team I care about, FC ‘Sharona Sharks.’ A team with no luck; a fan with no luck.
I didn't know who was on the line. I’d replaced too many phones in recent years, and when one of the backups crashed, I just stopped trying to sync contacts. My call log was a graveyard of digits. Most names no longer appeared identified, just numbers, like Holocaust survivors. Those who merited a name, everyone deserves one, after all, were usually labeled as "Blocked," "Do Not Answer," "Do Not Answer 3," or the more recent "Blocked, Do Not Answer Forever. New."
It was Datner. A pleasant enough fellow. I'd known him since he was a young, enthusiastic student. He was a good man, back during his internship. Pediatric residency hadn't done him any favors. His fair hair had receded and turned a premature gray, and his zest for life had almost completely evaporated. He was no longer light-hearted. I’d even known him while he was mourning his mother, and even then, he was more optimistic than he was now.
"Datner, I'm not a consultant for the NICU. Take your madness elsewhere. I had intended to spend the day in glorious, uninterrupted indolence," I shot back before he could even draw breath. Better to set the record straight before the request to claim my soul arrived.
He didn't stop. He was always stubborn. He apologized at length, babbling something incoherent about having been on duty in the NICU three days ago. Now, there were two isolates in a baby’s blood culture. The infectious disease specialist had dismissed it as contamination, but Datner feared it was real. He was truly sorry, he said, but maybe I could take a look?
It sounded like typical nonsense. I told him so. He insisted I come. Even just for five minutes.
I insisted I felt like hell. That was true; I hadn't felt well since the late 1980s. It didn't help. He insisted. The boy was relentless. I told him to shut up and let me drink my coffee, and that I’d be there in fifteen minutes.
"Promise?" he asked. "A sailor's promise, diseased with syphilis," I replied.
He hung up. Slow to take a hint, that one. But a good guy.
***
A few minutes later, I was already nodding my head towards several familiar faces from the past. A gaggle of nurses who I had no idea were still alive. I didn't know any of their names, of course. Except for one, Susan Schell, who stood at the edge of the ward, near the kitchenette. "Is she still alive?" I wondered internally (or perhaps I shouted it, I'm not sure). She hadn't changed much at all. Maybe a wrinkle here, a white hair there, but still the beautiful Susan. An American from hell.
I adopted what I call my 'Dreamy Genius' expression, the one that says 'don't interrupt my profound thoughts' and strode briskly toward the place of the incubator in question, ignoring the astonished gazes of all the occupants. Datner was already standing there, beside the incubator containing a small body and many tubes.
"The little guy doesn't look good, friend," I opened with an immediate taunt.
"Aging fast," the impertinent student replied.
"You were somewhat economical with the truth regarding the patient’s status," I bristled.
"It happened recently, just this morning," Datner tried to defend himself.
A weak, apologetic response. Total surrender.
At this point, I grew tired of the intellectual chess game. More accurately, the easy victory prevented me from feeling any sense of satisfaction, so I decided to get to the point. This way, I would at least significantly cut down on my stay in the NICU, a unit I hadn't tolerated, along with its people, for over sixteen years. I glanced at the patient's chart and even managed to read a few lines before returning to torment Datner. It’s important to arrive prepared for battle; otherwise, there is a danger that the opponent might have a fair chance of success, heaven forbid.
I remember being a young student, not even a resident, when I heard people speaking respectfully about me behind my back. Rumors were circulated about the new genius on the ward, who knew everything during rounds, even before the attending physician. I will reveal the secret of the aforementioned magic to you, even though a proper magician never reveals his secrets. The whole secret lies in arriving half an hour before everyone else, opening all the charts of the new admissions from the night, and memorizing the admission details. Especially numbers of vital signs and selected lab indices. That's it. That’s the whole secret. A little memorization and spurting out the numbers before everyone finishes their coffee, and the title 'genius' is thrown your way without a problem. The art of illusion. The art of the lie.
"So, I see we have a small preemie, ventilated on inotropes, with a borderline pulse and unstable blood pressure, oxygenating with difficulty, and prone to ending his visit on planet Earth. And you say the little prince wasn't like this until your shift?" I fired quickly. That's always my method. Stun them before they regain their composure.
If the fight is fair, there's a good chance you'll lose. After all, I was in enemy territory.
Datner was about to open his mouth when Dr. Katya appeared behind him.
***
"Exactly, Prof. B.S., exactly. Simply appalling. Seventy-two hours ago, this was a completely healthy baby. And now? What a disaster," she almost sobbed. Since when did she get so worked up? I remembered her as a cold fish, not spicy fish stew.
"How are you, dear Dr. Katya?" I mustered my most empathetic tone. I remember not tolerating her 20 years ago, when she first arrived at 'Sharona'. She was already a senior, and I was just a young, clueless resident. This whole meeting felt strange and unwelcome to me.
She didn't answer. She considered making a stinging comment but knew I'd fire back immediately. She gave up. Instead, Datner launched into a speech about cultures. I wasn't listening. There was a medical chart next to the incubator, and I picked it up and saw the problem immediately. I silenced Datner with a finger, and immediately burst forth with the following sentence:
"Gram-positive cocci in chains and Gram-positive bacilli. In the same culture. From the same time. Strange. Definitely strange."
***
"What do you say, Datner? Can you explain to Dr. Pavlichuk and me the possibilities in the differential diagnosis?"
Datner puffed out his chest. It was clear he had prepared for this. He launched into a monologue so long it felt like movie exposition.
"Three big possibilities. All of them are quite strange. First, contamination. The two growths are meaningless. This doesn't explain the child's condition, but it eliminates the need to understand the strange culture result." I smiled; there was an echo of my own words from the past in his reply, it was clear the youth enjoyed quoting me. He continued:
"The second possibility is that only one bacterium is real, and the other is a contaminant. In that case, we need to analyze each possibility regarding each bacterium."
"And the third possibility?" I decided to intervene, even though it was completely unnecessary.
"Both bacteria represent real infections, which are not necessarily related, and may not even have been acquired in the same way, but both led to the child's deterioration." The defense rested.
"I feel almost superfluous here, Datner and Katya. It's clear you've considered all the options. I'm sure you've already discussed the possible identity of the bacteria," I said, injecting a hint of mild insult into my words.
"Of course," Katya shrieked.
That woman needs sedatives; I decreed to myself. I nearly had a heart attack because of her sudden franticness.
"And?" I pressed.
"Datner, tell him," Katya said, with a semblance of quasi-authoritativeness.
It was clear to me that she was afraid of making a mistake, and even more than that, trembling with fear at the possibility that I would correct her.
"The Streptococci are probably GBS," Datner began lecturing, "That's the most common cause of neonatal sepsis, even this late."
"And...?" I continued to press.
"It could also be Enterococcus, though you taught me that without risk factors, it almost never does anything," chirped the visibly unshaven student. This didn't bother me; I had made a point of not arriving clean-shaven at work for over twenty years. I always replied to supervisors' questions about my poor shaving capabilities with the same answer: "When I have time to sleep, I'll shave and maybe even shower." I liked Datner's answer, even though he didn't list every possibility in the world. I decided to let it go and not press the point right now. This was uncharacteristic of me.
"And the second bacterium, Datner?" I continued.
"The second is contamination or Listeria," he answered.
"Excellent," I smiled, "And what about that entire list of Gram-positive bacilli I taught you a million times? Won't you repeat it for me?" I purred sweetly.
"Sure. Listeria, Diphtheroids including Diphtheria, Actinomyces, Nocardia, Clostridium, and something else I forgot," Datner rattled off. I must have taught him that at least two hundred times. Or perhaps I'm exaggerating, and it was only six times.
"You forgot Bacillus, Anthrax, and Cereus," I fired back conspicuously...

@DeptNatSel @CroweFam_  DNS dynasty week 0 of the 2031 season is here!!! army black knights breakdown below see you all tomorrow for kickoff! 2pm eastern!

HANGAR SPORTS NETWORK
DNS DYNASTY — OPERATION BLACKOUT
2031 PRESEASON: THE STANDARD HAS CHANGED AT WEST POINT

WEST POINT, N.Y. — There was a time when the question surrounding Operation Blackout was whether Coach Hawk could turn Army into a legitimate national program.

That question is dead.

Army enters 2031 ranked No. 11 in the country, carrying a 92 overall rating, 91 offense and 94 defense, a top-five recruiting class, one of the best collections of returning star power anywhere in the DNS Dynasty, and the scars of a 2030 season that took the Black Knights within one victory of playing for a national championship.

This is no longer a rebuild.

This is a program trying to finish the job.

And the most fascinating part of the 2031 Army season may be that virtually everything around Operation Blackout has changed — except the expectations.

THE SEASON THAT CHANGED WHAT ARMY EXPECTS

Army's final 14–2 record doesn't properly explain what happened in 2030.

The Black Knights ripped through the regular season 12–0, including a 28–0 demolition of Navy, and reached the American Championship undefeated.

Then came USF.

Coach Matt Merkz and the Bulls delivered the single most violent interruption of Army's season, beating the Black Knights 63–28 in the American title game. Army went from dreaming about an undefeated championship run to having its entire legitimacy questioned in the span of one night.

Operation Blackout responded.

Army drew No. 11 LSU in the opening round of the College Football Playoff and fell behind 14–0. The Black Knights recovered, controlled the final three quarters and won 28–21.

That victory carried more weight than an ordinary playoff win because of Coach Hawk's history. Before West Point, Hawk's coaching career ran through Mississippi State. LSU was familiar territory. So was the contempt.

Then came No. 3 Ole Miss.

Another Mississippi rival. More old SEC blood. More history Hawk had carried with him from Starkville.

Army beat the Rebels 31–23, advancing to the national semifinal at 14–1.

Waiting there was the monster of the DNS universe: Coach Derek's Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets.

Tech entered unbeaten, chasing a third consecutive national championship. Army's run finally ended there, and Georgia Tech ultimately completed the three-peat — 2028, 2029 and 2030 national champions.

For Army, that semifinal defeat established the measuring stick for everything that follows.

The Black Knights aren't trying to become nationally relevant in 2031.

They're trying to catch Georgia Tech.

THE COST OF BECOMING ELITE

The NFL came for West Point in force.

Army's 2030 roster produced an extraordinary draft exodus. Sixteen Black Knights were selected, including seven first-round selections.

That first-round group included WR D. Shaver, TE Kyle Levine, RT J. Beckner, edge defender C. Love, DT N. Forsett, linebacker R. Agramonte and safety J. Morey.

And the losses continued deeper into the draft.

Quarterback Kayd Coffman, receivers, offensive linemen, defensive pieces and multiple veteran role players departed from a roster that had spent years accumulating experience together.

That matters.

Last year's Army could walk into enormous games with veterans everywhere. The 2031 team is different. It may actually be more talented at the top, but the structure underneath those stars has changed dramatically.

The transition begins at quarterback.

DONAVAN BERRYMAN GETS THE KEYS

For the first time in years, Army enters a season without Coffman controlling the offense.

The new QB1 is Donavan Berryman, a redshirt junior currently rated 75 overall.

And that number doesn't tell the whole story.

Berryman brings legitimate athleticism to the position: 87 speed, 85 acceleration, 84 agility and 90 change of direction. His arm strength is solid, and his movement ability gives Hawk an opportunity to alter the geometry of an offense that already possesses several nightmare skill players.

But this is still the biggest uncertainty on the roster.

Army can protect him.

Army can run the football.

Army can put one of college football's most explosive receivers outside.

What Army cannot manufacture is experience at quarterback.

Behind Berryman is true freshman I. Ha, rated 71 overall and possessing a huge arm, including 95 throw power. The talent is interesting. The present belongs to Berryman.

How quickly he settles into the job could determine whether Army spends December chasing another playoff berth or wondering what an experienced quarterback might have changed.

Fortunately, his supporting cast is absurd.

DOMINIQUE CARTER: THE FACE OF OPERATION BLACKOUT

There may not be a more dangerous returning player in the country than Dominique Carter.

The junior receiver enters 2031 at 95 overall with 98 speed, 97 acceleration, 99 agility and 99 catching.

Those numbers fit the reputation.

Carter finished second in the 2030 Heisman Trophy voting, earned First-Team All-American honors, and won the Paul Hornung Award as the nation's most versatile player.

He enters 2031 not merely as Army's WR1.

He is the face of the program.

The question now becomes whether Carter can convert a Heisman runner-up season into the trophy itself while breaking in a new quarterback.

Hawk doesn't need Berryman to become Coffman immediately.

He needs Berryman to understand one basic principle:

When No. 2 gets space, give him the football.

And Carter isn't alone.

R. Boireau returns as an 88-overall receiver, T. Flannery checks in at 86, and N. Jones gives Army another athletic option.

That means opposing defenses cannot simply bracket Carter and assume the problem disappears.

K.J. CRUISE HAS ONE MORE RUN

Then there's K.J. Cruise.

The veteran running back returns for another season after earning Second-Team All-American honors in 2030.

Cruise enters the year rated 88 overall, carrying 89 speed, 91 acceleration, 93 agility, 95 change of direction, 98 awareness and 99 ball-carrier vision.

At this stage, there isn't much mystery surrounding Cruise.

Everybody knows what's coming.

Defenses still have to stop it.

The more intriguing piece is how his presence can protect Berryman. Hawk does not need to throw a new quarterback into 40-pass-game chaos. Army has Cruise, a veteran offensive line and Marquez Lamm, an 88-overall senior fullback capable of keeping the traditional physical identity of the offense intact.

If Army stays ahead of the chains, Berryman can grow into the role instead of being asked to rescue the offense from third-and-long.

That could be the defining offensive formula of the first month:

Cruise controls the game. Carter breaks it open. Berryman manages the space between them.

THE OFFENSIVE LINE MAY BE ARMY'S SECRET WEAPON

For all the attention Carter and Cruise receive, Army's offensive front may be the reason the quarterback transition works.

The projected starting five is loaded:

PositionStarterOVR
LT Nolan Moe 90
LG Carlos Balducci 91
C Gideon Mebane 85
RG Terrell Yoder 88
RT Finau Truong 89

That's an average starting rating just under 89 overall.

For a team introducing a new quarterback, that is a luxury.

Balducci surged during offseason training. Moe gives Army an established blind-side presence. Truong anchors the other edge. Yoder provides veteran strength inside, and Mebane has developed into a strong center despite still having eligibility remaining.

Army lost significant offensive experience to the draft.

It did not lose the ability to block.
That distinction matters enormously.
A NEW TARGET EMERGES AT TIGHT END
Kyle Levine is gone after an All-American season and first-round selection.
His replacement represents one of the most interesting young players on the roster.
True freshman Jamari Cleeland has climbed directly to the top of the depth chart at 80 overall.
Cleeland brings 90 speed and 97 acceleration to the tight end position.
That isn't a developmental profile.
That's a weapon.
Veterans M. Lord and M. Vazquez provide depth, but Cleeland has the athletic traits to become the next major matchup problem in Hawk's offense.
Carter outside. Cruise in the backfield. Cleeland attacking linebackers and safeties.
Berryman may be inexperienced.
His playbook certainly isn't short on answers.
THE DEFENSE MAY BE BETTER
The offense carries the biggest question.
The defense carries expectations.
Army enters the season rated 94 defensively, the strongest of its three team ratings.
And the centerpiece is still there.
Greg Bland is back.
Bland enters his senior season at 91 overall after winning the Dick Butkus Award and earning First-Team All-American honors in 2030.
He is no longer just an excellent linebacker.
He has become one of the foundational players of the entire Operation Blackout era.

Bland returns with a secondary that may be every bit as important.

That was postseason production against LSU.

THE FRONT SEVEN

The veteran linebacker room gives Army unusual flexibility.

Alex Zukauskas enters at 87 overall on the strong side. Jose Quick is an 85-overall WILL. Bland controls the middle.

This is where the 94 defensive rating will be tested.

Army lost first-round-caliber production from the defensive line.

Replacing ratings is possible.

Replacing disruption is harder.

The secondary should give the front time.

Bland should erase mistakes behind it.

Craig Rodenhauser remains Army's primary kicker.

John Enunwa handles the punting role.

Dominique Carter remains first in line on both kick and punt returns.

One of the best athletes in college football does not leave the field when the offense does.
