RECRUITING: HAWK ISN'T BUILDING A MOMENT

Army followed its CFP run by signing the No. 5 recruiting class in the country.

Twenty-five commitments.

Four five-stars. Seventeen four-stars. Four three-stars.

That is probably the most important number in this entire preseason preview.

Because it means Operation Blackout has crossed the hardest line in dynasty building.

Winning with a veteran roster is one thing.

Replacing veterans with nationally elite recruiting classes is something else entirely.

Army just sent 16 players into the draft and somehow enters the next season rated 92 overall.

That's how programs stop having windows.

That's how they build eras.

Ohio State finished No. 1 in recruiting, followed by Oregon, Miami and Michigan.

Then Army.

USF finished seventh.

Georgia Tech ninth.

The Black Knights are no longer trying to recruit like an outsider crashing the national party.

They're recruiting like they expect to stay.

THE DNS POWER STRUCTURE

And staying at the top won't be easy.

The 2031 preseason rankings are loaded with programs carrying direct relevance to Operation Blackout:

No. 4 Georgia Tech — Coach Derek.
Three consecutive national championships. The standard everyone is chasing.

No. 5 USF — Coach Matt Merkz.
The team responsible for Army's most brutal defeat of 2030.

No. 8 Tennessee — Coach AugieGG.

No. 11 Army — Coach Hawk.

Four major user programs sit inside the opening top eleven.

That is what the DNS Dynasty has become.

Georgia Tech is the empire.

USF proved it can punch Army directly in the mouth.

Tennessee has a new user-led era beginning with national expectations.

And Army begins the year close enough to see all of them.

The preseason top is led by No. 1 Oregon, followed by USC and Oklahoma before Georgia Tech and USF.

For Hawk, No. 11 is a useful position.

High enough to control the path.

Low enough to keep the chip.

THE 2031 ROAD

The strangest feature of Army's schedule isn't an opponent.

It's the calendar.

The Black Knights have four byes before October 11.

Then none.

Army plays Boise State, rests, plays Colorado, rests twice, plays Florida Atlantic, rests again — and then begins a nine-game run to the finish.

The first half gives Hawk enormous practice time to develop Berryman, rebuild the defensive front and work younger players into the rotation.

The second half offers virtually no mercy.

Army will play nine consecutive weeks from Rice through Navy.

And the final two games could determine everything.

NOVEMBER 29: ARMY AT USF

Circle it now.

Army travels to face No. 5 USF in Tampa on November 29.

There will be no need to manufacture a storyline.

63–28 already did that.

Coach Matt Merkz's Bulls didn't simply beat Army in last year's American Championship.

They ripped apart an undefeated team that entered championship weekend believing it might be the best Army squad of the Operation Blackout era.
Hawk remembers.

The players who returned remember.

It could also become something more important for the long-term DNS record:
the beginning of an actual Army–USF heavyweight rivalry.

Not manufactured hatred.

Not promotional material.

Results.

AND THEN NAVY

Navy.

At Michie Stadium.

December 6.

No bye.

No chance to emotionally reset.

One week Army could be playing for the American title picture and CFP positioning.

The next, none of it matters.

It's Army–Navy.

That is a spectacularly difficult way to close a season.

And it is exactly the kind of stretch championship teams eventually have to survive.

WHAT 2031 IS REALLY ABOUT

Army doesn't need 2031 to validate Operation Blackout.
That happened already.
The program has produced national award winners.
It has produced All-Americans.
It has produced first-round draft picks.
It has signed a top-five recruiting class.

The floor for this team should be extremely high.

The ceiling remains Atlanta.

There is no Cinderella story left at West Point.

text:
Trolls will never understand a self-sacrificing leader... Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that.
With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.
Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.
So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.
This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.
You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty
1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.
2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.
3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.
4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.
10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.
11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.
13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?
15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”
16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.
22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.
23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.
24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.
Now, Act Like It Matters
Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.
Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.
And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that “news” happens to be.
Today’s conservatives have more ability to find whatever you want to know than any group of people in human history, yet half of them couldn’t name any of the accomplishments in this essay, and if they were to read it, they would just complain that something else they wanted hasn’t happened fast enough to suit them.
This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.
So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not Heaven on Earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.
Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.
Because it does.

NBC, TRUMP'S RUSSIAN DIESEL, CONGRESS'S IMPORT BAN, THE CEASEFIRE AND THE SAME STANDARD FOR EVERYONE

Evidence cutoff: October 13, 2026.

Manhattva: https://t.co/Zeer7GNHL7
NBC: https://t.co/vR0UwHensP
NBC report: https://t.co/YPJ4TfPXio

THE SECOND CLAIM BEHIND THE SCREENSHOT: Why criticize the United States for buying a relatively small amount of Russian diesel while Europeans continue buying Russian energy? That is a legitimate consistency challenge to investigate. The ANSWER is not that European purchases are automatically acceptable. They have been repeatedly criticized, tracked and progressively restricted, including by European officials themselves. But Trump's NEW authorization must still satisfy U.S. statutes, its stated economic purpose and its actual diplomatic consequences. One country's inconsistency is not a legal waiver for another. (I–III)
WHAT NBC ACTUALLY POSTED. NBC's visible October 12 X text describes Ukrainian bewilderment at Trump's diesel announcement and concern about American support. It says the agreement reverses years of U.S. sanctions policy. That description is consistent with Reuters/AP reporting about the policy reversal, but it must NOT be expanded into a claim that Trump lifted EVERY Russia sanction. The underlying NBC web article was blocked from direct automated reading during this audit, so the accessible NBC X caption and corroborating original records are the verified bases here; do not invent quotes from the full article. (I–II)
WHAT TRUMP ANNOUNCED. On October 9, after speaking with Putin, Trump announced Russian supply of over 300,000 tons of diesel to the American AND GLOBAL marketplace, then 500,000 in November, 1 million thereafter, and a further 3 million in a later phase. Added as prospects these are over 4.8 million tons, not a verified 4.8-million-ton U.S. purchase order or fuel already unloaded at American docks. The initial quantities were accompanied by an explicit consumer-price rationale for farmers, truckers and households. On October 12 Trump defended his decision by asserting that the EU had paid Russia $250 billion for energy. He gave no clear period for his dollar figure, and dollar figures cannot be compared unconverted with euro support amounts. (III–IV)

THE SANCTIONS DOCUMENT, NOT THE COMMENT SECTION. On OCTOBER 9 the U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued GENERAL LICENSE 135. It authorizes otherwise prohibited transactions under two named OFAC regulatory regimes involving the sale, delivery, offloading or importation, INCLUDING into the United States, of Russian-origin diesel THROUGH APRIL 7, 2027. It excludes certain debits from U.S.-bank accounts of Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund and Ministry of Finance. Importantly, the actual one-page license does not contain a blanket condition limiting imports to diesel already loaded on October 9; reporting that says it does must be reconciled to the controlling document. (V)

HERE IS WHY THE EU COMPARISON DOESN'T SETTLE LEGALITY. Congress passed the ENDING IMPORTATION OF RUSSIAN OIL ACT in 2022. Section 2 bans imports of Russian-origin products in Harmonized Tariff Schedule CHAPTER 27, which includes petroleum fuels. Section 3 specifies a special process for terminating that ban: advance committee consultation, written certification about Russian withdrawal, reduced NATO threat and Ukrainian political independence, followed by 90 days for congressional review. A license under OFAC sanctions regulations does not on its face REPEAL an independent statute. Any other claimed authority or valid exception must be shown. Whether a future shipment is legally permissible remains a legal question; the public record does not establish a final judicial ruling invalidating the deal or prove completed prohibited imports. (V–VI)

THE OBJECTION IS BIPARTISAN, NOT SIMPLY AN NBC EDITORIAL POSITION. On October 11, Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Susan Collins, Richard Blumenthal, Lisa Murkowski, Ron Wyden, Thom Tillis and John Curtis issued a joint statement alleging the administration had not satisfied the statutory congressional process. Four are Republicans and three are Democrats. Their objection is a documented interpretation and demand for reversal, not a court judgment. Answer it with statutory documents and transaction records, not an accusation that critics ignore European gas invoices. (VII)

THE ENERGY-PRICE CLAIM NEEDS A COUNTERFACTUAL. American diesel was about $6.28 per gallon around the announcement, according to the contemporaneous AP/AAA account, following broader global supply disruption and the 2026 Iran-related crisis. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries have also constrained Russian output. Those are relevant mechanisms, not a proven proportional attribution of the entire price rise to either war. Economists interviewed by AP and other outlets doubt the announced early volumes would materially change U.S. pump prices because shifting scarce Russian diesel to American buyers can divert existing customers rather than produce equivalent NEW global supply. A short futures-market drop is not proof of lasting consumer savings. Track delivered barrels, incremental global production, wholesale and retail differentials, refinery constraints and transport costs. (III, VIII)

THE NUMERICAL TRAP: Russia's promised 300,000 tons is not automatically 300,000 tons SOLD TO THE U.S.; the additional scheduled amounts are announcements, not completed cargoes. Neither Trump nor Manhattva has supplied the contract, identity of U.S. buyers, Russian seller, exact purchase price, vessels, banks, sanctions pathway, taxes reaching Moscow or reconciliation with Chapter 27. Even a relatively small cargo can create strategic or legal precedent; conversely, an analyst must not inflate a tiny preliminary delivery into billions of verified government payments. (III, V–VI)

A SECOND STATED OBJECTIVE: DIPLOMACY. Reuters reported October 12, citing people familiar with conversations, that U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner described the diesel relief as a possible incentive to bring Putin back to peace talks. This is sourced reporting about what the envoys reportedly told Ukrainian representatives, not a signed reciprocal bargain proving Moscow stopped its offensive. The administration's argument should be tested against concrete concessions, not just the existence of a telephone call. (IX)

THE CEASEFIRE TEST WAS ALREADY PROBLEMATIC ON OCTOBER 12. Trump said a Russia–Ukraine “energy ceasefire” existed, but Kyiv reported Russian attacks on power and gas infrastructure afterward; Zelenskyy said Ukraine would reciprocate a real halt. Kremlin statements did not provide an independently confirmed, monitored general ceasefire. A promise to stop attacks on energy facilities is narrower than stopping military offensives, occupation or attacks against civilians. Calling the diesel deal a “peace trade” requires verified ceasefire terms and compliance. (X)

WHAT IS AND IS NOT HYPOCRISY? Europe continuing Russian LNG imports can undermine its declared goal of restricting Russian energy revenue. That is a real and measurable tension. The United States previously banning Russian-origin energy and then selectively authorizing NEW diesel trade raises a different—and potentially sharper—domestic-law question. The EU is moving through documented phased contracts and bans; that does not absolve its slow transition. The U.S. is acting under an OFAC license while a separate congressional prohibition remains central to the dispute; that is not answered by pointing to Hungary's gas pipeline. Apply one evidentiary standard but DO NOT PRETEND EVERY LEGAL REGIME IS IDENTICAL. (V–VII, XI)

FOLLOW THE MONEY, FIVE LEVELS DEEP:

DIRECT: a delivered cargo leads to payments, fuel supply, transportation and potential domestic price effects; a Kyiv grant or weapons shipment meets a different need.

FISCAL: export firms and Russian tax authorities may capture revenue; NATO allies bear sanctions, welfare and energy-security costs; aid disbursements shape Ukraine's survival.

MILITARY: weaker Russian export revenue can constrain budgets over time, while Russian refinery disruptions, fuel scarcity and Ukrainian energy outages alter military logistics and civilian welfare.
STRATEGIC: sanctions exceptions alter expectations of other buyers, shippers, insurers and governments, while a deal offered without enforceable concessions may weaken negotiating leverage. Conversely, a tightly monitored deal that achieves a real ceasefire or sizeable supply benefit would have to be evaluated on that documented result.
INSTITUTIONAL: how Washington and Brussels comply with their OWN laws, scrutinize corporate beneficiaries and disclose real costs influences whether future embargoes and security commitments are credible. These are potential causal pathways, not already quantified effects of these particular promised cargoes.
PUBLIC QUESTIONS THAT COULD SETTLE THIS ARGUMENT: (1) Which time window and geographic perimeter produced Manhattva's Europe figure? (2) Which aide metric—disbursed, allocated, committed, grants plus loans, refugees—was used? (3) Which named EU firms bought Russian energy in 2026, under what contract and exemption? (4) Where is the U.S. diesel contract, and who is paying whom? (5) What legal authority satisfies the 2022 import ban? (6) What barrels actually entered the market and what measured price impact followed? (7) What commitments did Putin make in exchange? (8) What independently verified ceasefire or withdrawal occurred? (9) What Russian tax revenue resulted? (10) Which officials or firms bear responsibility for failed predictions or unlawful conduct?
FINAL ACCOUNTABILITY STANDARD: The Europe-energy comparison has factual support under specific definitions and exposes shortcomings in European sanctions. Treating that fact as permission to disregard the legal and strategic questions around Trump's U.S. diesel deal is an unsupported leap. NBC's visible account of Ukrainian uncertainty is compatible with those questions; its claims should still be confined to what the records establish. We need the EUROPEAN invoices, UKRAINIAN aid ledger, U.S. LEGAL TEXT and actual RUSSIAN shipment trail—not a contest over which side's hypocrisy is louder.
END — CORRECTED FACT-CHECK–FULL-SITUATION-REPORT–ASSIST, source cutoff Oct. 13, 2026.

text:
"Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
Hola, soy palestino. 🇵🇸
Y como la honestidad es poco común en mi política, permítanme confesar algunas cosas.

1947. La ONU me ofreció un estado. Junto a Israel. Fronteras, independencia, reconocimiento. Dije que no. Mis líderes prometieron que la guerra "arrojaría a los judíos al mar". En cambio, lo perdí todo y lo llamaron catástrofe. No porque no me ofrecieran un estado, sino porque lo rechacé.

1948–2025. Los estados árabes podrían haberme integrado, dado derechos, pasaportes, dignidad. En cambio, me encerraron en campos de refugiados durante generaciones, para que siguiera siendo un arma contra Israel. Construyeron palacios para ellos y cárceles para mí. Me usaron como propaganda, no como personas.

1967. Tras otra guerra perdida, podría haber construido un estado en Cisjordania y Gaza. En cambio, insistí en "ni paz, ni reconocimiento, ni negociaciones". Tres noes.  Cincuenta años después, sigo sin Estado. Resulta que el rechazo no paga el alquiler.

Oslo, década de 1990. Israel dijo: «Intentémoslo». Me dio autonomía. Armas para la policía. Miles de millones en ayuda. ¿Qué hicieron mis líderes? Robaron el dinero, armaron milicias y lanzaron una intifada. Atentados suicidas en lugar de escuelas. Cohetes en lugar de fábricas.

Gaza, 2005. Israel se fue por completo. Sin colonos, sin soldados. Tuve la oportunidad de convertir Gaza en un Singapur mediterráneo. Voté por Hamás. La convirtieron en Mogadiscio junto al mar. ¿Miles de millones en ayuda? Túneles, cohetes y palacios para sus líderes, mientras mi gente come comida enlatada en la oscuridad.

¿Democracia? No he tenido elecciones en casi 20 años. Hamás mata a los disidentes en Gaza. Fatah los encarcela en Cisjordania.  Mis líderes cancelan elecciones porque están demasiado ocupados luchando por el poder.

Religión. En lugar de construir un futuro, pongo a clérigos en televisión enseñando a los niños a odiar a los judíos. Glorifico a los "mártires" que hacen estallar autobuses. Crío a mis hijos con canciones de sangre y fuego en lugar de libros y ciencia. Cambio la esperanza por la guerra santa.

Mundo árabe. Los regímenes árabes me llaman "hermano". Pero pregúntenles cuántos palestinos pueden vivir libremente en Líbano, Siria, Egipto o Kuwait. Me excluyen, pero celebran mi muerte, porque mi muerte es su excusa.

Absurdo. Sigo diciendo que quiero "construir un estado". E irónicamente, justo al lado está Israel: el vecino que construyó una democracia próspera, una potencia tecnológica, granjas en el desierto, ciudades de polvo. Sin petróleo, sin riqueza infinita, solo coraje. Podría haber aprendido, copiado, colaborado. En cambio, elegí la envidia y la rabia.

Obsesión antijudía. Podría haber aceptado a los judíos como vecinos.  Podría haber dicho: "Dos naciones, dos estados". En cambio, repito: "Del río al mar". En lugar de exhibir el honor, la hospitalidad y la rica cultura árabe, mostré solo la cultura de la espada: la ira, el extremismo y la sangre. En lugar de gritar salaam (paz) a los israelíes, grité muerte a los judíos. Y luego finjo sorprenderme cuando los israelíes no confían en mí, cuando están enojados, decepcionados y convencidos de que no quiero coexistencia en absoluto.

Responsabilidad. Culpo a Israel de todo. Siempre. ¿Mis líderes roban miles de millones? Culpa de Israel. ¿Hamás dispara cohetes desde hospitales? Culpa de Israel. ¿Glorifico la muerte más que la vida? Culpa de Israel. La responsabilidad no es mi fuerte.

Soy palestino.
Podría haber construido una nación, muchas veces. Elegí el rechazo, la corrupción y la guerra sin fin. Podría haber vivido en paz con Israel, pero elegí vivir a la sombra de su destrucción.

Así que sí, soy una víctima.  Pero con demasiada frecuencia, soy víctima de mis propios líderes, de mis propias decisiones y de mi propia negativa a abandonar el odio.

Y esa, querido lector, es la tragedia que nadie quiere admitir.

I’ve written an essay for @techpolicypress on the SIR and the faith in digitisation that has shaped Indian elections. I wanted to understand how decisions about who can vote came to depend on software whose workings are closed to public scrutiny.

For the research, over some weekends in the IIC library, I read books by former Chief Election Commissioners. I enjoyed them, particularly the accounts of the logistical work involved in conducting elections at this scale. Technology, though, is almost always presented as a success. For instance, former CEC S.Y. Quraishi recalls facial recognition software in Manipur detecting a woman who had come to vote more than 60 times in different guises. H.S. Brahma began linking voter IDs with Aadhaar on the promise that almost every complaint about the rolls would be resolved. These accounts say much more about what technology promises than about its limits.That faith extends well beyond the Commission as across Indian public policy, digitisation is routinely offered as the answer to failures of administration (in panels called, "state capacity constraints"). 

However, when the rules, or more properly the updates in the software builds in a system are kept secret, or changed to vary from the officially notified forms, however, discretion becomes harder to examine. People affected by an arbitrary decision have fewer means of understanding or challenging it. I also went back to an earlier attempt to make voters prove their entitlement to remain on the rolls. In 1992, the Commission under T.N. Seshan instructed its officers that the burden of proving citizenship lay on the voter. An officer in Delhi then declared an entire slum colony of 18,000 residents suspected foreigners. More than 16,000 lost their vote. In Lal Babu Hussein in 1995, the Supreme Court held that an existing entry on the roll carried a presumption that the registering officer had followed the law. The intensive revision of 2002–04 proceeded on that basis. Enumerators did the verification, and existing voters were presumed to belong on the rolls.

The SIR reverses that presumption through a process dependent on software. Today, more than 130 million names have come off draft rolls. The software treated “Md” and “Mohammed” as different people, flagged siblings born less than nine months apart, including twins, and found seven siblings sharing a father suspicious. Its rules, error rates and audit results have not been published. Voters are left to correct these errors, often by standing in queues and responding to notices in languages they cannot read. Nandan Nilekani, whose book advocated a centralised voter database and digitisation, has himself received an SIR notice. Finally, I would like to thank Tech Policy Press and its patient editorial team for being kind and gentle with me. Please read the essay and let me know what you think of it.

text:
Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸 And since honesty is rare in my politics, allow me to confess a few things.
The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that the war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything, and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.
1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me up in refugee camps for generations, so that I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.
After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I'm still stateless. Turns out rejection doesn't pay the rent.
Oslo, 1990s. Israel said, "Let's give it a try." It gave me autonomy. Guns for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.
Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.
Democracy? I haven't had elections in almost 20 years. Hamas kills dissidents in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.
Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children on songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but they celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurd. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a technological powerhouse, desert farms, dusty cities. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.
Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said, "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of showcasing honor, hospitality, and the rich Arab culture, I displayed only the culture of the sword.Anger, extremism, and bloodshed. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to the Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I feign surprise when the Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced that I don't want coexistence at all.
Accountability. I blame Israel for everything. Always. Do my leaders steal billions? Blame Israel. Does Hamas fire rockets from hospitals? Blame Israel. Do I glorify death more than life? Blame Israel. Accountability is not my strong suit.
I am Palestinian. I could have built a nation, many times over. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction. So yes, I am a victim. But all too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hatred. And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.

text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

THE JESTER VI

Violanté climbed upon a chair and announced that he had a toast of his own.

"To the road!" he cried. "May it be straight, may it be broad, and may every man who has laboured upon it be able to walk home upon his own two feet, since the treasury has not provided him with a horse!"

The laughter shook the hall.

Herod wiped his eyes.

"Another!" he demaunded.

Violanté bowed, delyghted.

He did not know the names of the men outside, nor did he care to learn them. He had never considered what it meant to wait for wauges with an empty purse, to retourn to a household without bread, or to explain to a childe that the man who governed the cité had spent the money intended for one's supper.

He knew onlie that the joke had pleaused his patron.

And because his patron had been pleaused, the joke was counted a success.

As the seasons passed, the jester became inseparable from Herod's publick image.

Painters depicted him standing near the Hegemon's chair, a grin upon his face and one hond raised in mock salute. Poets included him in verses concernyng the grandeur of the Malvezzi court. Foreign envoys wrote home describing the extraordinary freedom enjoyed by the Hegemon's fool, who could mock the greatest lords without fear of punishment.

These reports were received abroad as evidence of Herod's liberalité.

In Bològne, they were understood differentlie by those who had cause to endure the jester's privileges.

servaunts learned to avoid him whenever possible. Women chaunged their routes through the palays, or arranged to be accompanied when they must pass through chambers where he was likelie to be found. Pages took care not to laugh at his jokes unless the Hegemon was present, for Violanté regarded an unwilling audience as an insult requiring correctioun. Men who had incurred his displeausure discovered that a careless remark myght be repeated before Herod in an altered form, and that the altered form would be remembered more readilie than the original.

The jester began to understand that his positioun myght be used for purposes beyond entertainment.

He could obtain small favours for his companiouns, secure places at table, influence the choice of performers, and recommend a man for employment. He could also make trouble for those he disliked. A servaunt whose complaint irritated him myght be described as insolent; a clerk who refused to lend him money myght be presented as disloyal; a woman who rejected his attentiouns myght be accused of having attempted to seduce him.

Such accusatiouns were rarelie serious enough to require a formal inquiry.

They were serious enough to cause inconvenience.

Violanté enjoyed these discoveries.

He had always believed that a man should make use of whatever advauntages fortune provided, and he had no difficulty extending this principle to the privileges of his new office. If a servaunt carried his belongings, he regarded the serwyse as proper. If a woman avoided him, he considered the avoidaunce evidence of his desirabilité. If a clerk feared offending him, he took the fear for respect.

And if Herod laughed, Violanté considered the matter settled.

The Hegemon himself began to relie upon the fool's presence as a kind of assuraunce. Whenever a conversatioun became too grave, whenever a report revealed an inconvenience he did not wysh to consider, or whenever the complaints of others threatened to impose an unwelcome seriousnesse upon the court, Violanté could be summoned to dissolve the difficulty in laughter.

The jester did not resolve disputes.

He made the disputaunts appear ridiculous.

This was often more agreeable to Herod than resolutioun.

A treasury account myght show a deficit; Violanté would imitate the treasurer and make the deficit a subject of amusement. A merchaunt myght complain of a confiscated warehouse; Violanté would suggest that the merchaunt had been unfortunate to possess a warehouse where the Hegemon required a road. A widow myght petitioun for compensatioun; Violanté would describe her as a woman whose principal talent consisted of surviving long enough to make others feel guilty.

Herod would laugh.

The court would laugh.

The petitioun would remain unanswered.

There were moments when the laughter did not come easilie. Certain courtiers, older men who had known the Citie before the ascendancie of Herod, found the spectacle increasinglie distasteful. They had not become virtuous merelie through the passauge of years, and many had profited from the same arrangements which now injured others. Yet they retained enough memory to recognize that the publick affairs of Bològne were being converted into the private entertainment of its ruler.

Some attempted to withdraw from the court. Others found themselves too deeplie involved in contracts, debts, and offices to depart without sacrificing their fortunes. A few tried to warn Herod that the jester's behaviour was damaging the dignité of the Hegemon.

Herod listened, then asked whether they had ever observed how easilie a companie could be governed when it was in good humour.

They replied that good humour was one thing, and the contempt of law another.

Herod smiled.

"Must a law be solemn to be obeyed?"

The questioun was not answered.

Violanté, who had been listenyng from a nearby chair, raised his woden swerd.

"My lord, I propose that we replace all the laws of Bològne with a single ordinaunce: whoever laughs at the Hegemon shall be rewarded, and whoever fails to laugh shall be punished."

Herod clapped his honds.

"An excellent proposal!"

The courtiers laughed.

Violanté continued.

"To ensure fairnesse, every man shall be permitted one laugh upon entering the cité, a second upon entering the market, and a third upon entering the palays. Those who have used their allowaunce elsewhere must purchase an additiounal laugh from the treasury."

Herod was nearlie overcome.

"How much shall it cost?"

"That depends upon the man, my lord. A merchaunt shall pay according to his purse, a magistrate according to his dignité, and a labourer according to the number of stones he has carried that day."

The hall roared.

Herod leaned back, wiping his eyes.

"See that this is entered into the ordinaunces."

The secretary, who had been taking notes upon the Hegemon's instructiouns, stared at his page.

He was uncertain whether the command had been issued in jest.

Herod looked at him.

"Did you hear me?"

The secretary bowed.

"Yes, my lord."

"Then enter it."

The secretary wrote the words into his notebook.

They did not become law.

Yet the incident was remembered by those who had witnesseed it, for it revealed the peculiar conditioun of the court. A joke had been issued as a command; a command had been recorded as though it myght become a law; and no one present could confidentlie determine where the one had ended and the other begun.

The jester laughed.

The Hegemon laughed.

And the secretary, having completed his note, placed it among the papers awaiting review by the office of the One Way.

There came a day when Herod requested that Desiderata accompanie him upon an inspectioun of the new avenue.

The weather was fair, the principal sectioun of the road had been cleared of scaffolds, and a processioun of officiauls had been arranged to receive the Hegemon at intervals along the route. The architects were present with their drawings, the contractors with their accounts, the magistrates with their formal expressiouns of approval, and the captaines with sufficient armed men to ensure that no obstructioun should occur.

Desiderata had been instructed to wear a gown of crimson and a mantle edged with gold.

She did not ask why.

The processioun began at the western entraunce, where the new arch had been completed to a height sufficient to dominate the surrounding buildings. Its pale stone gleamed in the mornyng sun. The sculpted figures upon its face stood in their appointed poses, and the frieze depicting the victories of Bològne under Herod's protectioun had been polished until the outlines appeared almost luminous.

The Hegemon halted beneath the arch and looked upwards.

"This," he declared, "is but the beginnyng."

The architects bowed.

"The Citie shall be made beautiful from end to end," he continued. "No traveller shall enter Bològne without understanding that he has arrived at a place governed by reason, order, and noble ambitioun."

Desiderata looked along the avenue.

The road was indeed broad. Its paving stones had been laid with considerable skill, and the covered arcades offered shelter from rain and sun. In the distaunce, however, she could see the unfinished stretches, the temporary barriers, the exposed foundatiouns, and the irregular remains of houses whose walls had been removed.

Beyond the avenue, life continued in the old streets, cramped and crooked, where carts still struggled to tourn at narrow corners, merchaunts displayed their goods beneath the porches, and women carried baskets from the markets to their homes. The One Way did not abolish the cité's needs. It merelie imposed a new and expensive arrangement upon them.

Herod tourned to the architects.

"How long before the eastern sectioun is completed?"

They explained that the work would require another season, perhaps longer, depending upon the conditioun of the foundatiouns and the availabilité of materials.

"Another season?"

"My lord, the constructioun is proceeding according to the revised schedule."

"Then the schedule must be revised again."

The chief architect opened his mouth, then closed it.

Herod looked towards the treasurer.

"And the cost?"

The treasurer gave the latest sum.

It was considerablie greater than the amount originallie approved.

Desiderata watched her husband's expressioun.

He did not appear troubled. He appeared offended, as though the figures had insulted him by failing to conform to his wyshes.

"Why does the cost increase every time I ask the questioun?"

The treasurer replied that certain conditiouns could not have been anticipated at the outset.

"Then anticipate them now."

The treasurer bowed.

Herod tourned away.

They proceeded along the avenue, passing a series of newlie constructed façades intended to present a uniform appearaunce to the road. Behind these façades, in several places, stood older buildings whose inner chambers had not been altered. The owners had been required to modify their street-facing walls in accordaunce with the design, and some had received loans to meet the expense. Others had been compelled to sell their properties when the cost of conformité exceeded their means.

Herod pointed towards one of the façades.

"Observe the harmony."

The architect explained that the proportiouns had been determined according to a mathematical scheme intended to produce a pleausing relatioun between the windows, arches, and upper galleries.

Herod nodded.

"Such harmony should extend throughout the Citie."

Desiderata tourned towards him.

"Must every house be made to resemble every other?"

Herod regarded her as though she had asked whether every soldier should carry a different weapon.

"Why should a house be irregular merelie because its owner was born before the new design?"

"Because the house was built to serve the people who live within it."

"The people who live within it shall have better houses."

"If they can afford them."

Herod's eyes narrowed.

"My lady, you have taken a peculiar ynterest in the affairs of builders."

"They are the affairs of the Citie."

"Preciselie. And the Citie is being improved."

Desiderata looked towards the old streets beyond the avenue.

"Improved for whom?"

The questioun was quiet enough that onlie Herod and the nearest attendants heard it.

He did not answer.

For a moment he seemed to contemplate the possibilité that his wyfe had chosen this occasioun to challenge him in publick. Then he remembered that the processioun was proceeding according to plan, that the architects stood nearby awaiting his judgement, and that a display of displeausure myght disturb the very harmony he had come to admire.

He smiled.

"For those who possess the foresight to understand what is being built."

They continued.

At the eastern sectioun, the party encountered a small group of men who had assembled near a barrier. They carried tools and wore the garments of labourers, though their clothing was dirty and their faces bore the tired expressiouns of men who had been waiting for something that should already have been delivered.

One stepped forward.

"My lord, we ask leave to speak."

The captain of the guard moved to intercept him.

Herod raised a hond.

"Let him speak."

The man bowed.

"We have laboured upon the eastern foundatiouns. Our wauges have been withheld for many weeks. We have been told repeatedlie that pyment shall be made, but the clerks retourn us to the same office and the office retourns us to the contractors. We ask onlie that the sum owed be settled."

Herod listened.

The labourer's words were simple, but they carried the weight of an inconvenience which could not readilie be transformed into a joke. The man did not accuse the Hegemon of tyranny, nor did he questioun the magnificence of the avenue. He asked to be payd for work already performed.

Herod looked at the overseer.

"Is this true?"

The overseer began an explanatioun concernyng delays in the accounts, disputed measurements, and the conditioun of the foundatiouns.

Herod interrupted him.

"Have these men been payd?"

"Not yet, my lord."

"Why not?"

"The disbursement has been delayed."

Herod's expressioun hardened.

"Then see that it is made."

The labourer bowed his head.

"Thank you, my lord."

Herod felt the familiar satisfactioun of having resolved a matter by the exercise of authorité. He imagined that the companie would remember his interventioun as an act of liberalité, and that the labourers would carry the report of his generosité to their households.

He did not ask when the pyment myght be made.

He did not ask whether the treasury possessed the necessary funds.

He did not ask how many times the men had already received similar assuraunces.

The processioun continued.

By the following week, the pyment remained outstanding.

The overseer had been instructed to prepare the necessary documents, but the contractor had not yet submitted the revised account. The contractor declared that the measurements required verificatioun. The surveyor was occupied upon another sectioun of the avenue. The clerk who had been assigned to the matter was absent through illnesse.

The labourers were told to retourn after the next market day.

Herod never heard of the delay.

Or, if he heard of it, he did not consider it sufficientlie importaunt to remember.

The great dream of the One Way had begun to alter the Hegemon's understanding of the cité itself.

He no longer regarded Bològne as a collectioun of households, trades, parishes, guilds, towers, markets, and streets, each possessing a history which myght complicate the work of government. He regarded it as a design awaiting completioun.

The people were inhaibitaunts of the design.

Their houses were obstacles or ornaments.

Their labour was a resource.

Their complaints were irregularities.

Their memories were attachments to the past, and their expectatiouns were habits which myght be corrected by proper instructioun.

The One Way was, in this sense, more than a road. It was an attempt to prove that the whole of existence myght be arranged according to the preference of one man, provided that man possessed sufficient money, sufficient authorité, and sufficient indifference to those who must bear the expense.

Herod did not understand the project in these terms.

He believed he was bringing order into the world.

He had, since childehood, detested the feeling that events myght proceed without his consent. The old cité, with its twysted lanes and independent households, reminded him that the world had been made by people who had never imagined his arrival. Every crooked street was a declaratioun that some earlier desyre had been permitted to shape the future without his approval.

The One Way corrected this insult.

It placed his intentioun upon the very ground through which generatiouns had travelled. It forced the stones to conform to his design, the houses to submit to his proportiouns, and the people to alter their lives in accordaunce with a plan conceived within the palays.

If a house obstructed the route, it was removed.

If a market interfered with the view, it was relocated.

If a guild complained, its charter was examined.

If the treasury lacked money, new revenues were discovered.

If the revenues proved insufficient, loans were obtained.

If the loans could not be repayd, the future prosperité of the Citie was invoked.

The project could never fail, for its failure would require Herod to acknowledge that his judgement had been mistaken, and his judgement was the one thing he had ceased to regard as capable of errour.

His ministers understood this.

Some had come to admire him, others to fear him, and others to profit from the conditioun of affairs. Each discovered a means of accommodating himself to the new arrangement. The architects learned to present cost increases as necessary refinements. The contractors learned that the Hegemon preferred a grand promesse to a modest result. The clerks learned that records could be made to demonstrate success even when the actual work lagged behind the account. The magistrates learned that a questioun asked too insistentlie myght be interpreted as disloyaltie.

The poets learned all these lessons more quicklie than the rest.

One composed a new work in which Herod was likened to an ancient lawgiver who had found Bològne in a state of confusioun and bestowed upon her the gyft of proportioun. Another compared the One Way to the path followed by the sun across the heavens. A third declared that the new avenue would become a measure by which every other cité myght be judged, and that the age of Herod would be remembered as the moment when humanité fyrste discovered the true relatiounship between beauty and obedience.

The poems were read at feasts.

Copies were sent abroad.

The poets received further commissiouns.

And the Hegemon, hearing his own ambitioun retourned to him in language more noble than the thoughts from which it had arisen, began to believe that he had been chosen for a purpose beyond the ordinary limits of human conduct.

He was no longer merelie a riche man who wyshed to be admired.

He was becoming a man who believed that admiratioun was owed to him by the structure of the world.

This belief was not born in a single moment. It accumulated through thousands of small experiences, each confirming the same conclusioun. When he desyred a house, the house could be purchased. When he desyred a law, the law could be passed. When he desyred sylence, complaints were suppressed. When he desyred laughter, a jester was brought into his household. When he wyshed to be praised, poets were payd to praise him. When the accounts showed a deficit, the deficit became a temporary irregularité; when the avenue fell behind its schedule, the schedule was revised.

No one was willing to tell him that he could not have everything.

The people who myght have told him had either been removed, impoverished, sylenced, or trained to speak in ways he found agreeable.

Thus the Hegemon became mad from success, not because he had lost all understanding, but because the world around him had grown so obedient that he no longer encountered the ordinary restraints by which understanding is corrected.

He could not distinguish the voice of a flatterer from the voice of a witnesse, the enlargement of a treasury from the creatioun of wealth, the possessioun of a woman from her affectioun, or the constructioun of a monument from the achievement of greatnesse.

And because he could not distinguish these things, he began to demaund ever larger proofs of the conclusiouns he had already reached.

The avenue must be longer.

The arches must be higher.

The fountains must rise more brilliantlie.

The court must laugh more loudlie.

The Citie must admire more completelie.

And those who failed to admire him must be made to understand that their failure was a defect in themselves.

Desiderata knew that something in Herod had chaunged, though she could not say at what moment the chaunge had become complete.

In the earlie years of their marriage, he had still possessed the habit of concealment. He would offer a gyft when he desyred forgivenesse, display tendernesse when he required her compliaunce, and speak of duty when he wyshed to disguise an advauntage. He had understood that another person possessed a mind which myght resist him, and that the appearaunce of affectioun could sometimes secure what an open command would not.

Now he seemed increasinglie impatient with any distinctioun between his wyshes and the conduct of others.

He ordered her presence at publick ceremonies and was offended when she did not appear pleaused. He selected her gowns and was disappointed when she did not admire them. He arranged feasts, performaunces, and gardyn entertainments, then complained that she had become incapable of enjoying the life he had provided.

He had ceased to court her.

He had begun to display her.

At an evenyng receptioun, he myght summon her to stand beside him while he described the prosperité of the House Malvezzi. He would place a hond at her back, introduce her to foreign visitors, and speak of the advauntages she possessed as though she were a testament to his abilité to acquire and preserve valuable things.

Desiderata learned to remain still.

She had not forgotten the woman she had been before the calamities of Act I. She remembered the questiouns she had asked, the accounts she had examined, the confidence with which she had imagined that intelligence myght be used to improve the lives of those around her. She remembered Adonis, and the tendernesse that had existed between them before the world closed its hond upon their future.

Memory had become an uncomfortable possessioun.

It offered no escape, yet prevented her from fullie accepting the life into which she had been forced.

At times she drank until the edges of her thoughts grew indistinct. At times she sat before the fire and watched the coals collapse into ash. At times she allowed her attendants to dress her without speaking, and when they had finished, she would gaze into the mirror as though the woman reflected there belonged to a distaunt household whose name she had once known.

The wyne did not restore her.

The jewels did not comfort her.

The silks did not erase the past.

Yet they provided occupatioun, and occupatioun was sometimes preferable to remembraunce.

Herod found these habits intolerable.

"You have become a stranger in your own household," he told her one evenyng.

Desiderata sat beside the window, the lyght of a lamp falling upon the silver cup in her hond.

"I have always been here."

"Not as you were."

"No."

He waited, expecting an explanatioun.

She gave him none.

"You were once more livelie," he continued. "You took an ynterest in affairs. You had opiniouns concernyng the management of the house."

"I still possess them."

"Then why do you not speak?"

She looked towards him.

"Because you have taught the household what happens when a person speaks without your permissioun."

Herod's face drykened.

"You mistake firmnesse for cruelty."

"Perhaps."

"Do you think yourself ill-treated?"

Desiderata considered the questioun.

She myght have enumerated the humiliatiouns, the losses, the years of enforced sylence. She myght have reminded him that the marriage had not been a choice made in freedom, that her sorrow arose from events in which his ynterests had been deeplie entangled, and that the palays which surrounded her was built upon the ruin of a future she had once hoped to share with another man.

But she knew that he would tourn each accusatioun into a debate concernyng her ingratitude.

"Does it matter what I think?" she asked.

Herod stared at her.

"It matters greatlie."

"Then you should have asked before you decided."

He rose.

For a moment she thought he myght strike her, though he had rarelie permitted his temper to assume so simple a form. Instead he approached the table, took her cup, and poured the remainieng wyne into the fire.

The wyne hissed upon the coals.

"You shall have no more tonyght."

Desiderata watched the flames.

"Then I shall sleep sober."

He seemed offended by the answer, though he could not have explained why.

"You are my wyfe."

"Yes."

"I have given you everything."

She looked at him.

"No," she said. "You have given me everything that can be counted."

The sylence that followed was long enough for the fire to settle.

text:
whose methodical, purposeful intentions find expression in different leadership dimensions. One was the sound of a state at ease; the other are the silence of women who finally feels safe and the one who is afraid to die after waiting for death. I am told that more than 500 of such unique stories spread across the state have been turned around. I will try to visit as many as I can in the coming days.

Just before I left the state, I read that one of my friends who is aspiring to unseat the governor argued on radio that building a house for the poor should never be the remit of a governor because Local Government Chairmen exist to solve such little problems. At first, I felt not just a sense of shock but disappointment, regret, and pity for him. And I wished that he would climb down someday to meet these folks and experience the joy in their hearts, like I did.

*Postscript:*

I would be a dishonest witness if I only reported what pleased my eyes. Before leaving the state, I went to deliver a community crowd-funded lawnmower to St. Paul's Primary School, Midim Atan. I also used the opportunity to assess the Midim-Etim Ekpo Road Project handled by Nsik Engineering Limited. My findings were a disappointing anticlimax. I am taking this up privately with His Excellency, the governor.

But the primary school itself broke my heart entirely. There were only three teachers for seven classes of 109 pupils. No functional toilets or source of water existed. The buildings were a dilapidated shell. It was no wonder that seven teachers posted there recently immediately worked their transfers out. I could not walk away from children who have nowhere to relieve themselves, so I mobilized a local contractor on the spot to dig a soakaway from my pocket. The project is ongoing.

This rot lies squarely at the feet of Local Government Chairmen who now enjoy full financial autonomy but have mostly abandoned their responsibilities. Indeed, it was bittersweet that after I witnessed the unspeakable rot in that school, I also attended the unveiling of the bespoke residential quarters for the Local Government Chairman in my LGA. I refused to eat the snacks offered at that occasion as my silent protest against the indignity toward little children who are left to study in an environment as bad as I witnessed. Of course, the situation did not start under Governor Umo Eno. I am aware that state-funded model primary schools are being built in each LGA to stimulate grassroots education. Coincidentally, I returned to read that same day that the governor declared a state of emergency on education. I commend the critical first step, which must be backed by a brutal, uncompromising Marshall Plan. LG helmsmen MUST be corralled into deploying the huge resources at their disposal presently to complementing the efforts of the governor. The Commissioner for Education must wake up, think outside the box, and roll up his sleeves. A state that gives widows their dignity cannot allow its children to learn in squalor.

And so this series ends exactly where it began, with the question critics keep asking: Is Pastor Umo Eno doing anything with the money that comes into Akwa Ibom State? The critics will keep asking, as they should. A healthy democracy demands it. But I have now walked the ground where their arguments do not reach. I cannot settle every debate about every naira, but like the blind man, I can tell you what I have seen. Mrs. Immaculata Edet Nyong now sleeps and dreams good dreams. Mrs. Comfort Linus no longer prays for death. I went home to Akwa Ibom as a visitor, and I return to Abuja as a witness.

The eyes that have seen need no witness.

CONCLUDED

_+__+_+_*Celestine Mel* writes on public affairs, technology, and finance from Abuja-FCT.

text:
❯ Upgrades: Your Edited Config Survives the Upgrade on FreeBSD
Edit one line in a Debian config file, and the next update that ships a new version of it is held back by unattended-upgrades, security fixes included, until somebody answers a question. FreeBSD merges both changes and asks nothing.
⠀
■ THE HABIT
⠀
dpkg records an MD5 digest of every config file it ships. On upgrade it holds that digest against the file on disk and the file in the new package, and when both you and the package have changed it, Debian Policy says the user "must resolve the differences themselves". The prompt offers Y or I for the package's version, N or O for yours, D for a diff and Z for a shell (the brave option), and the default keeps what you have. Combining the two is not on the list, and cannot be: with only a digest, there is no common ancestor to merge from.
⠀
Automation picks a side in advance. --force-confold keeps your file, so the new default never arrives, and --force-confnew installs the new file over your change. I read the source of unattended-upgrades: a function called conffile_prompt compares the same three digests, and a package that would prompt is held back, pinned, logged as "has conffile prompt and needs to be upgraded manually", and the run counts as unsuccessful. Security updates get no exemption.
⠀
Debian does have a three-way merge in ucf, but a package must opt in, and even then the merge is one item in a menu whose default is to keep the current file; 132 of 37,478 source packages in Debian 13 depend on ucf at all. RHEL never asks: %config(noreplace) keeps your file and writes the new one beside it as .rpmnew, while plain %config renames yours to .rpmsave. rpmconf tidies up with a two-way diff and is not installed by default.
⠀
Both habits follow a fair rule, that a package manager must not guess. On forty machines the honest question becomes forty questions.
⠀
■ THE SAME JOB ON FREEBSD
⠀
FreeBSD keeps the file it shipped last time, so there is something to merge from. etcupdate, written by John Baldwin at a trading firm between 2010 and 2013, is "specifically tailored to assisting with mass upgrades. To that end it does not require user intervention while running." It merges /etc with diff3 against the previous release; in my measurement jail it keeps 388 files for that purpose. A collision is parked with conflict markers, your live file stays as it was, and no further merge starts until you have resolved it.
⠀
freebsd-update does the same with diff3 on release upgrades and shows every merged file for approval. pkg has carried a three-way merge for files marked @config since version 1.4 in 2014, borrowed from Fossil, and keeps the shipped version of each such file in its database; packaged base in 15.1 marks 374 files in 65 packages that way, sshd_config, master.passwd, login.conf and every rc.d script among them. rc.conf, fstab, pf.conf and jail.conf belong to no package, so no upgrade touches them. Ports install their defaults as .sample and never overwrite your file.
⠀
■ SHOWN
⠀
In my measurement jail I built three versions of a test package whose one config file holds, among other things, an address and a timeout. After installing 1.0 I changed the listen address, then upgraded to 2.0, which shipped timeout = 60. pkg merged both and left no extra file behind, without a word. When 3.0 changed the very timeout line I had set to 90, pkg reported "Unable to merge configuration file", kept my file and put its own beside it as .pkgnew. Under the rules above, Debian would have stopped at 2.0 and RHEL would have left timeout = 60 waiting in an .rpmnew.
⠀
■ THE LIMIT
⠀
A merge is textual, and two changes on different lines can still contradict each other. When a merge fails, pkg keeps your file and leaves its own as .pkgnew, and with MERGETOOL set it hands the conflict to a tool of your choice. freebsd-update asks during release upgrades, and patch-level updates leave modified files alone. Ports are not merged. On Linux, NixOS, etckeeper, Ansible and ucf each answer the question their own way.
⠀
etcupdate was written at a trading firm, where a server waiting for an answer is a server earning nothing. Thirteen years on, it still does not ask.

👉 Full essay: https://t.co/z0T4ybHXTN
⠀
Disclaimer: these pieces are written between half past seven and half past ten most mornings. AI serves as my secretary and as a second pair of eyes on the facts, so that what reaches you has been checked. Nothing here is automated apart from the deployment to the blog. The argument, the opinions, the examples and the measurements are mine.
⠀
