➡️ Wheelbase: 2,600 mm

🏷️ At over 4 metres, the BAYON has the right proportions to offer decent cabin space. 

🏷️ The real test, however, will be rear-seat comfort, practicality and overall space utilisation.

🏷️ Exterior Design ::

👉 The front, rear and side profiles look well-proportioned, with the familiar Hyundai design language. Nothing radically disruptive, but a decent-looking SUV that should appeal to buyers looking for a stylish, contemporary package.

🏷️ Interiors & Cabin Experience

👉 Hyundai has traditionally done a good job with interior design, perceived quality and feature integration. 

👉 The new VENUE reinforces that strength, and the BAYON appears to follow a familiar, well-established template.

Except the AC layout -switches this is unconventional for Indian buyers not everyone will like them 

🏷️ Powertrain: No Surprises Here ::

➡️ 1.5L naturally aspirated petrol engine
➡️ 6-speed Manual Transmission
➡️ Intelligent Variable Transmission (IVT)

👉 A familiar and predictable powertrain combination, prioritising everyday usability over outright performance.

🏷️ Intelligence & Connected Technology ::

👉 Hyundai is positioning the BAYON as an intelligent SUV, with Generative AI, connected technology, OTA updates and a digital cockpit taking centre stage.

👉 But here’s the catch: will these features actually drive volumes?

👉 For the average Indian buyer, purchase decisions still revolve around price, running costs, space, safety and value for money. 

👉 Moreover, if the headline technology is concentrated in the top variants, its appeal across the broader customer base could be limited.

I mean OTA ,ccNC,AI,connected tech.

👉 In my opinion, the BAYON could be Hyundai India’s attempt to create a fresh product template and generate renewed excitement around its portfolio, especially when the i20 ,VERNA haven’t been delivering the volumes the brand would ideally want even Exter (being a solid product) doesn’t gels 

👉 Plus with next gen Creta Hyundai India may make it more expensive thus creating a price pay for an additional product which is CNG -1.5 NA focus (remember Maruti plays That market) 

👉 A stylish SUV, a proven 1.5L petrol engine, the possibility of a CNG option & an attractive value proposition could give Hyundai a new opportunity.

👉 And with Indian buyers increasingly embracing CNG, that opportunity shouldn’t be ignored.

text:
CATL Has More Room to Turn Down Carmakers

Xiaomi left CATL off the supplier list for its September 4 Longjia battery launch, choosing CALB and Sunwoda cells. Li Auto also announced progress on self-developed batteries. We've argued the moat is cracking at both ends as automakers diversify away from CATL. The new detail from Caijing complicates that: domestic passenger vehicles contribute less than 40% of CATL's gross profit, so the shift may cost less profit than the debate suggests.

Storage already accounted for nearly a quarter of CATL's shipments in H1 2026. On September 20, its domestic storage solutions CTO said storage lines were running at full capacity, with Q4 scheduling extremely tight. A CATL manager told Caijing the company wouldn't reserve production lines for uncertain custom orders when storage and commercial vehicles offered higher unit prices and more predictable demand.

That choice has a practical basis. Passenger-car customers require different cell sizes and specifications, and CATL's Liyang plant changes production configurations hundreds of times a year. Each change requires replacing tooling, recalibrating equipment and running validation. Storage cells have fewer specifications, so different customers' orders can share a line. If one project delays delivery, another order can keep production running, spreading fixed costs across more cells.

text:
@realdonaldtrump @IlhanMN @WhiteHouse @Mike_Pence @AOC 
3/3
XENOPHOBIA, SCARE RHETORIC, FEDERAL POWER AND REAL PUBLIC SAFETY: ANALYZING THE TRUMP-OMAR EXCHANGE WITHOUT REWRITING THE FACTS
Evidence cutoff: October 13, 2026 | Original Omar response: https://t.co/lDdgsyqiJP
A president may lawfully criticize crime, demand better fraud controls, condemn gang leaders and request cooperation from a state. Politicians may also express forceful views about immigration. The constitutional and factual questions are WHETHER THEIR CLAIMS IDENTIFY ACTUAL WRONGDOERS, WHAT AUTHORITY THEY ASSERT, AND HOW THEY CHARACTERIZE INNOCENT PEOPLE. A president's powers are not unlimited, and presidential rhetoric is not a substitute for the findings of police, auditors, judges or juries.
WHAT THE TEXT ACTUALLY DOES. Trump's October 8 Truth Social statement constructs a recognizable sequence: first a formerly "great" state allegedly faces outside takeover; next an ethnic immigrant group is connected to pervasive murder, theft and contempt for existing residents; state officials are cast as corrupt and absent; readers are ordered to "fight back"; finally the president offers federal "rescue." The pattern is visible IN THE WORDING. Whether the author deliberately intended to incite violence, gain votes or intimidate Somali Americans cannot be proved solely from this text. (i)
CALL THE RHETORICAL DEVICES BY THEIR PROPER NAMES:
ETHNIC GENERALIZATION / COLLECTIVE GUILT: actions attributed to charged individuals or gang members are projected onto the Somali community. A suspect and an entire national-origin group are different categories.

XENOPHOBIC FRAMING: residents are portrayed as foreign occupiers regardless of citizenship or birth. This describes features of the language; it is not a psychiatric diagnosis of Trump or a judicial finding of illegal discrimination.

THREAT AMPLIFICATION / FEAR APPEAL: repeated references to statewide takeover, murder and rescue suggest an emergency without matching the claim to the latest complete state crime series.

SCAPEGOATING: complex issues involving pandemic program rules, agency control failures, fraud networks, state and federal enforcement, and local gangs become an accusation against one visible population.

FALSE CHOICE: the public is pushed toward accepting federal rescue or supposedly abandoning safety. In fact lawful enforcement, prosecution, state reform, minority rights and constitutional oversight can operate together.

DELEGITIMIZATION: describing Walz as a thief before presenting evidence of personal theft confuses political accountability with proof of a crime. (i-v)

ILHAN OMAR'S REPLY also contains factual and interpretive components. The screenshot reproduces her statement that repeated attacks on Somali Minnesotans are dangerous and that the community will not be intimidated. The first is a political assessment grounded in explicit generalization against Somali immigrants; the second is an expression of solidarity and determination, not a measured count of who supports her. Omar is a Somali-born NATURALIZED U.S. CITIZEN and the elected representative of Minnesota's Fifth District. She is not responsible for fraud or gang conduct because of ethnicity, nor does her elected office immunize her from lawful investigation or ordinary political criticism. The October 12 search of her residence is a subsequent investigation, not evidence of guilt or proof that her earlier response was fabricated. (ii, vi)

THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN MISINFORMATION AND DISINFORMATION MATTERS. A demonstrably false or misleading assertion can be classified without proving what a speaker knew. "Disinformation" implies deliberate deception and normally requires evidence such as internal instructions, coordination, editing records or verified knowledge of falsity. This article identifies unsupported group claims and misleading context; it does NOT assert an unseen political conspiracy, a secret order to commit violence or a proven plan to terrorize Somali residents. Conversely, legitimate crime reporting can become misleading when a headline leaps from a particular violent event to a general accusation about an ethnic population. (iii-v)

LEGAL TEST: NOT ALL DANGEROUS RHETORIC IS CRIMINAL INCITEMENT. The Supreme Court's Brandenburg standard generally protects advocacy unless it is directed at producing IMMINENT lawless action and likely to produce it. Whether an actual post crosses that threshold depends on audience, context, intent, likely imminence and more; no ruling reviewed here declares this post a crime. The absence of a criminal incitement ruling does not make the group accusation factually established or eliminate a leader's institutional responsibility to distinguish lawful mobilization from vigilantism. Americans may petition elected officials, report crimes, demonstrate peacefully and vote. Assaulting Somali residents or mosques is not lawful "fighting back." (vii)

WHAT WOULD "FEDERAL HELP" LEGALLY MEAN? Federal prosecutors and agents can pursue federal offenses within their lawful authority; joint FBI/state/local work already exists. A governor or mayor can request assistance for particular emergencies, but their request is NOT required for every federal investigation or immigration arrest. Military domestic-law-enforcement deployment is governed separately by the Posse Comitatus Act and limited statutory exceptions including 10 U.S.C. sections 251-253. The state-request mechanism under section 251 does not describe every possible federal intervention. The federal government cannot generally commandeer state and city officials into enforcing federal civil immigration policy. In June 2026 Judge Patrick Schiltz quashed DOJ grand-jury subpoenas concerning Walz, Frey and others, finding unconstitutional coercion and retaliation in those SPECIFIC proceedings. This is a judicial fact, not a general adjudication of every federal operation. (viii-xi)

REAL COMMUNITY RISK AND REAL SECURITY WORK CAN COEXIST. Minnesota police identified dangerous shootings involving youth gangs; the FBI and DOJ pursued a credible alleged terror plot; federal prosecutors secured convictions in major taxpayer fraud. Authorities should investigate organizers, shooters, fraudulent billers, recruiters, suppliers, money laundering and victims, and cooperate across county lines where the evidence warrants. Yet MPR documented mosques reviewing their security after the October 8 rhetoric. Hate incidents, threats, retaliatory vigilantism and fear of reporting crime can damage the SAME communities that benefit from stopping gangs and fraud. This is an observable concern, though no numerical causal effect from the post has been established. (iii-v, xii)

MEDIA AND GOVERNMENT SOURCE-INTEREST AUDIT. The White House is authoritative for ITS OWN accusations and enforcement announcements but is an interested political party; the Minnesota DHS is authoritative for its actions but has an interest in defending its record. The independent legislative audit, actual federal criminal judgments, FBI complaint, official BCA crime data and court order answer different evidentiary questions. Local reports about gang incidents rely partly on named police officials, whose claims may later be modified by arrests or trial evidence. Community advocates are essential witnesses about security concerns, not a statistical crime census. A headline or viral Truth Social image is no substitute for case numbers and statewide denominators. Nor is disagreement proof that a newsroom took a bribe or deliberately fabricated facts. (iii-v, ix-xii)

SECOND THROUGH FIFTH ORDER: When a national leader collapses individual offenses into ethnic identity, a story about 100 shots or a criminal food-site operator can begin influencing attitudes toward all Somali schoolchildren, business owners and worshipers. Increased precautionary security and reluctance to cooperate with police are POSSIBLE downstream risks; assess actual data instead of inventing numbers. Meanwhile failure to prosecute real fraud erodes welfare programs, and failure to confront youth gun violence permits further victimization, including of Somali-American families. Intergovernmental conflict can divert resources, provoke litigation and undermine trust; transparent, legally bounded cooperation can reduce both violence and discrimination.

A REPRODUCIBLE ACCOUNTABILITY PROGRAM WOULD REQUIRE: (1) local, county and state crime series with field dates and denominators; (2) named suspects and proven convictions, never an ethnic presumption; (3) independent audits of federal nutrition and Medicaid funding and a published recovery tally; (4) serious multi-jurisdiction gang intervention with youth protection and lawful gun enforcement; (5) civil-rights and religious-site security, with threats investigated; (6) published federal operational authority and independent review of agent shootings; (7) respect for all citizens' and noncitizens' procedural rights; (8) public corrections when officials overstate numbers or impute guilt without evidence.

THE FACTUAL SYNTHESIS: Minnesota has real violence, real organized fraud, and documented governance failures. Its latest complete statewide crime record nevertheless shows declining violent crime. Somali Americans include many U.S.-born and naturalized citizens; the conduct of defendants cannot be assigned to the entire population. Walz's decision not to run again is public, but personal theft is unproved; state officials have both failed in oversight and enacted reforms. The president's sentence uses a takeover-and-rescue structure that invites xenophobic and fear-based interpretations without furnishing demographic or community-wide crime evidence. Omar's objection describes that rhetoric; it does not itself prove Trump's secret intent. The constitutional standard is consistent regardless of who is in office: investigate individuals, protect victims, obey due process, and do not replace evidence with collective blame.

text:
I find Happymon Jacob’s middle-class analogy particularly interesting. He is one of the more pragmatic Indian scholars I read. His willingness to acknowledge India’s limits keeps his analysis focused on what the country can realistically do.

Mao’s discussions of two intermediate zones in 1963–64 offer another angle. In July 1964, he observed: “Some imperialists also oppose US imperialism.” A state can resist a stronger power while dominating weaker neighbours. 

Nor does cooperation require equal distance from both giants. China later worked with Washington against Soviet pressure. Today, a country can rely on a power for security while resisting its trade demands. Cooperation matters when it gives each member more room to act.

Shared anxiety also leaves fierce competition intact. These countries compete for the same investment and export markets. A common middle-power identity gives them little reason to surrender those interests. Moving closer to Washington or Beijing may serve them better.

For India, this raises a question about what its rise offers fellow members. Preserving India’s chance to become a third pole will struggle to unite countries pursuing ambitions of their own. They need a reason to believe India’s rise will also improve their position.

" Beauseant at .ontgisard 1177 "
By Artist Michael Rucker 
Copyright ©️ 

Description
This painting places a Templar knight at the heart of one of the most improbable victories of the Crusades. On 25 November 1177, sixteen-year-old King Baldwin IV of Jerusalem already marked by leprosy rode out with a few hundred knights to stop Saladins Ayyubid army from reaching the Holy City. With him came Grand Master Eudes de Saint-Amand and roughly eighty Knights Templar from Gaza.

Contemporary estimates give the Christians perhaps 375450 knights and several thousand infantry against a far larger Muslim host that had been allowed to scatter while raiding. Saladin, confident the leper king would stay behind walls, was caught crossing broken ground near Montgisard (Tell Gezer / Mons Gisardi), between Ramla and Yibna. Baldwin knelt before a fragment of the True Cross, then ordered the charge. The Templars formed the spearhead. Their war banner, the Beauseant black above white, black to enemies, white to friends was the signal that no brother might quit the field while it still flew.

The shock of heavy cavalry smashed the unready Ayyubid line. Saladin himself barely escaped; most of his army did not.The scene you see is not a portrait of one named man but an emblem of that hour: white mantle and red cross pattee of the Temple, kite shield, the Beauseant replacing later anachronisms, stone churches of the Latin East rising behind the dust. It is offered so visitors may remember that history is not only catastrophe. Sometimes a small, disciplined force, a young king who would not hide, and a banner that meant we do not leave changed the map for a season.

Baldwins victory bought the Kingdom of Jerusalem nearly a decade. Saladin would return; Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem still lay ahead. Yet Montgisard remains the day the Temples black-and-white standard flew over a field that should have been lost.Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam.

The one thing I am starting to notice is this: 

The types who call themselves "Uncompromising #Christian" (or something along those lines) on X will never debate a topic on scripture, or they will completely ignore being called out by fellow Christians.

IMHO, they will end up being the parents of kids who become Wiccans, Satanists, Reddit-tier atheists, or something else the moment they leave the house or go to college. It's these people's pride that causes this to happen to their children.

Lust does a massive amount of work when it comes to messing people up; it’s a constant onslaught from the enemy. But pride is the real general of the army. It’s what drives the devil's deepest work.

Yeah, you remained chaste, never looked at NSFW content, stayed straight-edge, etc. But you just had to let everyone know it. If not by explicitly telling them, it's that prideful, holier-than-thou attitude that did it for you.

Lust is overt and obvious. If you can control yourself, avoid it, and never get a taste of what it offers, it's really not as hard to resist because you don't know what's on the other side. It's just that this world throws lustful things at you every single hour of the day.

But pride? Pride is devious. Now, feeling satisfaction in hard work or being grateful for how far you've come isn't a bad thing. But pride takes that good feeling and quickly twists it.

Slowly, it tries to tell you, "I'm better than that." Then it says, "Look how far I've come, how much I have accomplished. I'm doing what scripture told me to do, so I must be in the right!"

Then, before you know it's: "I'm better than these people because I have proof I am right."

It's not just a Christian thing either—we all know a non-religious person who acts exactly like this.

Pride is the silent soldier of the enemy. It picks up where all of the fleshly sins fail to gain headway. It's the traitor in the castle who talks you into opening the gate yourself—your Gríma Wormtongue from The Lord of the Rings.

Pride is what goes in after the absolute best of people. It works because it uses the good you have done against you. Your strengths become your weakness. And the stronger you are, the more pride has to work with.

text:
🚨 PLEA DEAL: POLICE OFFICER ACCUSED OF MOLESTING TWO 9-YEAR-OLD CHILDREN AGREES TO PLEAD GUILTY TO LESSER FELONY CHARGES

📍 Indianapolis, Indiana

Former IMPD officer David McDaniel was originally charged with two Level 1 felony counts of child molesting following allegations involving two children who were just 9 years old when the alleged abuse occurred in 2016.

Now, McDaniel has reportedly agreed to plead guilty to two lesser Level 4 felony charges, including child molesting and attempted child molesting, in exchange for the dismissal of the more serious charges.

Let that sink in.

A former police officer accused of sexually abusing two children has negotiated a plea agreement that would eliminate the original, more serious charges.

But here’s where I believe the public deserves answers.

What evidence or legal considerations led prosecutors to negotiate this agreement? Were the victims’ interests adequately represented? And how will the proposed sentence reflect the seriousness of these allegations?

The reported agreement also includes restitution for the victims’ mental-health expenses.

That’s an important provision, but financial restitution and criminal accountability address different consequences of abuse. One should not be confused with the other.

A plea agreement doesn’t automatically mean justice has been denied. But it shouldn’t automatically be treated as justice served, either.

That distinction matters.

When someone who once carried a badge faces allegations of abusing children, the public has every reason to scrutinize how the justice system responds.

And the children at the center of this case deserve more than to become an afterthought in legal negotiations.

At the time of the reported agreement, judicial approval was still pending.

My concern isn’t simply that a plea deal was offered. It’s whether the outcome will deliver meaningful accountability while respecting the victims whose lives were affected.

Two children were just 9 years old when the abuse occurred. Their experiences deserve to remain central to how this case is understood and resolved.

text:
The Higher Office

On Friday President Trump said Russia would send diesel west: 300,000 tons at once, 500,000 in November, and a million more after that. A sanctions waiver, reported to run until April 2027, was issued so the purchase could go through. On Sunday he announced an “energy ceasefire,” the phrase set in capital letters and effective immediately. Both parties had agreed, he wrote. Do not break it. He offered no details. By Monday Moscow had not publicly confirmed the pause, and Al Jazeera, via Axios, reported that Zelenskyy first called the deal news to him. One office had spoken. An equal politics would have needed the others to agree, and they had not.

The reply inside the American system was a demand to be counted in. Seven senators, four Republicans and three Democrats, told him to reverse course. Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis, John Curtis, Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal, and Ron Wyden said Congress had banned Russian energy imports in 2022 so American money would not finance the war, and that the administration had neither consulted Congress nor explained itself, as the law requires. Tillis, on Meet the Press, said there was a legitimate case that the president was not following the law. A statute can sit above a Friday post, and on that point the letter defends hierarchy. Weeks before the midterms of 3 November, the same letter treats the missing consultation as the ground of illegitimacy.

Europe asked to be included on the same terms. In Luxembourg on Monday the Council adopted listings against 1,569 companies and executives in Russia’s military industry, the largest set it said it had ever agreed. Kaja Kallas called on the United States to put sanctions in place. Lithuania’s Kęstutis Budrys said the deal helped neither the price of fuel nor the unity of the transatlantic community, and that it was not the European way. Ireland’s Helen McEntee called it concerning. Britain’s Stephen Doughty said London was not planning to buy Russian energy. Macron, at a Paris auto show, said he had noted no energy ceasefire from the Russian side in forty-eight hours. Tusk said Russia was not interested in a ceasefire and that he would go to Brussels to press for more sanctions. Europe may keep its own list. It does not, by that keeping, become an equal author of an American purchase.

Line the authors up and the democratic claim is plain. A president, seven senators, a council of foreign ministers, and an electorate that on 3 November will be asked to price the arrangement. Each signature is treated as incomplete until the others have weighed the same. The Senate wants a consultation. The Council wants the purchase to pass a test of allied consent. The electorate wants a cheaper gallon. A decision cannot be made that way, because a decision is unequal: one judgment outranks the rest, and one person can be blamed for it. Democracy denies the inequality and then cannot name the owner of the waiver. Egalitarianism gives the denial its moral name and calls the heavier will an injustice.

The campaign at home already speaks that name. The Associated Press reports that more than three dozen voting laws in Republican-controlled states take effect this midterm year, many echoing a presidential demand for identification and proof of citizenship that Congress has not passed. Students in New Hampshire can no longer use student IDs to vote. Utah voters returning mail ballots must include more information on the envelope. The fight is over how easily an equal ballot can be cast, not over who may bind the republic, and not over whether the import ban of 2022 still outranks the man who waived it.

Hierarchy ranks office, statute, and responsibility. Egalitarianism refuses the ranking. Democracy issues the refusal a ballot.

Monday is a bad day for the refusal. A senator who must say whether a statute was bypassed is not the equal, on that question, of a voter weighing the price of diesel. The Council is not the equal of the president whose waiver it is asked to bless. A voter can be right that fuel is expensive and still hold no office that answers for the waiver. Calling those unequal duties equal is the egalitarian falsehood. Arming the falsehood with a vote, and calling the result the only legitimate government, is the democratic one.

The alternative keeps the ladder and drops the alibi. Citizenship sits beneath command, proven competence, and the offices that may not split the difference. The person who must answer outranks the person who only must be counted. Cruelty is not the discipline, and neither is birth. Birth confers no office. Hierarchy confers the office and a penalty for using it badly. Seven senators can be right about the 2022 ban and remain seven names, not a sovereign. A council can be right to keep its sanctions and still not author Washington’s purchase. Once everyone has voted, no one in particular has acted.

The morning comes back to the two doctrines it has to refuse. The ceasefire was spoken as if equal partners had agreed, and they had not. The waiver was scored as if the Senate, the Council, and the November voter had to weigh the same, and they do not. The ballot laws were drawn as if the trouble were an insufficiently equal count. Democracy cannot own a choice it must share with everyone in the room. Egalitarianism cannot set a statute above a post, an office above a poll, or a duty above a crowd. What the West needs is a ladder someone can be pulled down. A constitution is that ladder. It says which office outranks which while a waiver is in force and a ballot is being made easier to cast. Folding the signature, the statute, and the European list into one November consent is the aim democracy and equality share, and it is the wrong aim.

text:
The most unsettling idea in The Matrix is how easily a person can mistake a familiar life for a freely chosen one.

You do not have to believe reality is a computer simulation to recognise that feeling. You can wake up, go to work, pay your bills, scroll through your phone and repeat the routine for years without asking who decided this was the life you should want.

Much of what governs us arrives before we are old enough to question it. We inherit ideas about success, money, beauty, belonging and what makes a person valuable. Eventually, those ideas become so familiar that we hear them as our own voice.

Work harder. Earn more. Stay useful. Do not fall behind. Become someone other people approve of.

Some of these beliefs help us function. Others keep us chasing a finish line that moves every time we approach it. The difficulty is learning to tell the difference.

This is where The Matrix becomes a useful metaphor. A system does not need to hide the truth perfectly when it can keep people too occupied to examine their assumptions. A crowded schedule, a constant stream of information and the fear of losing your place can leave little room for the question: “Do I actually believe this?”

That question has a long philosophical history. Plato imagined prisoners who understood the world through shadows on a wall. Later thinkers questioned whether our senses could give us certainty. The film brings those doubts into a modern setting, where comfort and control can look remarkably alike.

But questioning appearances does not mean everything is false. Your body needs care. Your choices affect other people. Pain, affection and responsibility have consequences whether or not you have a perfect explanation of reality.

A useful awakening brings you into closer contact with those consequences. It helps you notice where you have been living automatically.

Perhaps you have confused your income with your worth. Perhaps an old failure has become the limit of what you think is possible. Perhaps you have spent so long defending an identity that you no longer know whether it fits.

These are beliefs you can examine. You can ask where they came from, what evidence supports them and what they are costing you.

The uncomfortable part is that awareness gives you something to do. Once you recognise a pattern, you have to decide how to respond. You may need to change a habit, disappoint someone, admit uncertainty or take a risk you have been avoiding.

Neo’s awakening captures that cost. Understanding his situation does not deliver an easy life. It leaves him vulnerable, disoriented and responsible for choices he could previously avoid. Freedom demands practice long after the revelation has passed.

The same is true outside the cinema. You can understand that comparison makes you miserable and still reach for your phone. You can recognise the need for approval and still organise your life around it. Insight opens a possibility; repeated choices turn it into a change.

And those choices belong to each person. You can offer someone another perspective, but you cannot force them to see through your eyes. Treating people as foolish because they disagree with you simply creates another hierarchy, with the supposedly awakened person at the top.

That is one reason to be careful with anyone selling certainty. A promise of secret knowledge can be persuasive when life feels confusing. Before handing over your trust, ask whether the teaching strengthens your judgment or makes you dependent on the teacher. Does it welcome questions? Can it withstand disagreement? Does it help you live more honestly?

The idea of “no spoon” can be read in that spirit. Our experience of a situation includes the meaning we bring to it. Changing that meaning will not remove every obstacle, but it can reveal options that fear or habit had concealed.

A setback can become information. A label can describe part of your experience without defining your entire future. An uncomfortable feeling can be noticed without becoming an instruction you must obey.

Even the sense of who you are deserves some curiosity. You have a history, a personality and commitments, yet you can also observe your thoughts changing. A belief that once felt inseparable from you can lose its authority. That capacity to notice gives you room to grow.

Perhaps that is the most practical lesson to take from the film: pay attention to what directs your life.

Notice what captures your fear. Notice whose approval you keep seeking. Notice the stories you repeat about yourself and whether they still deserve your loyalty.

Then begin with one choice you can make consciously.

An honest conversation. A boundary you have postponed. A few minutes without distraction. A decision based on what matters to you.

You do not need to solve the nature of the universe before you start living with greater awareness. You can begin wherever you are, by examining the life you have accepted and taking responsibility for the life you help create.

text:
The island of Kythira

Kythira sits between the Peloponnese and Crete, yet it has a distinctive identity that makes it feel like a destination apart. Its landscapes range from rugged coastlines and hidden coves to green valleys, waterfalls and traditional settlements.

The island is particularly rewarding for travellers who like to mix beach time with exploring. You can spend one day swimming in clear water and the next wandering through a historic village or following a countryside trail.

Some experiences worth adding to your itinerary include:
•  Exploring Chora and its Venetian castle.
•  Visiting the harbour village of Kapsali.
•  Discovering the waterfalls at Mylopotamos.
•  Swimming at Kaladi or other scenic beaches.
•  Wandering through traditional villages.
•  Sampling local dishes and sweets.

Chora, the island's capital, sits above the coast and offers wonderful views across the surrounding landscape. Its narrow streets and historic buildings are ideal for an unhurried wander.

At Mylopotamos, the scenery changes. Green vegetation, stone bridges and flowing water create a surprisingly lush setting, especially compared with the island's more exposed coastal areas.

The beaches are another highlight, with a variety of settings to choose from. Some are easier to reach, while others reward a little extra effort with dramatic scenery and a quieter atmosphere.

Kythira is best explored without trying to squeeze everything into one day.

Distances, winding roads and the temptation to stop for photographs can make even a short journey take longer than expected.

Give yourself time to discover the island at your own pace. It is often the places you stumble across between the main attractions that make Kythira memorable.

पिण्डजप्रवरारूढा चण्डकोपास्त्रकैर्युता।
प्रसादं तनुते मह्यं चन्द्रघण्टेति विश्रुता॥

Pindaja pravaraarudhaa chandakopaastrakairyutaa,
Prasaadam tanute mahyam Chandraghanteti vishrutaa.

I bow to the widely renowned Ma Chandraghanta, seated on her mount, armed with fierce weapons, who grants her grace to me

Her name comes from Chandra or moon and Ghanta or bell describing the half-moon marking on her forehead shaped like a temple bell Chandraghanta is Parvati again, the same goddess honoured through Shailaputri and Brahmacharini, now in the days following her marriage to Shiva. Where Day 1 showed her as the mountain's daughter, Day 2 as the ascetic seeking her husband, Day 3 shows what came after devotion was answered

Her arrival in this form carries a memorable story. On the day of the wedding, Shiva arrived not as a graceful god but leading a procession of ghosts and ascetics, covered in ash, which frightened Parvati's own family To calm the moment and protect those around her, Parvati took on the form of Chandraghanta, radiant and armed and it was this form that persuaded Shiva to appear as Chandrashekhara, gentle and composed, for the marriage itself

She is shown with ten arms, carrying a trident, a mace, a sword, a bow and arrow, a lotus, a japa mala and a water pot, with two hands held open in gestures of blessing and reassurance. She rides a tiger, unlike Shailaputri's bull or the lion ridden by some of the other Navadurga forms, and a third eye rests permanently on her forehead, always open, watching for anything that threatens her devotees

Her golden complexion is read as radiance drawn from deep inner strength and despite the weapons in her many hands, tradition holds her as a protector rather than a figure of alarm, someone who fights so that peace can return quickly

Bells rung during puja are believed to clear a space of negative energy before worship begins and Chandraghanta wears one permanently on her forehead, meaning her very presence carries out that same purification wherever she turns her gaze

Worship on this day is said to move the seeker's energy into the Manipura, the solar plexus chakra, the seat of courage and personal will, continuing the same rise that began at the root on Day 1 and moved through the sacral centre on Day 2. Where the earlier days built ground and patience, Day 3 asks for the courage to act on both

Her mantra is easy to carry through the day:

ॐ देवी चन्द्रघण्टायै नमः
Om Devi Chandraghantayai Namah

Milk and milk-based sweets, such as kheer, are offered to her and jasmine remains her favoured flower, carried over from her earlier form as Brahmacharini

Sources referenced: Devi Kavacham (Durga Saptashati, Markandeya Purana) · Navadurga Stotram · Devi Bhagavata Purana · Yogic tradition on the Manipura Chakra

text:
Ancient literature repeatedly describes encounters with presences that seem too powerful for ordinary language: a person whose gaze cannot be endured, a stranger whose appearance silences a gathering, a warrior surrounded by radiance, a god whose arrival changes perception or overwhelms the body. Witnesses tremble, avert their eyes, lose speech, fall down, or find themselves drawn toward the figure before them.

🧵

“Archetypal” offers one way of reading these encounters—as manifestations of sovereign power, beauty, terror, desire, or divine violence. The ancient accounts use their own images: fire, extraordinary stature, unbearable brightness, possession, and voices that shake the world. Mesopotamian tradition even names an awe-inspiring radiance, melammu, associated with gods, kings, and sacred places. 

The following collection brings together 37 examples from Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, and Rome. Some survive in Bronze Age texts; others are later accounts of heroic antiquity or encounters involving historical people. Myth, royal inscription, drama, and historical anecdote preserve different kinds of evidence: each entry identifies the text in which the encounter occurs, without assuming that every reported marvel happened literally.

1. Sinuhe overwhelmed before the pharaoh — Egypt, The Tale of Sinuhe.

    Returning from exile, Sinuhe enters the king’s presence and becomes almost incapable of functioning. His limbs tremble, his sense of himself disappears, and he cannot distinguish life from death—even though the king greets him kindly. This Middle Kingdom literary scene presents royal presence as a force experienced throughout the body. 

2. The golden serpent whose approach shakes the island — Egypt, The Shipwrecked Sailor.

    A stranded sailor hears what seems to be thunder: trees break and the earth shakes. An enormous serpent approaches, its body golden and its eyebrows lapis lazuli. The terrified sailor encounters a speaking being with divine attributes, who reassures him and foretells his rescue. 

3. The Sphinx speaks to the future king — Egypt, the Dream Stela of Thutmose IV.

    Resting beneath the Sphinx, the young prince falls asleep and encounters the monument’s divine presence in a dream. The god addresses him as a son and promises kingship while asking to be freed from the encroaching sand. The royal inscription makes a personal encounter with a sacred being foundational to sovereignty. 

4. Huwawa’s seven terrors — Sumer, Gilgamesh and Huwawa, Version A.

    The guardian of the cedar forest radiates powers described as terrors or auras. His manifestation is followed by sleep, bewilderment, and helplessness among the intruders. Gilgamesh must persuade him to surrender these powers before overcoming him: the guardian’s danger extends beyond bodily strength. 

5. Ninurta returns with a presence that frightens the gods — Sumer, Ninurta’s Return to Nibru.

    Returning victorious, Ninurta approaches with radiance that covers Enlil’s temple. Heaven and earth tremble. A divine messenger goes out to warn him against terrifying his own father. The victorious warrior carries such overwhelming power that even his homecoming requires restraint.

6. Inana clothes herself in terror — Sumer, Inana and Ebih.

    Inana confronts a mountain that refuses to acknowledge her supremacy. The poem describes her adorning herself with terror and fearsome radiance before attacking. Divine appearance is active power here: something she bears into the encounter, inseparable from her capacity to overwhelm opposition. 

7. Gudea encounters a figure as enormous as heaven and earth — Sumer, the Gudea Cylinders.

    In a dream, the ruler sees an immense being with a divine head, birdlike wings, a lower body resembling a floodstorm, and lions beside him. The figure is subsequently identified as Ningirsu. The encounter initiates a temple-building undertaking, but its meaning initially exceeds Gudea’s understanding.

🚨 COLUMBIA, MD: BLACK FLAG BREWING CO. COULD CLOSE AFTER 10 YEARS — PROSPECTIVE BUYERS HAVE SECURED ONLY 20% OF FUNDING.

Black Flag Brewing Company, one of Columbia’s established craft breweries, could shut down November 30 unless a pending sale is completed before its lease expires.

Founder Brian Gaylor is seeking backup buyers as the current deal faces major financing problems.

KEY DETAILS:

▪️ 20% FUNDED: Prospective buyers have secured only about one-fifth of the money needed to purchase the business.

▪️ NOVEMBER 30 DEADLINE: Black Flag’s original 10-year lease expires at the end of November.

▪️ PENDING SALE: Gaylor signed an agreement earlier this year to sell the brewery to another Maryland brewing brand.

▪️ EMPLOYEE JOBS: The proposed arrangement would allow both brands to operate from the Columbia location while retaining existing staff.

▪️ BACKUP BUYERS: Gaylor is seeking alternative offers, prioritizing purchasers willing to keep employees.

▪️ FAMILY DECISION: The birth of Gaylor’s first child this year contributed to his decision to step away from operating the business.

▪️ STILL OPERATING: The brewery remains open, and its owner emphasizes that closure is not yet certain.

Black Flag opened in 2016 at 9315 Snowden River Parkway and became known for its IPAs, Belgian-inspired beers, and specialty releases.

Gaylor says the business has an established sales pipeline and additional brewing capacity, but the approaching lease expiration leaves little time to finalize a deal.

The bottom line: With approximately 80% of the purchase funding still unsecured, Black Flag’s future depends on whether its prospective buyers can complete financing or another buyer steps forward before November 30.

SOURCES: Baltimore Business Journal; Black Flag Brewing Company.

text:
Language: Humanity’s Living Inheritance
Language is one of humanity’s most remarkable creations. It lets people share practical information, tell stories, preserve memory, express identity, and imagine things that do not yet exist. Every language offers a distinct way of organizing sound and meaning—and each changes as people use it.
1. Thousands of languages, many ways to communicate
A widely used 2025 edition of Ethnologue recorded more than 7,000 living languages. The exact total depends on how researchers distinguish a language from a dialect, and new research can change how varieties are classified. One standard count includes languages still used as someone’s first language.
Languages differ in their sounds, vocabulary, and grammar. Some commonly put the verb after the object; others put it before. Some mark grammatical relationships with word endings, while others rely more on word order or separate words. A language may have grammatical categories that English lacks, or express a distinction English makes in another way.
Language is not limited to speech. Sign languages have their own vocabularies and grammars, expressed through hand shapes, movement, facial expression, and space. They are natural human languages, not signed versions of spoken languages. A community may use more than one language, and the same language may be written in more than one script.
2. How children acquire grammar
Children do not need formal grammar lessons to begin learning the language around them. They hear or see language used in everyday life, learn patterns, and gradually use those patterns to understand and form new sentences. Their learning involves more than copying: children generalize, test patterns, and sometimes produce forms they have never heard exactly that way.
For example, an English-speaking child might say “goed” after learning that many past-tense verbs take -ed. The child is applying a pattern to an irregular verb. That kind of mistake can reveal a developing understanding of grammar.
Research on language development examines how the structure of what children hear or see interacts with learners’ abilities to detect patterns and generalize. The details remain an active area of study; researchers continue to debate how much is learned from experience and what expectations children bring to learning.
Children who grow up with more than one language can acquire both. Mixing words or grammatical patterns at times can be part of bilingual development; by itself, it does not mean a child is confused.
3. Languages can disappear
A language is at risk when fewer children learn it and use it in daily life. UNESCO reports that nearly 40% of the world’s languages are endangered, most of them Indigenous languages. The figure is an estimate, and the level of risk varies: some languages still have many speakers but are losing transmission to younger generations, while others have very few speakers left.
Language shift can happen for many reasons. Communities may face pressure to use a dominant language in school, government, work, or public life. Displacement, discrimination, and policies that punish people for speaking their language can weaken its use across generations. Families may also decide that a more widely used language will give children better access to education or employment.
When a language stops being passed on, the loss reaches beyond words. A language can carry place names, family histories, oral literature, specialized knowledge, humor, and ways of describing relationships with the natural world. These are not always impossible to express in other languages, but the original details and associations can be difficult to preserve fully.
Revitalization efforts often support the things that keep a language in everyday use: children learning from elders, community classes, Indigenous-language education, recordings, dictionaries, books, and digital materials. UNESCO’s International Decade of Indigenous Languages (2022–2032) supports efforts to promote language rights, education, digital inclusion, and transmission between generations.
4. Writing systems: ways to make language visible
Writing is a way to represent language, but languages and scripts are not the same thing. A language is a system people use to communicate; a script is a set of written symbols used to record language. One script can be used for several languages, and a language can be written in more than one script.
Writing systems represent language in different ways:
Alphabets generally use letters for consonants and vowels.
Abjads primarily represent consonants, with vowels often omitted or marked separately.
Abugidas use consonant symbols with a default vowel that can be changed by marks.
Syllabaries use symbols for syllables.
Logosyllabaries combine symbols associated with words or meaningful parts of words and symbols representing sounds.
These categories are useful, though real writing systems do not always fit neatly into one box. Japanese, for example, combines kanji with hiragana and katakana, and may also use Latin letters. Unicode’s script guide describes dozens of writing systems and notes that individual scripts can behave differently across languages.
Not every language has a widely used writing system, and spoken language does not depend on writing to be complete. Communities may develop a writing system for a language, adapt an existing script, or use a language primarily through speech or signing. Writing can preserve records beyond a person’s lifetime, but it is only one part of a language’s life.
5. Translation: carrying meaning between languages
Translation makes communication across languages possible. It allows people to share stories, religious and philosophical works, news, scientific findings, laws, and everyday messages. Interpreters do related work in spoken and signed exchanges, conveying meaning in real time.
Translation is more than replacing each word with a corresponding word. Words carry associations, tone, history, and cultural context. Idioms, humor, poetry, and wordplay may depend on features that do not exist in the target language. A translator may need to preserve the sense and effect of an expression even when its literal form cannot be carried across.
This is why different translations of the same work may make different choices. A very literal translation can preserve the original structure but sound unusual; a freer translation may read naturally while making the translator’s interpretation more visible. Good translation involves judgment about what matters most in each passage and what the intended readers need to understand.
6. Words that reach back thousands of years
Historical linguists compare related languages to identify regular sound patterns and reconstruct forms from an ancestral language. A reconstructed form is written with an asterisk to show that it is inferred from evidence rather than directly found in a surviving document.
The University of Texas Indo-European Lexicon illustrates this method with words for three, sister, and mother. Forms in Latin, Greek, Sanskrit, and other related languages can be compared to infer ancestral forms. For example, the familiar resemblance among English mother, Latin māter, Greek mētēr, and Sanskrit mātā is part of a wider pattern—not merely a coincidence of similar-sounding words.
A reconstructed word is not a recording of ancient speech. Linguists infer it from the way related words correspond across languages. The reconstruction offers a strong historical explanation, but the ancient speakers left no direct written record of that particular form.
Words can also survive while changing in sound or meaning. A word’s history may include gradual sound change, new uses, borrowing from another language, or changes in how it is written. A word that looks similar in two languages may be a true relative—or simply a borrowing or coincidence—so etymology depends on patterns and historical evidence, not resemblance alone.
Conclusion
Languages hold human knowledge in a living form. Children learn them through participation in communities; writing systems make some of their words visible across time; translation carries meaning between communities; and historical linguistics traces relationships among words that have changed for thousands of years. The world’s languages are numerous, varied, and vulnerable—and their future depends in large part on whether people can keep learning and using them in everyday life.

text:
October 13, 1926 — Why Were Foreign Warships in China's Civil War?

Why were American warships operating deep inside China during its civil war?

In September 1926, the British steamer Kiangwo, carrying wounded people and British passengers from Wanhsien, came under heavy fire between Wuchang and Hanyang on the Yangtze River.

The American destroyer USS Stewart (DD-224) intervened, rescuing wounded passengers and British nationals and transporting them to Hankow.

On October 13, 1926, Britain formally expressed its gratitude to the United States for the swift assistance provided by the American warship.

But this rescue was part of a much larger story.

During the 1920s, American and other foreign warships operated along China's rivers to protect their nationals, shipping, and commercial interests. These activities were rooted in a system of unequal treaties and foreign privileges increasingly challenged by Chinese nationalism.

The USS Stewart rescue revealed the complexity of that era: a humanitarian act carried out amid civil war, foreign intervention, and China's struggle for sovereignty.

A century later, one diplomatic document offers a glimpse into the tensions that shaped modern China.

https://t.co/I06t01Xo2e

Historical Reconstruction Notice

This documentary combines authentic historical photographs, archival documents, and AI-assisted visual reconstructions.

Reconstructed scenes are illustrative and should not be interpreted as original footage of the events. Ship movements, rescue activities, public gatherings, and some environmental details have been recreated for historical storytelling.

References

U.S. Department of State, Foreign Relations of the United States, 1926, Volume I, Document 507 — British diplomatic communication dated October 13, 1926.

Naval History and Heritage Command — Historical photographs and records of U.S. Navy vessels operating in Chinese waters.

Historical Photographs of China, University of Bristol — Historical photographs of Hankow and Yangtze River shipping.

University of California, Berkeley — Julean Arnold photographic collection, China, 1920s.

🇺🇸 In 2014, Chicago woman Dawn Michelle Hunt thought she had won the trip of a lifetime.

She received an email saying she had won an all-expenses-paid trip to Australia. 

At first she was suspicious, but after checking out the company she believed the offer was legitimate.

The trip included a stopover in China to collect prize documents and designer handbags she was told to take with her to Australia.

Then, at the airport in Guangzhou, security searched the handbags and found more than 4.5 pounds of methamphetamine sewn into the linings. 

Hunt was arrested. 

Chinese authorities later acknowledged she had likely been used as an unwitting drug mule, but the court still convicted her saying she “should have known better”

She was originally sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve, which was later reduced to life in prison.

More than a decade on, she remains locked up in Guangdong Women’s Prison and her family continues to fight for her release.

text:
Yes Candace, some people always accuse others of the uncomfortable truth they refuse to face —

“Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.” @CocaCamhi

text:
Will Spencer: From Outside, America Looking In
The United States of America is a big country. We’re home to 344 million people, the third most populous nation, after India and China. We occupy 3.8 million square miles, also third largest, this time behind Russia and Canada. We span six time zones from Hawaii to New York City and are ringed by more than 95,000 miles of shoreline. And in no other nation on earth can you find such a diversity of ecosystems. From the arctic tundra of Alaska to the bayous of Louisiana, from the misty rainforests of Washington to the sun-scorched deserts of Arizona, from the alpine peaks of the Rockies to the steamy swamps of the Everglades, in our one country we find the glorious natural beauty of God’s creation in microcosm.

The strength of this diversity obscures a weakness: if America has so much to offer, why go anywhere else? An estimated two-thirds of Americans (around 64%) have never traveled outside North America (including Mexico and Canada), and 11% have never even left their home state. Our country is large enough, varied enough, and most importantly abundant enough that most of us never feel the need to leave.

This is hardly a lamentable problem. But I want to suggest that there are things about America we cannot see from inside it. The abundance that gratifies us also surrounds us, and a man surrounded by something often struggles to take its full measure.

Which is why I believe that to really understand our country, to know what it is and what it isn’t, you have to leave. You have to stand somewhere else and look back.

text:
Image and Video Analysis: Can We Verify What We See?

A video does not have to be AI-generated to mislead someone. Sometimes, the footage is genuine, but the date, location or event attached to it is false. This makes image and video verification a much bigger problem than just deepfake detection.

During Hurricane Milton in October 2024, a video shared as footage of traffic in Florida was traced by Reuters to an earlier post showing flooding in Mumbai. In May 2023, a fake image of an explosion near the Pentagon spread online and briefly unsettled US markets. One involved real footage used in the wrong context; the other involved a fabricated scene.

Technically, these require different approaches.

A useful verification pipeline could begin with provenance. EXIF metadata, video container information, timestamps and C2PA Content Credentials can be inspected for clues about origin and edits. C2PA uses cryptographic signatures to make provenance claims tamper-evident, but it cannot establish that the event shown actually happened. Metadata can also be missing after a file is shared.

Next comes content retrieval. Scene-change detection can split a video into representative keyframes. Perceptual hashing (pHash) and Hamming-distance matching help find near-duplicate images, even after resizing or compression. Vision-language embeddings can retrieve visually similar scenes, although a high similarity score is not proof that two images show the same event.

The next layer is visual and temporal analysis. OCR can extract signboards and street names; landmark matching and satellite imagery can support geolocation. Compression patterns, noise residuals and inconsistent lighting may offer clues to manipulation. For video, optical flow and frame-to-frame consistency can help identify suspicious motion, while audio-visual synchronisation can be examined where speech is involved.

There is a catch: recompression, cropping and poor lighting can create similar artefacts. Domain shift is another challenge: a detector trained on known manipulations may fail on new generators or compression settings. One confidence score is not a verdict.

What interests me most is how these signals can be combined into an evidence-based system: linking each finding to its source, recording contradictions and expressing uncertainty instead of forcing every result into “real” or “fake”.

This could be valuable in journalism, investigations, disaster response, financial risk and public safety, where the cost of getting the context wrong can be significant.

I would love to connect with researchers, startups and people working on computer vision, multimodal AI, digital forensics and media provenance to discuss how such systems can be built and evaluated at scale.

How should we measure verification quality when the original source is unavailable?

#ComputerVision #DigitalForensics #MultimodalAI #MediaVerification

text:
@GHWTowler talks about this here

Sergei Lavrov had his line ready. Sitting beside the British Foreign Secretary in Moscow in December 2017, he told the press that his guest had already conceded Russia hadn’t interfered in the referendum. Boris Johnson cut across him. “Not successfully,“ he said, and then said it again, in case the interpreter had ignored it.

Lavrov, who was already a Russian deputy foreign minister while Johnson was in Brussels inventing straight bananas, purred that the poor man feared for his reputation at home. Johnson said it was Lavrov’s reputation that worried him. Then he went off to lay red roses on the bridge where Boris Nemtsov was shot.

Those two words were the British position for the best part of a decade. Russia tried. Russia failed. Nobody in government seriously disputed either half, and Carole Cadwallader and her Remain diehards who did were mostly ignored.

Then on Sunday our new PM Andy Burnham went on a podcast.

The podcast was The Rest Is Politics, which is to say Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart, which is to say the warmest bath in British broadcasting for a Prime Minister who wants to talk about rejoining the EU. Burnham had just come back from Berlin, where Friedrich Merz had been telling him the AfD were Moscow’s creatures. He offered his hosts something to match.

On arriving in Downing Street, he said, he’d asked whether Russia interfered in 2016, and “I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.” He wanted it on the record, he explained, so that voters in France and Germany would understand that some of their politics is instigated by our enemies.

Who gave him the answer? He didn’t say. What evidence? None offered. What kind of interference, and did it change a single vote? Silence. HuffPost ran it as the first time a British Prime Minister had confirmed Russia’s role in Brexit, which is what anyone would take from it, and what it was meant to sound like.

By breakfast on Monday it had come apart. Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, was put up on LBC and said what the Foreign Office has always said. “We know what the result was. I don’t think they’ve succeeded in their efforts.” He leaned on the security minister, Dan Jarvis, who had already given evidence that Russia attempted and failed. So a minister of the Crown went on morning radio and corrected his own Prime Minister with Boris Johnson’s two words. Lavrov must have enjoyed that.

Number 10 followed him into the bunker. The spokesman called it inconceivable that Russia hadn’t tried to use the referendum, agreed it hadn’t succeeded, and added that the Prime Minister absolutely accepts the result. Nigel Farage, in Dover, was less diplomatic and called Burnham a liar.

Then came the dispatch box. Kemi Badenoch reminded the House that the head of MI5 said in 2018 that he’d seen no evidence Russia influenced the result, and asked whether the Prime Minister now thought it illegitimate. Burnham wincing, told her he had “implied no such thing”, that he was not reopening the referendum, and then changed the subject to Russian meddling in the 2019 general election.

Implied. A man who says he asked a question and got a clear yes has not implied anything. He has asserted it. What he left out was the word successfully, and he left it out for a reason. You don’t warn French and German voters about interference that failed. The whole point of the remark, as he framed it himself, was that it worked here and might work there. Unsay that and the podcast clip is a Prime Minister telling foreign electorates that Russia tried something in Britain ten years ago and got nowhere, which isn’t much of a warning.

Johnson, never one to leave a stage to someone else, walked back on. When he became Foreign Secretary in the weeks after the vote, he says, the intelligence services told him they had no evidence of foreign interference. So one of two things is true. Either the agencies have changed their assessment since, in which case Parliament and the rest of us would like to see the new one, or the Prime Minister is misrepresenting what he was told.

It’s a neat fork, and Burnham can’t sit comfortably on either prong. If the assessment has changed, what changed it, ten years on? If it hasn’t, he dressed up a routine briefing (Russia probes everything, Russia probed this) as a revelation, for a foreign audience.

I’ll be fair to the other side, because the record deserves it. The Intelligence and Security Committee’s Russia report in 2020 was scathing that nobody had gone looking. MI5’s first written submission to the inquiry ran to six lines. Johnson’s government replied that it had seen no evidence of successful interference and that a retrospective assessment wasn’t necessary, and you can argue that “we found nothing” sits awkwardly beside “we didn’t look”. Remainacs have argued it for ten years.

But look at what was actually found in the open. The Commons Library records that RT spent $1,031.99 promoting six referendum posts during the regulated campaign. Vote Leave was allowed to spend £7 million. Seventeen point four million people voted to leave. Moscow’s documented outlay comes to rather less than a hundredth of a cent per Leave voter, and the Pembrokeshire Herald, of all papers, has noticed that much of the Russian-linked online chatter researchers identified came after polls closed. That is the great Kremlin operation that decided Britain’s future.

Of course Russia tried. The ISC said Moscow regards Britain as one of its top Western intelligence targets, and I’d be mildly insulted if it didn’t. A hostile state with a large foreign intelligence service and a state broadcaster will push whatever divides its rivals, in every election and every referendum, from Edinburgh in 2014 to Washington in 2016. Expecting otherwise is like being shocked that foxes visit the henhouse.

And so, I’m quite sure, do we. The Foreign Office ran the Information Research Department for thirty years after 1948, feeding carefully sourced stories to friendly journalists from Lagos to Jakarta. When the Integrity Initiative’s papers leaked in 2018 they showed a Foreign Office-funded outfit cultivating networks of journalists and academics across Europe. Nobody in Whitehall or in Moscow fainted. The BBC World Service is paid for by the same department. Statecraft has always included the manufacture of opinion abroad, and Britain was rather good at it.

So was it naivety or stupidity?

The naivety would be to imagine that “Russia interfered” is news. Every intelligence officer in Europe assumes it of every vote. The stupidity is to announce it as news, in a form your own minister has to correct before the nine o’clock pips, and then to stand at the despatch box claiming you never said it.

I don’t think Burnham is naive, and he isn’t stupid. I think he found the line useful. He had just been in Berlin making the case for drawing Britain back towards Brussels, and Merz had handed him a story about Russian puppets on the German right. Seventeen million British Leave voters made a handy exhibit for it. Nobody asked them whether they minded being cast as Moscow’s dupes to help a German chancellor with his domestic problem.

Watch what the taint is for. If the 2016 result was nudged by Moscow, then it’s a little less sacred, and a little less sacred is all you need to skip asking the people again.

Emily Thornberry has now floated the idea that a line in a Labour manifesto would do the work of a second referendum. Jess Phillips told the Cliveden Literary Festival at the weekend that she’d love rejoining in the next manifesto, and that she doesn’t “run towards having another referendum”. Burnham himself told the BBC after conference that a future referendum pledge was possible, and has conspicuously declined to promise one.

Thornberry has form here, though not the form she’d like remembered. On the Marr programme in November 2018 she said, flatly, “We had a referendum and the results of the referendum ought to be abided by.” On Question Time around the same time she predicted that a second vote would come back Leave, with the public asking whether politicians had heard them the first time. Her party’s 2024 manifesto promised to make Brexit work, which most voters took to mean making it work rather than quietly unpicking it.

I’m no friend of referenda. They’re blunt instruments and they let MPs dodge the jobs they’re paid for. But once you’ve asked the country a direct question and it has answered, only the country can take the answer back. A manifesto is a bundle of three hundred promises voted on for a hundred reasons, and nobody has ever been elected on paragraph forty-seven. Treating one line of it as a mandate to reverse 17.4 million votes is the politics of the small print, and Labour knows it, which is why they need Russia.

If Burnham wants a Russian influence campaign with a paper trail, Maurice Cousins has been pointing at one. It isn’t about a vote ten years ago. It’s about the gas under Lancashire.

Russia’s interest is simple arithmetic. Every cubic metre of shale gas Europe produces for itself is a cubic metre it doesn’t buy from Gazprom, and a Europe that heats itself is a Europe Moscow can’t freeze. So in June 2014 the then Secretary General of NATO, Anders Fogh Rasmussen, told an audience at Chatham House that allies had reported Russia engaging with environmental groups campaigning against shale gas, to keep Europe dependent on Russian imports.

The Americans went further, and they put it in writing. The January 2017 assessment by the US Director of National Intelligence, the same document that set out Russia’s meddling in the presidential election, noted that RT runs anti-fracking programming, and read it as Moscow worrying about American shale and Gazprom’s profits. A House Science Committee staff report in 2018 followed the trail into social media. RT was not shy about bringing the campaign to England either. In January 2017 it ran a breathless piece about frackers threatening the Major Oak in Sherwood Forest, Robin Hood’s old hideout. Putin as protector of the greenwood.

I’ll concede the limits, as I did on 2016. Nobody has shown evidence Russian money reaching British anti-fracking groups. The Ferret’s fact-checkers rated that claim unsupported, the green groups denied it, and Rasmussen later called his remark an interpretation. But the propaganda is documented by the intelligence agencies of our closest ally, and the motive is written on every gas bill in the country.

Burnham might have asked Merz, while he was in Berlin, who handed Moscow the keys to Germany’s gas in the first place. It wasn’t the AfD. Gerhard Schröder signed the Nord Stream deal with Putin in 2005, in his last weeks as an SPD chancellor, and spent his retirement chairing Nord Stream’s shareholders’ committee and sitting on Rosneft’s board. Angela Merkel, leader of Merz’s own CDU, opened the first pipeline in 2011, defended Nord Stream 2 for years as a purely private enterprise, closed the nuclear stations after Fukushima and presided over a law in 2016 that all but banned shale fracking. By 2021 Russia was supplying 55% of Germany’s imported gas, up from 39% a decade before. Asked in 2022 whether she regretted any of it, Merkel said no, and explained that cheap Russian gas had let Germany phase out nuclear and coal.

Read that answer again. The green transition was paid for in roubles, and the people who signed the cheques sat in the chancellery, not on the fringes. When Donald Trump warned the UN General Assembly in 2018 that Germany was making itself dependent on Russian energy, the German delegation was filmed smirking. Merz now tells a British Prime Minister that Russia’s friends sit on the AfD benches. Russia’s most useful friends in Germany wore SPD and CDU rosettes, and they were doing exactly what RT asked.

And look how it turned out. Labour went into the 2024 election promising to ban fracking for good. The Bowland shale stays where it is. Britain buys gas from Norway’s pipelines and from tankers out of Qatar and Texas, at whatever price the world sets that winter. Whether or not Moscow lifted a finger, it got exactly the British energy policy RT spent years asking for, and Burnham’s government is the one delivering it.

So here’s a question for the next time he walks into Number 10 asking what the Russians have been up to. Not the referendum. Ask about the shale.

“Not successfully,” Johnson told Lavrov. Nobody can say that about fracking
