Anybody who doesn't follow @GHWTowler free substack writings is missing out on such a good thing. Every article is a gem. Please read and get his articles delivered free to your inbox. Here's another doozy.

Sergei Lavrov had his line ready. Sitting beside the British Foreign Secretary in Moscow in December 2017, he told the press that his guest had already conceded Russia hadn’t interfered in the referendum. Boris Johnson cut across him. “Not successfully,“ he said, and then said it again, in case the interpreter had ignored it.

Lavrov, who was already a Russian deputy foreign minister while Johnson was in Brussels inventing straight bananas, purred that the poor man feared for his reputation at home. Johnson said it was Lavrov’s reputation that worried him. Then he went off to lay red roses on the bridge where Boris Nemtsov was shot.

Those two words were the British position for the best part of a decade. Russia tried. Russia failed. Nobody in government seriously disputed either half, and Carole Cadwallader and her Remain diehards who did were mostly ignored.

Then on Sunday our new PM Andy Burnham went on a podcast.

The podcast was The Rest Is Politics, which is to say Alastair Campbell and Rory Stewart, which is to say the warmest bath in British broadcasting for a Prime Minister who wants to talk about rejoining the EU. Burnham had just come back from Berlin, where Friedrich Merz had been telling him the AfD were Moscow’s creatures. He offered his hosts something to match.

On arriving in Downing Street, he said, he’d asked whether Russia interfered in 2016, and “I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.” He wanted it on the record, he explained, so that voters in France and Germany would understand that some of their politics is instigated by our enemies.

Who gave him the answer? He didn’t say. What evidence? None offered. What kind of interference, and did it change a single vote? Silence. HuffPost ran it as the first time a British Prime Minister had confirmed Russia’s role in Brexit, which is what anyone would take from it, and what it was meant to sound like.

By breakfast on Monday it had come apart. Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, was put up on LBC and said what the Foreign Office has always said. “We know what the result was. I don’t think they’ve succeeded in their efforts.” He leaned on the security minister, Dan Jarvis, who had already given evidence that Russia attempted and failed. So a minister of the Crown went on morning radio and corrected his own Prime Minister with Boris Johnson’s two words. Lavrov must have enjoyed that.

Number 10 followed him into the bunker. The spokesman called it inconceivable that Russia hadn’t tried to use the referendum, agreed it hadn’t succeeded, and added that the Prime Minister absolutely accepts the result. Nigel Farage, in Dover, was less diplomatic and called Burnham a liar.

Then came the dispatch box. Kemi Badenoch reminded the House that the head of MI5 said in 2018 that he’d seen no evidence Russia influenced the result, and asked whether the Prime Minister now thought it illegitimate. Burnham wincing, told her he had “implied no such thing”, that he was not reopening the referendum, and then changed the subject to Russian meddling in the 2019 general election.

Implied. A man who says he asked a question and got a clear yes has not implied anything. He has asserted it. What he left out was the word successfully, and he left it out for a reason. You don’t warn French and German voters about interference that failed. The whole point of the remark, as he framed it himself, was that it worked here and might work there. Unsay that and the podcast clip is a Prime Minister telling foreign electorates that Russia tried something in Britain ten years ago and got nowhere, which isn’t much of a warning.

Johnson, never one to leave a stage to someone else, walked back on. When he became Foreign Secretary in the weeks after the vote, he says, the intelligence services told him they had no evidence of foreign interference. So one of two things is true. Either the agencies have changed their assessment since, in which case Parliament and the rest of us would like to see the new one, or the Prime Minister is misrepresenting what he was told.

It’s a neat fork, and Burnham can’t sit comfortably on either prong. If the assessment has changed, what changed it, ten years on? If it hasn’t, he dressed up a routine briefing (Russia probes everything, Russia probed this) as a revelation, for a foreign audience.

I’ll be fair to the other side, because the record deserves it. The Intelligence and Security Committee’s Russia report in 2020 was scathing that nobody had gone looking. MI5’s first written submission to the inquiry ran to six lines. Johnson’s government replied that it had seen no evidence of successful interference and that a retrospective assessment wasn’t necessary, and you can argue that “we found nothing” sits awkwardly beside “we didn’t look”. Remainacs have argued it for ten years.

But look at what was actually found in the open. The Commons Library records that RT spent $1,031.99 promoting six referendum posts during the regulated campaign. Vote Leave was allowed to spend £7 million. Seventeen point four million people voted to leave. Moscow’s documented outlay comes to rather less than a hundredth of a cent per Leave voter, and the Pembrokeshire Herald, of all papers, has noticed that much of the Russian-linked online chatter researchers identified came after polls closed. That is the great Kremlin operation that decided Britain’s future.

Of course Russia tried. The ISC said Moscow regards Britain as one of its top Western intelligence targets, and I’d be mildly insulted if it didn’t. A hostile state with a large foreign intelligence service and a state broadcaster will push whatever divides its rivals, in every election and every referendum, from Edinburgh in 2014 to Washington in 2016. Expecting otherwise is like being shocked that foxes visit the henhouse.

And so, I’m quite sure, do we. The Foreign Office ran the Information Research Department for thirty years after 1948, feeding carefully sourced stories to friendly journalists from Lagos to Jakarta. When the Integrity Initiative’s papers leaked in 2018 they showed a Foreign Office-funded outfit cultivating networks of journalists and academics across Europe. Nobody in Whitehall or in Moscow fainted. The BBC World Service is paid for by the same department. Statecraft has always included the manufacture of opinion abroad, and Britain was rather good at it.

So was it naivety or stupidity?

The naivety would be to imagine that “Russia interfered” is news. Every intelligence officer in Europe assumes it of every vote. The stupidity is to announce it as news, in a form your own minister has to correct before the nine o’clock pips, and then to stand at the despatch box claiming you never said it.

I don’t think Burnham is naive, and he isn’t stupid. I think he found the line useful. He had just been in Berlin making the case for drawing Britain back towards Brussels, and Merz had handed him a story about Russian puppets on the German right. Seventeen million British Leave voters made a handy exhibit for it. Nobody asked them whether they minded being cast as Moscow’s dupes to help a German chancellor with his domestic problem.

Watch what the taint is for. If the 2016 result was nudged by Moscow, then it’s a little less sacred, and a little less sacred is all you need to skip asking the people again.

Emily Thornberry has now floated the idea that a line in a Labour manifesto would do the work of a second referendum. Jess Phillips told the Cliveden Literary Festival at the weekend that she’d love rejoining in the next manifesto, and that she doesn’t “run towards having another referendum”. Burnham himself told the BBC after conference that a future referendum pledge was possible, and has conspicuously declined to promise one.

Thornberry has form here, though not the form she’d like remembered. On the Marr programme in November 2018 she said, flatly, “We had a referendum and the results of the referendum ought to be abided by.” On Question Time around the same time she predicted that a second vote would come back Leave, with the public asking whether politicians had heard them the first time. Her party’s 2024 manifesto promised to make Brexit work, which most voters took to mean making it work rather than quietly unpicking it.

I’m no friend of referenda. They’re blunt instruments and they let MPs dodge the jobs they’re paid for. But once you’ve asked the country a direct question and it has answered, only the country can take the answer back. A manifesto is a bundle of three hundred promises voted on for a hundred reasons, and nobody has ever been elected on paragraph forty-seven. Treating one line of it as a mandate to reverse 17.4 million votes is the politics of the small print, and Labour knows it, which is why they need Russia.

If Burnham wants a Russian influence campaign with a paper trail, Maurice Cousins has been pointing at one. It isn’t about a vote ten years ago. It’s about the gas under Lancashire.

Russia’s interest is simple arithmetic. Every cubic metre of shale gas Europe produces for itself is a cubic metre it doesn’t buy from Gazprom, and a Europe that heats itself is a Europe Moscow can’t freeze. So in June 2014 the then Secretary General of NATO, Anders Fogh Rasmussen, told an audience at Chatham House that allies had reported Russia engaging with environmental groups campaigning against shale gas, to keep Europe dependent on Russian imports.

The Americans went further, and they put it in writing. The January 2017 assessment by the US Director of National Intelligence, the same document that set out Russia’s meddling in the presidential election, noted that RT runs anti-fracking programming, and read it as Moscow worrying about American shale and Gazprom’s profits. A House Science Committee staff report in 2018 followed the trail into social media. RT was not shy about bringing the campaign to England either. In January 2017 it ran a breathless piece about frackers threatening the Major Oak in Sherwood Forest, Robin Hood’s old hideout. Putin as protector of the greenwood.

I’ll concede the limits, as I did on 2016. Nobody has shown evidence Russian money reaching British anti-fracking groups. The Ferret’s fact-checkers rated that claim unsupported, the green groups denied it, and Rasmussen later called his remark an interpretation. But the propaganda is documented by the intelligence agencies of our closest ally, and the motive is written on every gas bill in the country.

Burnham might have asked Merz, while he was in Berlin, who handed Moscow the keys to Germany’s gas in the first place. It wasn’t the AfD. Gerhard Schröder signed the Nord Stream deal with Putin in 2005, in his last weeks as an SPD chancellor, and spent his retirement chairing Nord Stream’s shareholders’ committee and sitting on Rosneft’s board. Angela Merkel, leader of Merz’s own CDU, opened the first pipeline in 2011, defended Nord Stream 2 for years as a purely private enterprise, closed the nuclear stations after Fukushima and presided over a law in 2016 that all but banned shale fracking. By 2021 Russia was supplying 55% of Germany’s imported gas, up from 39% a decade before. Asked in 2022 whether she regretted any of it, Merkel said no, and explained that cheap Russian gas had let Germany phase out nuclear and coal.

Read that answer again. The green transition was paid for in roubles, and the people who signed the cheques sat in the chancellery, not on the fringes. When Donald Trump warned the UN General Assembly in 2018 that Germany was making itself dependent on Russian energy, the German delegation was filmed smirking. Merz now tells a British Prime Minister that Russia’s friends sit on the AfD benches. Russia’s most useful friends in Germany wore SPD and CDU rosettes, and they were doing exactly what RT asked.

And look how it turned out. Labour went into the 2024 election promising to ban fracking for good. The Bowland shale stays where it is. Britain buys gas from Norway’s pipelines and from tankers out of Qatar and Texas, at whatever price the world sets that winter. Whether or not Moscow lifted a finger, it got exactly the British energy policy RT spent years asking for, and Burnham’s government is the one delivering it.

So here’s a question for the next time he walks into Number 10 asking what the Russians have been up to. Not the referendum. Ask about the shale.

Europe Buys Israel’s Weapons. Israel Builds America’s Defence Industry at the Expense of Its Own Independence.

👇 A Line of State statecraft note on defence industrial sovereignty, first published in Hebrew at Walla Money (@WallaNews) and now in English at @TimesofIsrael.

In 2025, Europe accounted for 36 per cent of Israel’s defence export contracts. North America accounted for just 13 per cent. Israel’s customers have shifted. Its industrial priorities have not.

Washington’s strategy is clear: foreign arms purchases and investment should expand American production. By 2028, US military aid will no longer finance Israeli domestic procurement. Yet Israeli defence companies continue investing in American facilities even where American demand cannot justify the expense.

European alternatives are sometimes suppressed inside those companies before reaching Israel’s Ministry of Defence. Washington need not exercise a veto when Israeli management does it first.

Greece offers a different model.

Its approximately €3 billion Achilles Shield programme integrates Israeli air and missile defence systems with Greek industrial participation and technology transfer. It could anchor a European hub for development, manufacturing and maintenance, turning Greek demand into shared industrial capacity.

That also changes the political equation. Excluding an Israeli exporter is easier than excluding technology embedded in European employment, suppliers and production.

The EU’s €150 billion SAFE loan programme reinforces this shift. It finances genuine European industrial capacity, not subsidiaries with European addresses. Sensitive systems require sufficient local design authority. Israel must preserve its intellectual property, future revenues and enforceable priority for wartime production.

A European factory that cannot supply Israel in war is an export asset, not strategic depth.

Nor does Achilles Shield eliminate American approval requirements for jointly developed systems. Israel needs a parallel missile-defence architecture it can develop, manufacture and export independently. BARAK MX demonstrates the principle: international cooperation that creates capability without surrendering control over its successor.

Meanwhile, Europe is integrating Ukrainian technology and production into its defence industry. It is building alternatives, not waiting for Israel.

America puts its own industrial interests first. Israel’s strategic failure is putting its own second.

text:
🌍 GLOBAL MARKET RECAP — OCTOBER 13, 2026
Chips, Earnings & CPI Week | Updated around 08:15 CEST

1️⃣ GLOBAL EQUITIES — THE AI TRADE CRACKS IN SEOUL WHILE WALL STREET ROTATES INTO VALUE
Global equities open Tuesday on the defensive, and this time the pressure is coming less from the battlefield than from the semiconductor supply chain. Wall Street finished Monday mixed: the Dow gained 0.38% to 51,850, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.06% to 7,807 and the Nasdaq fell 0.44% to 27,246, as a U.S. chip index dropped about 2.7% and higher oil prices limited risk appetite. The rotation was visible at sector level, with investors moving toward value and financials ahead of bank earnings. Overnight the weakness turned into a sharp sell-off in Asia, led by South Korea, and Nasdaq 100 futures were down roughly 0.5% in early trading. The S&P 500 celebrated the fourth anniversary of the current bull market on Monday, but from a starting point almost 120% above its 2022 low, the market now needs earnings to justify valuations rather than narratives to extend them. This week will provide that test through bank results, Wednesday's inflation data and Thursday's TSMC report.

2️⃣ U.S. MACRO — CPI AND BANK EARNINGS WILL MEASURE THE REAL DAMAGE OF EXPENSIVE ENERGY
The American economy enters a decisive 48 hours. Today JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and BlackRock open the third-quarter earnings season, followed by Bank of America and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday. Their reports matter beyond the financial sector: net interest income will show how banks are coping with the Federal Reserve's September hike, credit provisions and card charge-offs will reveal whether consumers are cracking after a weak September jobs report, and investment-banking commentary will indicate whether corporate confidence survives the energy shock. On Wednesday the September CPI is expected to show headline inflation around 3.6% year on year, up from 3.4% in August, with energy as the main driver, followed by producer prices on Thursday. Household sentiment is already fragile, and U.S. diesel still costs around $6.28 per gallon. A hot inflation print would strengthen the case for additional tightening; a softer reading would support the view that the energy shock has not yet become a broad inflationary spiral.

3️⃣ BONDS & FED — THE CASH TREASURY MARKET REOPENS AND MUST CONFIRM WHAT FUTURES ONLY SUGGESTED
After Monday's Columbus Day closure, the cash Treasury market reopens today and will finally price a weekend of military escalation, contradictory diplomacy and higher oil. The U.S. 10-year yield was last quoted around 5.24%, close to the highest levels in roughly two decades, after the 30-year briefly touched 5.70% last week. The Federal Reserve, led by Chair Kevin Warsh, raised its target range to 3.75–4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023. Futures had moved to price a pause at the October 27–28 meeting, with hike odds falling to around 20% after a solid auction and the September minutes, but a further move before year-end remains heavily priced. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack argued that smaller, more frequent adjustments can help anchor inflation expectations, without explicitly backing an October hike. The key issue is the long end: persistent deficits, energy-driven inflation and the financing needs of AI infrastructure are pushing term premia higher regardless of the policy rate.

4️⃣ EUROPE & FX — EUROPEAN STOCKS RESIST, BUT THE DOLLAR REMAINS THE DEFENSIVE ASSET OF CHOICE
European markets showed surprising resilience on Monday. The Stoxx 600 rose about 0.6%, with the DAX and FTSE 100 up roughly 0.8% and the CAC 40 up about 0.3%, led by banks and utilities, despite the attacks on Saudi airports and higher crude prices. Investors also welcomed the U.S.–Russia diesel arrangement, which may ease Europe's refined-product shortage at the margin. Company news was mixed: Volkswagen reported a 14.3% fall in third-quarter deliveries, mainly because of China. In currencies, the Dollar Index closed Monday up about 0.3% and trades near 102.6, close to its strongest level in around 18 months, while EUR/USD is near $1.116 and GBP/USD near $1.321. Analysts describe demand for "defensive USD exposure" as the dominant force. For Europe, the combination of a strong dollar, oil priced in dollars and fragile French public finances remains an imported inflation problem that the ECB can observe but cannot fully neutralise.

5️⃣ ASIA — KOREA'S MEMORY SELL-OFF TRIGGERS THE FIRST CIRCUIT BREAKER IN TWO MONTHS
Asia is the epicentre of this morning's risk aversion. South Korea's Kospi fell more than 5% and broke below 6,000 intraday, triggering a sell-side sidecar for the first time since August 19. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix dropped between roughly 5% and 9%, while SK Square lost more than 11%. Foreign investors sold about 1.8 trillion won of local shares in the morning session, while retail investors bought the dip. The trigger was China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, which said it will unveil next-generation server DRAM products within the year, raising fears of tougher competition in one of the most profitable segments of the AI supply chain. Japan's Nikkei fell about 2.3% as traders returned from a long weekend, Taiwan's TAIEX lost about 1.2% and the MSCI Asia-Pacific index is heading for its weakest close since mid-August. In India, the Reserve Bank launched its most aggressive currency defence in more than a decade, while the yen holds around 158.4 per dollar under constant intervention risk.

6️⃣ OIL, GOLD & COMMODITIES — BRENT RETURNS ABOVE $105 AS THE CEASEFIRE NARRATIVE FADES
Monday's oil reversal proved short-lived. Brent climbed back above $105 per barrel, a two-week high, and trades around $105.8 this morning, down about 0.8% in Asia; WTI is near $93. The weekend's diplomatic optimism faded as the Kremlin declined to confirm the energy ceasefire, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued and Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed strikes on tankers near Hormuz. The market is pricing not only lost barrels but the cost of transporting them: insurance premiums, rerouting, delayed cargoes and refinery bottlenecks. Gold closed Monday around $4,195 per ounce, down about 0.5%, as a stronger dollar and elevated real yields offset geopolitical demand. This is the uncomfortable configuration for central banks: energy-driven inflation pressure combined with weaker growth expectations, a mix that limits their room to support the economy.

7️⃣ GEOPOLITICS — THE HOUTHI CAMPAIGN AGAINST SAUDI ARABIA IS BECOMING A REGIONAL TEST
The Houthi campaign against Saudi airports has killed at least 20 people in a week, according to CBS News, including 13 in Saturday's strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport. Saudi authorities extended the airport's closure until Saturday, the coalition reported intercepting ballistic missiles aimed at the Khamis Mushait air base, Etihad cancelled Saudi flights and Delta postponed its planned Atlanta–Riyadh route to March 2027. President Trump said the Houthis are "misbehaving very badly" but has not yet announced whether the United States will join strikes in Yemen. Pakistan pledged to honour its defence commitments to Riyadh, the UK said it would consider further Saudi requests, and Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered to facilitate Saudi–Houthi talks.

On the wider war, Tehran described Washington's latest response to its seven-point proposal on reopening Hormuz as "inadequate", while acknowledging that some conditions had been accepted. The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports remains in force, and reports on tanker attacks near the Strait remain contradictory between the IRGC's claims and UKMTO's assessments.

In Europe, the Kremlin did not confirm the "energy ceasefire" announced by Washington. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said only that "contacts are ongoing", while Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia would not "fall for assurances and promises once again". Until both sides confirm reciprocal terms, the ceasefire remains a political announcement rather than an operational reality.

8️⃣ ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE — COMPETITION, NOT DEMAND, IS THE NEW RISK FOR THE CHIP TRADE
This morning's Korean sell-off highlights a shift in how markets assess artificial intelligence. Until recently, the main question was whether demand for AI infrastructure would remain strong. Now investors are also asking who will capture the margins. A credible Chinese challenger in server DRAM threatens the pricing power that has made memory one of the most profitable parts of the AI supply chain, and Monday's weakness in Micron and the U.S. chip index shows that the concern is global. Rising borrowing costs add another layer: with long-term yields above 5%, the financing of data centres, power capacity and chips becomes more expensive and future profits are discounted more heavily. Thursday's TSMC results, alongside ASML's report, will be critical. Analysts expect another record quarter, but forward guidance on capital expenditure, pricing, capacity and customer concentration will matter more than the headline profit. The AI cycle is not over, but it is entering a phase in which valuation discipline becomes as important as growth.

9️⃣ CRYPTO — BITCOIN LOSES $82K AS LEVERAGE AND ETF OUTFLOWS MEET RISING YIELDS
Bitcoin failed to hold Monday's recovery. After trading near $84.2K, BTC slipped to around $81.4K overnight, Ethereum fell to about $2.43K and Solana dropped roughly 7.5% toward $104. According to CoinGlass data, about $771 million of positions were liquidated in 24 hours, around $686 million of them long bets, confirming that leverage had rebuilt during the weekend bounce. Flows are also weakening: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $681 million of net outflows last week, their worst week since late June, while spot Ether ETFs lost about $542 million. Analysts link the move to elevated Treasury yields, a stronger dollar, the Korean equity sell-off and positioning ahead of CPI. Structurally, $80K remains the key support to monitor, while the $85K–87.4K area is now a more distant resistance. For long-term accumulation, BTC, ETH and SOL should continue to be assessed through disciplined DCA and portfolio allocation, kept separate from speculative trading exposure. In this phase, Bitcoin is trading as a liquidity asset, not as a geopolitical safe haven.

🔟 MARKET STRUCTURE — THE MARKET IS MOVING FROM GEOPOLITICAL HEADLINES TO HARD DATA
The weekend's lesson was that diplomatic headlines can move prices for a few hours, but they cannot change the underlying conditions. This week, the market's focus shifts from announcements to measurable evidence: inflation, bank balance sheets, corporate guidance and Treasury demand.

The principal transmission mechanism remains Geopolitics → Energy & Shipping → Inflation → Central Banks → Sovereign Yields → Dollar → Equities → Crypto. Alongside it, a second chain is becoming more fragile: AI Demand → Chip Pricing Power → Infrastructure Financing → Earnings & Valuations.

This week I am monitoring Brent between $100 and $108, the U.S. 10-year Treasury between 5.20% and 5.35% now that cash trading resumes, the Dollar Index around 103, the Kospi around 6,000 as a barometer of AI sentiment, and Bitcoin at $80K support and $85K–87.4K resistance. The key catalysts are today's bank earnings, Wednesday's CPI, Thursday's PPI and the TSMC and ASML reports.

The constructive scenario requires inflation in line with or below expectations, bank results that show contained credit stress, stable long-term yields and TSMC guidance capable of restoring confidence in the AI supply chain. In that case, the correction in chips and crypto could remain a leverage reset rather than a trend change.

The negative scenario involves a CPI surprise above 3.6%, a 10-year yield breaking above 5.35%, a new attack on Gulf energy infrastructure or a disappointing outlook from TSMC. text:
As the Cold War froze into decades of uneasy détente, the heroic dissident slowly curdled into a crushing diplomatic liability. Hungarian leader János Kádár refused to grant Mindszenty safe passage out of the country unless he signed a humiliating confession of guilt and renounced his moral authority. Meanwhile, the Vatican under Pope Paul VI adopted the pragmatic diplomacy of *Ostpolitik*, seeking accommodation with Eastern bloc regimes to secure the appointment of new bishops. To Rome and Washington, the unbending, uncompromising old cardinal stubbornly refusing to strike a deal in Budapest was an awkward relic obstructing superpower negotiations.

Mindszenty refused to budge. He believed that accepting a conditional pardon or leaving without the freedom of his church would validate his tormentors. American diplomats treated him with deep personal reverence, but successive administrations—from Eisenhower to Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon—found their Budapest legation perpetually paralyzed, unable to elevate the mission to a full embassy as long as its permanent houseguest occupied the second floor.

The standoff finally cracked in September 1971 under relentless pressure from President Richard Nixon and direct orders of obedience from Pope Paul VI. Broken in health and deeply bitter that his own church was urging him to surrender, the seventy-nine-year-old Cardinal climbed into an American diplomatic limousine, drove under armed escort to Ferihegy Airport, and flew into Austrian exile. 

Even freedom offered no peace. When Mindszenty published his memoirs exposing the full horrors of his torture and rejected Vatican gag orders, Pope Paul VI stripped him of his title as Archbishop of Esztergom in 1974 to appease Budapest. Cardinal Mindszenty died in Vienna the following year, having survived Nazi prisons, communist torture dungeons, and fifteen years in a locked room—only to discover that realpolitik had no room for martyrs who refused to compromise.

text:
Tuesday morning headlines from #Georgia, 13 October

● EU foreign ministers discussed the situation in Georgia in Luxembourg. According to EU High Representative Kaja Kallas, democratic backsliding in Georgia is deepening, the threat of banning opposition parties is growing, and civil society activities are being restricted. Kallas said the EU’s current approach was not putting enough pressure on the Georgian authorities to bring about change. A more in-depth discussion of Georgia is scheduled for January.

● EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said Georgia’s EU candidate status existed only on paper. She said the EU was ready to resume cooperation with the Georgian authorities, but this would require halting democratic backsliding and changing controversial laws. Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said the Georgian people wanted a European future, but the authorities had failed to take the necessary steps. She added that diplomatic dialogue with Georgia was continuing.

● Following the meeting of EU foreign ministers, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the government was ready to reset relations with Brussels, but this would require the European Commission’s leadership to change its attitude towards Georgia. He said relations with some EU member states were showing positive changes, but “bureaucrats in the EU leadership continue to act against Georgia”. Kobakhidze said the government was ready to discuss all controversial laws with the EU, but would not give up the country’s sovereignty, peace or national identity in exchange for European integration.

● Irakli Kobakhidze again claimed that the EU was demanding that Georgia allow same-sex couples to adopt children and allow anyone who wished to legally change their gender, which the prime minister said was unacceptable.

● Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling party, actively participates in political decision-making. According to the prime minister, Ivanishvili is in regular contact with party representatives, offers advice and takes part in discussions on important issues. Kobakhidze nevertheless maintained that decisions are not made unilaterally. Ivanishvili holds no government office in Georgia.

● Irakli Kobakhidze commented on Russia’s ban on imports of products from several Georgian companies. The prime minister said the government was working to clarify the issue and hoped Russia would reverse its decision. The ban affects products from TbilWine, Teliani Veli, Dzmebi Askaneli, Nabeglavi and other companies.

● Russia’s Foreign Ministry again said Georgia should sign a non-use-of-force agreement with Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) and begin the delimitation of what Moscow calls their “state borders”. Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin made the statement during an online meeting with the co-chairs of the Geneva International Discussions on the conflicts in Georgia. In response, Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said Georgia continued to demand the withdrawal of Russian occupying forces from Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, as well as the return to their homes in those territories of hundreds of thousands of displaced people.

● The Constitutional Court rejected Judge Manana Kobakhidze’s request to recuse herself from the case seeking to ban opposition parties. The judge said she had co-founded the ruling Georgian Dream party, served as an MP and repeatedly publicly criticised the opposition United National Movement, calling for its dissolution. The party is now among those whose activities the authorities are seeking to ban. Kobakhidze said this background could raise questions about her impartiality, but the Constitutional Court found no grounds for her recusal.

Context: On 6 October, the Constitutional Court agreed to hear Georgian Dream’s lawsuit seeking to ban five pro-Western opposition parties. The ruling party accuses them of denying the legitimacy of the current government and the country’s constitutional order.

● Tbilisi Court of Appeals will consider the cases of those convicted over the events of 4 October 2025 on 13 October at 17:00. Reports suggest that plea agreements may be reached with Murtaz Zodelava, Lasha Beridze, Guri Zhvania and Irakli Chkhvirkvia. Zodelava and Beridze are reportedly facing likely sentences of one year and one month, although neither the prosecution’s agreement nor the court’s decision has been confirmed.

● Opposition leader Giorgi Gakharia, who lives in Germany, plans to file a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg over the criminal cases brought against him in Georgia if domestic legal remedies are exhausted. His lawyer told journalists that video evidence submitted in the case proves Gakharia’s innocence, but the defence has little hope that Georgian courts will act impartially. More details on the criminal cases against Giorgi Gakharia here https://t.co/slX9Q93hCN

● Irakli Kobakhidze denied allegations by prisoner Giorgi Davitadze that prison staff had sexually assaulted and humiliated him. Kobakhidze said there was no evidence to support the allegations and that the actions shown in surveillance footage released by the prison administration “fully complied with the principle of proportionality from beginning to end”. According to the prime minister, the prosecutor’s office announced on 10 October that it had closed the investigation, stating that no criminal offences against the prisoner had been proven.

● OSCE Chairperson-in-Office and Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis will visit Tbilisi on 16 October. Meetings with the prime minister and foreign minister are scheduled. The visit will focus on the consequences of the August 2008 war with Russia and the Geneva International Discussions on resolving conflicts in Georgia. Before arriving in Georgia, Cassis will visit Yerevan on 15 October.

● MPs from the ruling party have introduced amendments to the rules governing compulsory psychiatric treatment. Under the draft legislation, a special commission would review the grounds for continuing treatment every month, while a court would reconsider the matter every six months. The amendments are intended to implement a Constitutional Court ruling.

● Under a draft law submitted by the government, the maximum authorised strength of the Georgian Defence Forces in 2027 will remain at 37,000, unchanged from previous years. The figure sets the maximum permitted number of servicemen, not the actual number serving.

● Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III of Georgia met representatives of UNESCO’s World Heritage Centre and international expert organisations to discuss the restoration of Gelati Monastery. According to the Patriarchate, specialists gave a positive assessment of the restoration work and discussed whether it complied with the recommendations.

● From 1 January 2027, pensions for people under 70 will rise by 45 lari (about $12) to 415 lari (about $160). The prime minister said the initial plan had been to increase pensions by only 20 lari, but the government had decided on a larger rise.

● The government will offer internally displaced families from Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region the option of receiving cash compensation instead of housing. Participation in the programme will be voluntary, with compensation set at 10,000 lari (about $4,000) per family member. The offer applies to families that have not yet received housing or equivalent compensation from the state.

● Georgian media reported that Iran’s ambassador to Tbilisi had been attacked by stray dogs, fallen and broken his leg. The ambassador himself posted a statement saying the report was mistaken and that the person injured was another embassy employee.

text:
Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.

text:
NOBLE Prestige Ultra-Flagship Series Roundup: QILIN, VKRP, Sultan Prestige & K10L

Overview

NOBLE is one of the most representative names in ultra-flagship IEMs. The Shogun, launched early in 2025, shows bold personality in both looks and sound. Old hands know and prize the Prestige series more. The Prestige line is tuned by founder Wizard and offers custom shells. Each Prestige IEM has a clear sonic lean.

The Viking Ragnar Prestige (VKRP) sold out as a phenomenon-level benchmark the moment it landed. The Sultan Prestige, on the market for over five years, is still cited for its unique timbre. The Kublai Khan Prestige wins tinkerers with its pairing potential. In the ultra-flagship and Hi-End space, price and quality don't map one to one.

For high-end listeners, raw specs are not the first thing — finding the most fitting, most loved sound matters most. Top IEMs don't win by stacking drivers. A memorable tuning catches the ear more than spec sheets. The Prestige line shares a solid technical base across models. They all show outstanding density, full detail, and an open sense of space.

This guide is for listeners who want to try @noblebywizard 's ultra-flagships but don't know where to start. It lays out each model's traits and best fit, with the verdicts up front.

QILIN: class-leading tech, open stage and very high density. Its upper mids are full and lush, with gorgeous coloration. It leans broadly all-round.

Viking Ragnar Prestige: fine, delicate imaging with strong line definition. It renders instrument timbre most accurately, with less low-end quantity, fitting all kinds of classical. It has the biggest desktop-amp potential.

Sultan Prestige: clear vocal coloring, sweet, soft, and relaxed. It has a rich sense of atmosphere and is very forgiving of recordings, asking little of the source.

K10L Prestige: the entry model of the P line. Solid tech, clean and dense base, even three-band balance. Wide song fit and tweakable, with the best value.

P.S. To keep a consistent reference and stay accurate, all the listening above uses my most-used AZLA ORIGIN earbuds cover.

QILIN

QILIN is the only one of the four above $7,000, and its raw technical skill is the most eye-catching. Its strongest point is not detail but a smart control of coloration. Its gorgeous upper-mid coloring brings vivid life to instruments and vocals. The bright, dazzling tone with an open stage gives it both a striking first listen and broad fit. It also has decent long-term listenability.

QILIN's tuning is rounded, so you don't need a player with too much character. The Lotoo PAW GT2, with solid yet understated tech, brings out QILIN's unique beauty best. A well-controlled desktop amp also gives audible gains in dynamics and stage scale. Its better partners are cross-over 'brick' amps like the C9 II and EA4. Their output matches better and they keep hiss low.

QILIN suits an end-game listener as the one main IEM. I own many IEMs of different styles, yet my top pick right now is the VKRP, about $1,500 cheaper. QILIN builds a rare stage for an IEM; VKRP goes further with an unbelievable speaker-like feel. Its stage escapes the shell, wider in bound and looser in layout. The whole scene expands to over-ear or even small-to-mid speaker scale.

On Bach's "Violin Concerto No. 1," the QILIN version puts violin and harpsichord in front with sheen; the band feels weak and a bit crowded. The VKRP clearly shows the violin, harpsichord, and band in their places, neatly ordered.

Viking Ragnar Prestige (VKRP)

VKRP has a strong character and gets mixed reviews. Some say its low-end atmosphere is poor or its vocals lack flavor, and it fits the public less than QILIN. In fact its low end is not big in quantity but has good cohesion and layering. It fully restores the changes of small snare, timpani, and double bass in classical.

Its clean, low-colored upper mids and excellent density serve the ultimate classical restore. Playing R&B or electronic with strong beats feels less fun, and casual pop is less catchy. Picking it as main needs trade-offs. Later NOBLE tuned the similar Kronos a bit more restrained.

I found some high-value tricks to make VKRP more all-round. Switching to a more mid-low or thicker earbuds cover clearly lifts its vocal feel. The best match is AZLA MAX, giving thicker mids placed more forward. VKRP also gains most from desktop among the four.

Paired with the TEAC HA-507 amp, its large-scale show steps up. The HA-507 has a fine, transparent, soft base that suits IEMs well. With VKRP it gives open space and precise placement. The low end is solid and steady with mighty dynamics, and vocals are clear and gentle. It turns broadly all-round.

Sultan Prestige

Sultan Prestige has been out about five years, and next to today's ultra-flagships its taste still feels current. QILIN's coloring dazzles with power and luxury; Sultan Prestige shows a flowing tolerance and sweet lushness. Its mids carry warm coloring and a fine velvet feel, sanding sibilance nearly away.

The treble is soft and gentle with middle brightness, trading some transparency for listenability. This pop-leaning tuning could easily turn soft and dull. Wizard opened the stage so the mid energy spreads in a huge space. The whole listen feels open and fluid. Its raw tech lags the later P-line members.

But on all kinds of female vocals, especially J-POP females with plain recordings, its recording tolerance and vocal beauty are the best of the four. Sultan Prestige avoids the worry that faster gear upgrades make your music harder to enjoy. It is not picky about source; a mid-to-high player drives it well.

K10L Prestige

Next to the others, the ~$3,800 K10L is more approachable. It is the door to the Prestige series. For most, it is the best balance of tech, pairing, and value. With no special taste, buying it won't disappoint. Built on the broad-pop lean most audiophiles like, its coloring is more restrained than Sultan Prestige.

Sultan Prestige sometimes over-decorates certain male pop, turning a bit greasy. K10L has better tech and keeps more vocal grain, so throat tones, chest resonance, even small flaws are felt. Keeping these details makes K10L more immersive than Sultan Prestige on live concert recordings. Its chase for true, natural sound makes it not just a pop-specialized IEM.

Through K10L, piano, violin sonatas, or complex chamber music reveal rich playing detail and lay the structure out in good order. Even if a listener later moves to desktop with a desktop amp, K10L's upgrade headroom keeps up. I drove K10L with a few studio desktop amps; dynamics and separation both lifted clearly.

The best match was a warm, luxurious-colored amp like the Goldmund THA3. Its sound is smooth and elegant, vocals full and lively, low end full and powerful with clear layers.

Conclusion

QILIN and VKRP differ sharply but both carry a commanding air. They take skill and careful pairing to enjoy. By contrast K10L and Sultan Prestige suit most daily listening. They adapt better and tune easier to enjoy.

In recent years portable HiFi's top IEM prices get refreshed almost yearly. After the settle, buyer fever cools and spending turns rational; few top IEM brands survive. NOBLE's worth is not selling IEMs dear, but giving the ultra-flagship IEM class diverse taste — and that taste has strong foresight and lasting life.

Most IEMs stay hot only months. Prestige models out one to two, even over three years, still stay active in online groups and offline meets. It became the spoken tuning benchmark, unique in a fickle IEM world.

#KOSPI PLUNGES 7.4% AS AI FINANCING WARNINGS DEEPEN A GLOBAL CHIP SELL-OFF

Key Details: 
The Kospi closed down 7.4% at 5,914.35 on Tuesday, its lowest since late July, after a sell-side trading curb was triggered for the first time in nearly two months, as fears of AI overheating and Chinese competition drove rotation out of technology. Foreign investors had net sold ₩1.98tn of Kospi stocks and ₩191.9bn of Kospi 200 futures by mid-morning, after ₩2tn of net selling on Monday, while retail buyers absorbed ₩1.43tn. Tech stocks also fell in Tokyo and Taipei, with the Nikkei down 2.5% at 67,292.39. Broadcom's chief executive likened market sentiment to a casino, and the chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that rising borrowing costs and uncertain returns could become bigger obstacles to AI expansion than chip or power shortages, while expecting strong computing demand through 2029, potentially into 2030. Eugene Asset Management CIO Ha SeokKeun said uncertainty over whether the upcycle can last into 2028 and beyond is weighing on Korean chipmakers' valuations. Falling equities and lower oil prices lifted bonds, with the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.19% as cash trading resumed.

Impact Assessment: 
Industry leaders naming financing as the binding constraint ties AI equity valuations directly to 5% Treasury yields and credit spreads, compressing multiples at Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron and Broadcom. Foreign exits weigh on the won and Taiwan exporters. Rotation into duration offers bonds temporary relief, but a hot CPI would remove that cushion while record index concentration leaves equities exposed.

text:
Trump has repeatedly offered practical, success-oriented life advice—especially on hard work, mindset, family, and perseverance—that many find useful. It’s not rarefied philosophy, but it’s explicit and repeated.

Ask yourself and Grok:

2025 University of Alabama commencement — Delivered an explicit list of “life-changing lessons”: love what you do (rarely succeed without it); think big (same energy as thinking small, bigger payoff); work hard and don’t lose momentum; trust your instincts/common sense; believe in the American Dream; think of yourself as a winner (reject victimhood); be an original (“God only created one of you”); never give up. Perseverance framed as the key. 

The most important thing in life is to love what you’re doing, because that’s the only way you’ll ever be really good at it.” Also: listen to your gut over paper analysis; sometimes your best investments are the ones you don’t make; if you’re going to think, think big; experience teaches focus and knowing when to walk away.

Parenting rules (repeated to his kids, including Barron) — No drugs, no alcohol, no cigarettes. Rooted in his brother’s alcoholism; practical, moral boundary-setting he says he still repeats

 “When you open your heart to patriotism, there is no room for prejudice.” And the formulation that Americans of every background “all bleed the same red blood of patriots.”

These are conventional success and character maxims (work hard, love the work, positive mindset, family boundaries, national solidarity). Whether one finds them profound is taste; the existence of the statements is not in doubt.

text:
It’s hilarious how you get proven wrong over and over again. Cope and seethe. 😆

“Could the Discord statement by Tyler Robinson, “Hey guys, I have bad news for you all. It was me at UVU yesterday. I’m sorry for all of this. I’m surrendering through a sheriff friend in a few moments.”, also be used as an admission of confession during the actual trial when it comes?

Yes. That Discord message can be offered at trial as an admission by Robinson.
Under Utah Rule of Evidence 801(d)(2), a statement by a party-opponent is not hearsay. A defendant’s own words acknowledging the crime (“It was me at UVU yesterday”) fit that rule. Prosecutors would present it as a confession or at least a statement against interest.
To get it in they still have to authenticate it: show the account was his and that he sent the message. They already have several routes that courts routinely accept:
•  Discord’s own records produced under warrant
•  Screenshots from Lance Twiggs’ phone (Exhibit 16.2 at the prelim)
•  Account identifiers matching Robinson
•  Timing that lines up with his surrender
The defense can fight weight, not usually admissibility. Typical arguments would be: the account wasn’t proven to be his beyond dispute; the message was a joke consistent with the earlier “doppelganger” banter; “at UVU yesterday” is ambiguous; or the chat should be shown in full so the jury sees the joking context. Those go to the jury. They do not automatically keep the statement out.
The same message was already used at the preliminary hearing and cited in the bindover. That does not guarantee trial admission of every surrounding exhibit, but a defendant’s own written admission, authenticated by the platform and a chat participant, is standard trial evidence. A judge would almost certainly let the jury hear it.”

text:
The public concerns regarding the diversion or detouring whatever of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway within the Ondo section to connect with the East-West Road are understandable, particularly given the expectations that the project should follow a direct coastal alignment. However, it is important to objectively consider the technical, economic, and environmental realities associated with constructing major road infrastructure across the Niger Delta region.

The East-West Road remains the most critical transportation corridor linking the Niger Delta states, including Ondo, Edo, Delta, Bayelsa, and Rivers States. Given its strategic importance to regional mobility, commerce, oil and gas operations, and national economic activities, the decision to reconstruct and integrate sections of the East-West Road into the broader coastal highway network can be viewed as a practical and prudent engineering solution.

The terrain across much of the Niger Delta consists of coastal wetlands, mangrove forests, deep swampy plains, and flood-prone areas. Constructing a completely new coastal highway through these challenging environments is technically complex, highly capital-intensive, and likely to require a significantly longer completion period. These difficult geographical conditions may partly explain why successive governments over several decades were unable to deliver a comprehensive coastal highway despite recognizing its importance.

Rather than abandoning the vision of a coastal highway, integrating and upgrading existing strategic corridors such as the East-West Road offers an opportunity to accelerate connectivity while reducing implementation risks. Such an approach enables the government to leverage existing road alignments, minimize environmental disruption, and direct available resources toward delivering a functional transportation network within a shorter timeframe.

However, for this strategy to gain public acceptance, the reconstruction of the East-West Road must be undertaken to the highest engineering standards. Given the challenging terrain and recurring flooding experienced in many sections, the road should be reconstructed using reinforced concrete pavement rather than conventional asphalt where necessary. Additionally, the carriageway should be elevated above flood plains and designed with adequate drainage infrastructure, embankment protection, and climate-resilient engineering features to ensure long-term durability and reduce future maintenance costs.

An upgraded East-West Road would also serve a critical dual purpose. During the construction of the more difficult coastal segments, it would provide a reliable alternative route for commuters, businesses, and logistics operators. This would help sustain economic activity across the region while allowing work on the coastal highway to progress in phases.

Ultimately, the success of this approach will depend on transparency, stakeholder engagement, and clear communication of the long-term vision. The government should reassure affected communities that the diversion is not a cancellation of the coastal highway concept but rather a strategic adaptation to the realities of the terrain, funding requirements, and engineering challenges. If properly executed, the reconstruction of the East-West Road and its integration into the coastal highway network could provide immediate transportation benefits while laying the foundation for the eventual completion of a resilient and sustainable coastal corridor across the Niger Delta.

In this context, the diversion should be seen not as a departure from the original objective, but as a pragmatic step toward achieving it in a manner that balances engineering feasibility, economic efficiency, environmental considerations, and the public interest.

text:
“Give me the photograph,” Uncle Michael demanded.

I held it tightly.

“Why? What are you hiding?”

He laughed, but there was no warmth in it.

“Your father was a foolish man. He believed money was more important than family.”

“You stole his inheritance!”

His expression changed instantly.

“Watch your mouth, Daniel.”

“You forged documents. You made him disappear. Didn't you?”

He stepped closer.

“Your father wasn't innocent. He was planning to take everything from me.”

“Then why did he disappear?”

Michael looked at me for several seconds before answering.

“Because he had a choice.”

“What choice?”

“He could leave the country and never return, or he could stay and watch everyone he loved suffer.”

I felt sick.

“You threatened him?”

“I offered him a way out.”

“And my mother? What did you do to her?”

He shook his head.

“Your mother made her own decisions. She chose to remain silent because she knew what would happen if she spoke.”

I couldn't believe what I was hearing.

Before I could respond, someone knocked violently on the study door.

“Michael! Open this door!” my mother shouted.

My uncle ignored her.

Then he leaned toward me and whispered, “Your sister is making a terrible mistake by coming here.”

My phone vibrated in my pocket.

A message from Sophie.

“I'm outside your house. I have proof that our father is alive. Please come out alone.”

I stared at my uncle.

He had seen the message on my screen.

For the first time, his confident expression cracked.

“You're not going anywhere,” he said.

He reached for my phone, but I shoved past him and unlocked the door as my mother pulled it open from the other side.

I ran outside.

A black car was parked across the street.

A young woman stepped out.

She looked almost exactly like my father.

“Daniel?” she asked.

I nodded.

She hugged me, trembling.

Then she handed me a sealed envelope.

Inside was a recent photograph of my father sitting in a wheelchair outside a small house.

On the back was a handwritten note:

“My children, if you are reading this, Michael has finally made his move. Trust no one until you hear my side of the story.”

“Where did you get this?” I asked.

“Someone delivered it to my apartment. There was also an address.”

She showed me the paper.

It was an address in a quiet coastal town several hours away.

“We need to go,” she said. “Tonight.”

But before we could enter my car, headlights flooded the street.

A vehicle screeched to a halt beside us.

Two men stepped out.

One pointed directly at Sophie.

“The girl comes with us,” he said.

I grabbed my sister's hand.

And then a familiar voice came from inside the vehicle.

“Don't be afraid, children.”

My father stepped into the light.

He was older, thinner, and walking with a cane.

But he was alive.

And the first thing he said was:

“Your mother has been lying to you about more than my disappearance.”

THE HIDDEN COCKROACHES. PART 1 OF 5.

The Untangling

Delhi police detained the party's founder at the airport this morning. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were taken off their flights. The YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was picked up in Gurugram. 45 Metro stations are shut, 23,000 personnel are deployed, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 cover the capital.

Today's orders stopped a march. The march was against the chief election commissioner. The map shows who that man is already connected to.

The judge who called the protesters "cockroaches" has graft allegations on file from 2019. They have sat unadjudicated since. His bench declined to watch the videos of the July 20 police charge. He said "cockroaches" twice, on May 15 and again on July 22.

The chief election commissioner drove the voter-roll purge over 14 written objections from his own commissioners. Before the job he served as Cooperation Secretary under Amit Shah. Shah's home ministry blocked the party's X account in May. The Delhi High Court ordered it restored in July.

One panel picked that commissioner and both of his objectors in a single day. It showed the opposition 6 names out of 212, ten minutes before the meeting. The 2023 law had removed the Chief Justice from that panel.

The previous commissioner, Rajiv Kumar, retired in February 2025. HDFC Bank made him part-time chairman in June 2026.

A 2006 suicide note naming the current commissioner went back under probe this month. He had set up the Ram Mandir trust before taking the election job.

The Times of India ran zero stories on the roll purge across 120 days. Hindustan Times ran zero. Aaj Tak ran zero. Adani's NDTV ran three. The Indian Express ran fourteen.

Punjab Police says it broke two ISI-linked modules in August that planned an attack at the protest site. Nine were taken in, four of them juveniles.

Delhi Police says 200 people were detained today. The party says 10,000 across India.

text:
The Great Commission in Matthew 28 does not place Gentile believers under the Sermon on the Mount as a continuing legal code.

Jesus’ earthly ministry was directed to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24 KJV). The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) was given in that context—raising the standard of the law in anticipation of the kingdom offered to Israel, not inaugurating a new law for the Body of Christ. After the resurrection, the apostles were commanded to teach “all things whatsoever I have commanded you,” yet the very same apostles later met in council and determined that Gentile believers were not required to observe the Law of Moses:

“For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things; That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication.” Acts 15:28-29 KJV

Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles (Romans 11:13; Galatians 2:7–9), received the further revelation of the mystery of the Church, which had not been made known in other ages (Ephesians 3:1–9). He taught the same gospel of Christ crucified, buried, and risen (1 Corinthians 15:1–4), yet he also declared:

“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.” Romans 6:14 KJV

“Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.” Galatians 5:1 KJV

The new covenant was ratified by the blood of Christ (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 9:15–17). Believers are justified by faith apart from the works of the law (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). To insist that Gentile disciples must observe the full content of Matthew 5–7 as binding commandments is to collapse the distinction the Scriptures themselves maintain between the program offered to Israel and the present dispensation of grace. There is one gospel of salvation; there is not one continuous legal program for both Israel and the Church.

text:
INGREDIENTS OF A FAILED STATE
(Views of a Palestinian Refugee) 

Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.

text:
When he is rejected and betrayed by those once called friends. When allies grow weary, politicians negotiate, and some are already poised to shake the hand of the executioner. When his life and the life of his country are daily targets for rockets, drones, bombs, and lies. I have no idea how this man has endured all this. And continues to endure it.

He does not look like a movie hero. He looks like a man who hasn't slept in years. He has been cast aside. With eyes burning for the homes of Kyiv, Kharkiv, Dnipro, and Odesa. With eyes that see all of Ukraine. He asks for no pity. He courageously asks for weapons. He does not flee. He stands his ground and bares his chest. When offered evacuation, he says: "I need ammunition, not a taxi." And this is not just a catchy phrase. It is a choice proven over years. Every day. Every night. Right now.

He has been betrayed and continues to be betrayed. He has been underestimated and continues to be underestimated. He has been insulted and continues to be insulted. He has been put to the test and continues to be put to the test. And he stands tall. In the shadow of ruined cities. With weary soldiers. In the shadow of a world that is also weary—a world that wants to forget this war in Ukraine and think of something that causes no suffering or stress, something pleasant. Yet he reminds everyone. He speaks to people as if holding their hands. And there is something in that which brings a lump to one's throat.
In all my life, I have never admired any public figure more than him. And I think, perhaps, I never will again. Because such admiration is not about politics. It is about a man who, when everything is falling apart, does not ask "Why me?" but—like a knight—does what must be done. I am certain he will stand firm, even if it costs him his life. Even if all his friends leave. Even if the whole world turns its back on him. He will not betray his principles.

The entire world respects him—not because he is perfect, but because he is the strongest of them all, because he has raised the banner of the highest values: human dignity, freedom, and democracy. And all of Ukraine stands with him—weary and wounded, yet unbowed. Perhaps in the future, you will vote for someone else in the presidential election. That is your right. But today, let us respect him. We have a president who deserves respect and of whom we need not be ashamed. May he have strength and patience.

Volodymyr Oleksandrovych deserves kind words and every form of support today. So let us give it to him—it is our duty!

First, Google demonstrated that the same predictive capability derived from behavioral surplus that could enrich surveillance capitalists could also help candidates win elections. To prove it, it was ready to enter the fiery battlefield of the new millennium’s electoral campaigns, beginning with Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign. Schmidt played a leading role in organizing his team, taking charge of the most modern data-based strategies capable of rendering the old political arts obsolete thanks to the science of behavioral prediction.
“At Obama’s headquarters in Chicago, […] the electorate was remodeled, every single weekend […] the staff could observe the impact of events on the predicted behaviors and beliefs of every voter across the nation.”
Research by media scholars Daniel Kreiss and Philip Howard indicates that the 2008 Obama campaign compiled significant data on more than 250 million Americans, including “a vast array of online behavioral and relational data collected from use of the campaign’s web site and third-party social media sites such as Facebook.” Journalist Sasha Issenberg, who documented these developments in his book The Victory Lab, quotes one of Obama’s 2008 political consultants who likened predictive modeling to the tools of a fortune-teller: “We knew who… people were going to vote for before they decided.”
Obama used his closeness to Schmidt to confirm that he was the most innovative candidate, intent on ousting the usual faces of Washington. Once elected, Schmidt joined the Transition Economic Advisory Board and appeared alongside Obama at his first press conference after the elections. According to Politico, “the mere image of Schmidt arm-in-arm with Obama’s economic advisers was enough to send shivers down the spine of Google’s competitors. ‘Microsoft will be terrified,’ declared a Democratic lobbyist who knows the sector thoroughly. ‘There are good reasons to be terrified of Google.’”
Schmidt’s role in the election of President Obama was only a chapter in a long, by now legendary relationship that someone has described as a “love story.” It is no surprise that Schmidt played an even more important role in the 2012 reelection campaign, in fundraising and the use of new technologies, “personally overseeing the turnout data on election night.” The New York Times political correspondent Jim Rutenberg […] offers a very realistic picture of how the collection and analysis of behavioral surplus were used as a political methodology. They knew “the name, address, race, sex, and income of every single undecided voter” and the way to deliver targeted television ads to them. One key was the persuasion score that identified how easily an undecided voter could be convinced to vote for the Democratic candidate.

text:
He paid $8,000. Three jewelers offered $1,250. He lost $6,750 on a product the industry told him was precious.

The diamond wasn’t fake. The certification was real. The stone was genuine. The price was the lie.

Diamonds are not rare. De Beers controlled 85% of the global supply for a century — stockpiling stones in vaults and releasing them slowly to manufacture scarcity. The rarity was a boardroom decision.

The engagement ring tradition didn’t exist before 1938. An advertising agency invented it. The “two months’ salary” rule was a marketing campaign. “A Diamond Is Forever” was designed to stop resale — not to symbolize love.

A diamond loses 40–60% of its retail value the moment you buy it. The retail markup is 50–200%. You’re not buying a $8,000 diamond. You’re buying a $1,250 diamond in an $8,000 experience.

Lab-grown diamonds are chemically, physically, and optically identical. They cost 80–90% less. The FTC says they’re real diamonds. Sixty-one percent of American engagement rings now have lab-grown center stones. De Beers — the company that built the natural diamond monopoly — launched its own lab-grown brand.

Natural diamond prices have fallen 60% since 2022. De Beers reported a $189 million loss. The “store of value” narrative is collapsing under real market data.

The Kimberley Process — the ethical certification — was abandoned by one of its own founders, who called it an accomplice to diamond laundering.

“The diamond industry is the only industry in the world that spent a century convincing consumers that a product with negligible resale value is an investment. That a common mineral is rare. That a marketing campaign is a tradition. That an advertising slogan is wisdom.”

“‘A Diamond Is Forever’ doesn’t mean your love is eternal.”

“It means: don’t sell the diamond. Because if you try — you’ll find out what it’s actually worth.”

“He found out. Three jewelers. Three offers. $900. $1,100. $1,250.”

“$8,000 in.”

“$1,250 out.”

“Same diamond.”

“That’s not an investment. That’s not a tradition. That’s a century-old marketing campaign that finally met a consumer who did the math.”

“Do the math before you buy. Not after.”

If this was useful, repost the first post so more people can learn the truth about diamond pricing before they spend $8,000 on a product worth $1,250 — because the industry is counting on one thing: that you’ll never try to sell it.

He said this is the math the industry needs you to never do — because nobody buys an $8,000 product that’s worth $1,250 the moment they own it. Unless they don’t know.

“The retail markup on diamonds at traditional jewelry stores is 50–200% above wholesale cost. That markup covers: the storefront lease (premium mall locations cost $50,000–$100,000/month), employee salaries, security, insurance, marketing, store design, and profit.”

“None of those costs are in the diamond. The diamond is the same stone whether it’s in a $15,000/month mall case or a FedEx box from an online retailer. The sparkle doesn’t know what building it’s in.”

“When you resell — the jeweler offers you wholesale. Not retail. The retail experience — the showroom, the lighting, the velvet box, the champagne, the ‘you’re making the right choice’ — evaporates the moment you walk out. What remains is the stone. At wholesale value.”

“His ring: $8,000 retail. Three jewelers offered $900, $1,100, and $1,250. The best offer was 15.6% of what he paid. He didn’t lose $6,750 because diamonds are bad investments. He lost $6,750 because he paid $8,000 for a product with a wholesale value of $1,250. The $6,750 was never ‘his.’ It was the store’s margin. He rented it for the length of time it took to walk to his car.”

“He said the resale moment is when the industry’s entire narrative collapses. ‘When a man buys a diamond for $8,000 — he believes he owns $8,000 worth of diamond. When he tries to sell it — he discovers he owns $1,250 worth of diamond and $6,750 worth of marketing, showroom lighting, and a velvet box he left on the counter.’”

text:
A guy tried to sell his $8,000 diamond ring. Three jewelers. Three offers. $900. $1,100. $1,250.

He paid $8,000. The best offer was $1,250. He lost $6,750 the moment he walked out of the store with it.

Not because the diamond was fake. Not because the market crashed. Because diamonds have never held retail value. Ever.
