text:
A 4-gram piece of foam and paint just sat dead still for 40 minutes. Then it moved 2 millimeters. And every adult who saw it stopped breathing.

Watch the video first. Sound on. Then come back, because what you just saw is the most addictive 27 seconds of nothing turning into everything, and I'm about to explain why your brain can't look away.

---

PART 1. THE LIE OF STILLNESS

Nobody tells you this about water: it is never quiet.

It only looks quiet to people who aren't paying attention.

Under that flat grey surface there is a full-time economy running. Things eat. Things hide. Things panic. Things wait. A single square meter of a pond can hold more drama in an hour than your entire group chat has produced in a year.

And you, standing on the bank, holding a pole and a string, are trying to join that economy with one small, painted, brightly colored lie.

Because that's what a float is. A lie that happens to be very useful.

It says: nothing is happening here.

It says: relax.

It says: this is just a stick floating in a pond.

And then, in one beat, it stops lying.

That is the entire game. Everything else is decoration.

---

PART 2. WHY YOU CAN'T LOOK AWAY

Here's the weird part. You can watch a float for two hours and see nothing, and still refuse to blink.

That's not patience. Patience is passive. This is something else.

This is what psychologists would call variable reward, and it's the same mechanism that keeps people pulling slot machine levers and refreshing feeds at 2 a.m. The reward is unpredictable. It could come in ten seconds. It could come in ten minutes. It could not come at all.

Your brain hates that uncertainty and loves it at the same time.

Dopamine is not the chemical of pleasure, by the way. It's the chemical of anticipation. It spikes when something good might be about to happen. Not when it happens. When it MIGHT.

A float is an anticipation machine with a red tip.

Every ripple is a false alarm. Every false alarm is a tiny hit. Every tiny hit makes you more locked in than the last.

Now put that into a vertical video with a pink rod, flat grey water, and a float that has started to behave strangely.

You are not watching a video anymore. You are in it.

---

PART 3. THE TWITCH

Let me tell you what the first sign looks like, because most people miss it.

It isn't a dive. It isn't a dramatic plunge like in the cartoons.

It's a shiver.

The tip trembles. A little ring spreads out. The float lifts slightly, or sinks slightly, or drifts a few centimeters against the wind where nothing should be pushing it.

To a beginner, that's nothing. Wind. Current. A leaf.

To someone who has stood on a bank for ten years, that's a scream.

Because underneath that float, on the end of a very thin line, there is a hook the size of a fingernail clipping hiding a piece of bait. And something with a mouth and a very strong opinion about food has just walked up to it.

It hasn't committed yet.

It's thinking.

Yes. Thinking. We'll get to that.

The fish nudges. It tastes. It spits. It comes back. It circles. It tests the bait the way you test a stranger's offer: cautiously, with every sense turned up to maximum.

And all of that arrives at your eyes as a trembling, red-and-yellow dot on a sheet of grey.

That tiny dot is a live feed from a conversation you cannot hear.

---

PART 4. WHAT THE FISH ACTUALLY KNOWS

Let's kill a myth right now.

You've heard that a goldfish has a three-second memory. It's false. Goldfish can be trained, they can learn to respond to signals, and they can remember what they learned for months.

Carp are even more interesting. Research on anglers' lakes has found that fish which have been hooked once can become wary of baits and tackle for a long time afterward, in some studies for months. Fish don't just react. They file things away.

Think about what that means. The thing under your float might have seen this trick before.

It might have been caught, handled, and released three summers ago, and it might have decided back then, in whatever way a fish decides anything, that shiny things with strange food attached are worth a second look before a first bite.

Fish also feel the world in a way you never will.

They have a lateral line, a row of sensors running along their sides that detects tiny pressure changes and vibrations in the water. A fish can sense movement it cannot see. A footstep on the bank. A heavy boot. A sloppy cast.

Many carp species can taste with their lips and mouth, and even with the skin around them. Taste buds, all over, working like a second set of eyes.

So when that float shivers, understand the scale of what is happening.

A creature that tastes through its skin and hears through its body just examined your lie from six directions at once.

And it's still deciding.

---

PART 5. THE SECOND THAT STRETCHES

There is a moment in every bite that physics doesn't explain.

Clocks say it lasts one second. Your body says it lasts a year.

The float has moved. You saw it. Your hand is already tightening on the handle. Your shoulder is loaded. Your breathing has gone shallow and strange.

And you have exactly one decision to make.

Strike now, and you might pull the bait straight out of a mouth that was only investigating.

Wait too long, and a fish that wasn't convinced will decide it was.

This is what separates the people who catch from the people who say they "just came for the fresh air."

Not gear. Not bait. Not luck.

The decision inside the second.

The best anglers in the world will tell you they can't fully explain it. They just know. They've watched ten thousand floats do ten thousand slightly different things, and somewhere in the back of their skull a quiet little machine has sorted every wobble into one of three folders: nothing, maybe, and NOW.

You don't learn that folder from a book.

You learn it by being wrong in public, alone, at 6 a.m., while a heron stares at you like you've insulted its family.

---

PART 6. A 600-YEAR-OLD OBSESSION

You think this is a modern hobby? You think this is something people do on weekends because they discovered it on a screen?

Humans have been fishing for tens of thousands of years. We have found fishing hooks carved from shell that are older than farming, older than cities, older than writing.

Somebody sat by water, wrapped a line around a finger, and waited.

Before there was a single word on a page, there was a person staring at the surface of a lake, waiting for it to move.

In 1653, a man named Izaak Walton published a book called The Compleat Angler. It was part guide, part philosophy, part love letter to doing absolutely nothing beside a river. It has been reprinted again and again for hundreds of years, and people are still quoting it.

Why? Because the thing he was describing never changed.

The rods changed. The line changed. The floats went from quills and cork to foam and carbon.

The feeling is the same.

You, in the present, looking at a float on a screen, are connected by a straight line to a person on a riverbank before the pyramids were finished.

That is not a fishing video.

That is a very old human nerve being touched.

---

PART 7. THE ANATOMY OF A FLOAT

Let me ruin your ability to ignore floats forever.

A float is a tiny, brutally honest instrument. It was designed to do one job: tell you what's happening where you can't see.

The tip, usually painted bright red, orange, or yellow, sticks above the water. That's the display screen.

The body provides buoyancy.

The weights on the line below are balanced so that only a few millimeters of tip remain visible. This is called shotting, and it is an art form. Too much tip showing and the float is stubborn, it resists small movements. Too little and it drowns at the first breeze.

When it's right, the float stands as sensitive as a seismograph.

A fish lifting the bait off the bottom makes the float rise. A fish pulling it down makes it sink. A fish swimming sideways makes it glide. A fish pulling it under makes it vanish.

Four moves. Four messages. All delivered in silence, in a language that looks like nothing to anyone who doesn't speak it.

Once you speak it, you can never go back to seeing a pond as just water.

You see a message board.

---

PART 8. THE SOUND

Now the title of the video. Say it out loud.

Slup.

That is the sound a fish makes when it sips something from the surface. A tiny, wet, almost embarrassing noise. A kiss with no romance.

It's one of the most beautiful sounds in the natural world and almost nobody has ever consciously heard it.

Think about that. A whole sound, a whole behavior, happening in ponds, canals, and rivers around the planet every single second of every single day. Millions of little slups that no one is there to hear.

And somebody pointed a phone at it and captured it.

That's the entire content strategy of the universe: take something invisible, shrink it into 27 seconds, and make a person who has never held a rod feel their heart rate climb.

Turn the volume up. Put on headphones. Watch it again.

The second time you will hear what the first time hid.

---

PART 9. WHY SO MANY PEOPLE QUIETLY OBSESS

Let me say something that sounds exaggerated and isn't.

Millions of people around the world fish. Not as a career. Not for show. Just because.

They get up in the dark. They drive to the same bank. They set up the same chair. They pour the same tea. They sit.

And ask them why, and you get the same answer in forty different accents:

"It's the only time my head is quiet."

That's the secret. That is the whole sport.

We live in a species-wide state of overstimulation. Every minute of the day, something is asking for something. A phone buzzes. A screen glows. A voice demands a reply.

Then you stand at a pond, and the entire world shrinks to a single colored dot.

One object. One job. One question: will it move?

Researchers have studied time spent near water for years, and the general finding is hard to miss. People feel calmer, more focused, and less stressed near lakes, rivers, and the sea. There's even a name for it: blue space.

But there's a twist nobody sells you.

It isn't the calm that hooks people.

It's the calm with a charge inside it.

A meditation app gives you peace. A float gives you peace with a loaded spring underneath.

You are relaxed and ready to explode at the same time.

There is no other feeling quite like it.

---

PART 10. THE FIRST CATCH THAT CHANGES A PERSON

Everybody remembers their first one.

Not the biggest. Not the best. The first.

The way the float went. The way the line tightened. The way the rod bent into a perfect arc and something on the other end of that string pulled back with a will that felt totally out of proportion to its size.

A small fish can feel enormous at the end of thin line. A hand-sized fish can feel like a truck. Your brain has no way to calibrate this the first time.

You'll hear people laugh at the "tiny fish" photos online, the ones where somebody holds up something the size of a sandwich with the face of a lottery winner.

Don't laugh.

That face is real. That face is a human being who just completed a conversation with a wild animal using nothing but a thread and patience.

The animal said "no," then said "maybe," then said "okay."

And they answered it correctly.

---

PART 11. THE TINY DETAILS NOBODY NOTICES

If you've watched the video once, you've seen the main event.

Watch it a second time and notice what surrounds it.

The rings on the surface. The way they spread, overlap, fade. Each ring is a record of something that happened. A ripple is a timestamp.

The reflection of the sky sliding across the water, soft yellow clouds stretched thin like paint. Water is a mirror that lies about depth. You are looking at the sky and the lake at the same time and your eyes can't decide which is which.

A leaf, drifting by with absolutely no idea it's in a story.

The line, thin as a thought, drawing a pale diagonal between your hand and an invisible decision.

Each of these things is doing nothing and everything. They are the set dressing for a tiny play with one actor.

That actor wears red and yellow, and they are about to disappear.

---

PART 12. THE MATH OF A BITE

Here is a number that will bother you.

An experienced angler might spend a long stretch of time on the water for a single bite that matters. Hours of attention for a few seconds of action.

Run the ratio. If a session lasts four hours and the decisive moment lasts four seconds, then 99.97 percent of the experience is waiting.

So why do people come back?

Because the waiting is not empty. The waiting is where the story is loaded. It's the inhale before the shout. It's the staircase before the surprise.

Without the long quiet, the strike means nothing. With the long quiet, it means everything.

Great films understand this. Great jokes understand this. Great horror understands this best of all.

Tension is not the opposite of boredom.

Tension is boredom with a secret.

And the secret, in this case, is under the surface, hungry, curious, and about thirty centimeters from a hook.

---

PART 13. THINGS THAT LIVE UNDER THAT GREY SKY

Let me show you what's really down there, because the more you know, the harder you'll stare at that dot.

Carp, crucian, bream, roach, perch, tench. Different shapes. Different moods. Different tricks.

Carp are the heavyweights of freshwater. They can live for decades, and some individuals in well-kept waters reach ages that surprise even experienced anglers. They have no true stomach. They eat almost constantly, grinding food with teeth set deep in the throat.

Crucian carp are among the great survivors of the natural world. In oxygen-starved, ice-covered ponds in winter, some can switch their metabolism and produce alcohol in their tissues to keep going when there's no oxygen to burn. A fish that brews its own antifreeze to outlast a frozen pond.

Roach move in shoals and read danger faster than a stock trader reads a crash.

Perch hunt in packs and strike like thrown knives.

Every one of these animals has its own rhythm of biting. Its own way of making a float behave. Its own signature in the water.

A good angler doesn't just see a float move.

They read the handwriting.

---

PART 14. THE RULES NOBODY WRITES DOWN

Every serious angler follows a set of unwritten laws. Nobody teaches them. You absorb them like weather.

Rule one: never trust a quiet float. A float that hasn't moved for ten minutes is not safe. It is loading.

Rule two: the bite you ignore is always the big one. Always. This is not superstition. This is statistics wearing a hat.

Rule three: the moment you look away to pour tea, check a message, or scratch your nose, the float will do the one thing you've waited all morning to see. It knows. Nobody can prove it, but it knows.

Rule four: stillness is a skill. The less you move, the more the water forgets you exist. Fish can sense a heavy step on the bank. The patient angler becomes part of the furniture.

Rule five: the line between "I missed it" and "I read it perfectly" is about a third of a second.

Rule six: nobody ever wins an argument with a fish.

You can win a battle. You can win an afternoon. You can win a whole season.

But the fish always gets the last word, because the fish is the one who gets to decide whether the day was a story or a shrug.

---

PART 15. A SMALL EXPERIMENT FOR YOU

Try this. Right now. Don't scroll.

Scroll back to the video, press play, and for the next twenty-seven seconds do not look at anything else. No glance at the corner of the screen. No peek at the notifications. No reading the replies.

Just the float.

Notice what happens to your body.

Your shoulders will rise slightly. Your jaw will tighten. Your breathing will shorten. Somewhere around the middle, your eyes will stop wandering and lock to a single point the way a cat's do right before a jump.

You have not moved. You have not been threatened. You are in your kitchen, or a train, or a bed.

And a few square centimeters of water has taken control of your nervous system.

That is not a trick of editing.

That is evolution doing exactly what it was built to do.

For hundreds of thousands of years, the humans who watched water carefully were the humans who ate. The ones who could hold still, stay alert, and react in an instant to a tiny movement were the ones who survived. We are the descendants of people who stared at ripples.

Your attention span wasn't broken by the internet.

It was just waiting for the right ripple.

---

PART 16. THE SOCIAL LIFE OF A POND

There's a whole world at the edge of every fishing spot that has nothing to do with fish.

The dog that walks past every morning at the same time. The old man with the folding stool who arrives before dawn and has never once been seen to catch anything, and who has also never once looked unhappy.

The kingfisher that flashes by like a thrown jewel and makes everyone on the bank go quiet at once.

The ducks that investigate your bait box with the confidence of tax inspectors.

The tiny arguments over where to cast. The shared flask. The nod between strangers that means more than most conversations.

Fishing is one of the last places on earth where two adults can sit for three hours, say eleven words, and consider the day a perfect friendship.

There is a kind of masculinity and femininity and neither in it. Just a shared agreement. We are here. We are waiting. We are not in a hurry.

That alone is worth more than most things people pay for.

---

PART 17. WHY SHORT VIDEOS LIKE THIS EXPLODE

Let me break down, as someone who studies this stuff for a living, why a clip like this works.

First: it opens in the middle of a question. No intro. No logo. No explanation. Straight into a float on the water. Your brain immediately asks, "what's going to happen?"

Second: the frame has one focal point. In a chaotic feed, a single bright color on a flat background is the easiest thing in the world for the eye to lock onto.

Third: nothing is forced. There's no host shouting. No text screaming. The water does the talking. People trust things that aren't trying to sell them something.

Fourth: it has a real payoff. Not a fake one. Not a clickbait cut. The tension builds and then releases in the water, in front of you, in real time.

Fifth: it has sound. The small wet slup of a fish at the surface is the kind of detail that makes a clip feel like a place instead of a file.

Sixth: it's short enough to rewatch. And a rewatch is the strongest signal any viral post can send.

The best content in the world isn't loud.

It's specific, honest, and built around a question the viewer can't resist answering.

---

PART 18. THE QUESTION BEHIND THE QUESTION

Strip away the water, the rod, and the fish, and the video is asking you something.

How long can you stay with something uncertain before you demand an outcome?

Most of modern life trains the answer to be "three seconds."

Skip. Swipe. Next.

We have built an entire civilization on the idea that anything slow is broken. If a page loads slowly, we leave. If a person replies slowly, we spiral. If a plan takes years, we quit in months.

And then there's a man on a bank who has been staring at a single colored dot for three hours and is happier than anyone you know.

What does he understand that you don't?

That the outcome was never the point. The attention was.

The act of being fully, uselessly, wonderfully present for one small moving thing is the rarest luxury left on earth. You can't buy it. You can't automate it. You can't speed it up.

You can only stand there. And wait. And watch.

And if you're lucky, the water will answer.

---

PART 19. THE MOMENT BEFORE THE MOMENT

Let's go back to the float, because we've been away from it too long.

Picture it again. Red tip. Yellow bead. Grey water. The rings around it spreading slowly outward, getting fainter, getting wider, like thoughts that have run out of things to say.

Everything on the surface says calm.

Everything in your chest says otherwise.

Because you know something the water doesn't want you to know yet. You know that the stillness has a half-life. That nothing stays this quiet. That the quiet is just the part before.

You've seen what happens when the line draws tight. You've felt what it's like when the tip slides sideways, hesitates, and then simply goes.

And you know that when it goes, there will be no time to think.

Only a hand, a wrist, and the oldest reflex in the world.

---

PART 20. WHAT HAPPENS NEXT

I'm not going to tell you.

That's the point.

If I tell you, you'll nod, scroll, and forget it in nine seconds. If I don't, you'll go back to the video and watch the surface with a slightly different pair of eyes.

You'll watch the red tip more carefully. You'll notice how the rings change. You'll catch the instant where calm tilts into something else. You'll feel your pulse do that small, silly, ancient thing it does when something alive is about to happen near water.

That's the whole trick.

The story isn't in my words. It isn't in the caption. It isn't even in the fish.

It's in the half second where you realize you've been holding your breath for a minute and a half and you didn't notice.

Press play.

Then press it again.

---

PART 21. FOR THE ONES WHO ALREADY KNOW

If you fish, you already felt it.

You felt it in the first three seconds, before the float even moved. Something in the way the line sat. Something in the way the light hit the surface. A small tightness behind the sternum that says, "Here we go."

You don't need me to explain it.

You've stood there in the cold, in the heat, in the drizzle, in the wind, in the silence. You've sat through mornings that gave you nothing and afternoons that gave you everything. You've lost fish that you still think about and landed ones you'll never forget.

You know why people say they "go fishing" when they mean something else entirely.

They mean: I am going to go and be a person again.

And if you've never fished, and this is your first time paying attention to a float, I'll say one thing.

Welcome. You're one of us now. There's no cure.

---

PART 22. THE THREE THINGS EVERY GREAT VIDEO NEEDS

Since you made it this far, here are the three ingredients behind anything that makes people stop.

One: a question the viewer didn't know they had.

Two: a tension that builds without anyone telling them to feel it.

Three: a payoff that lands slightly differently from what they expected.

Everything else is lighting.

A float on the water gives you all three in under half a minute. That's not an accident. It's the oldest storytelling structure on earth, played out in a miniature theater where the stage is a pond and the lead actor weighs four grams.

Great creators learn from this. Great stories learn from this. Great lives, honestly, might learn from this.

Be still. Pay attention. Wait for the real thing.

And when it comes, don't flinch.

---

PART 23. WHY YOU'LL WATCH IT A THIRD TIME

The first time, you watch for the fish.

The second time, you watch for the float.

The third time, you stop watching either one. You watch the water itself: the slow breathing of the surface, the way light slides across it, the way a whole afternoon seems to fit inside a single frame.

That's when the clip stops being a clip.

It becomes a window.

And through that window you can see something that's very hard to find anywhere else online: a moment that isn't trying to be anything. No filter. No script. No performance. Just a small piece of the real world, doing what it has always done, while you hold still and let it.

Most of the internet wants your reaction.

This asks only for your attention.

That's why it works.

---

FINAL WORD

Somewhere right now, a float is sitting on a surface that looks perfectly empty.

Nobody is watching it. No camera. No audience. No applause waiting.

And under it, a living creature is deciding whether to believe a lie.

That's happening on a canal in the Netherlands. A reservoir in Texas. A river in Finland. A rice-field pond in China. A crumbling concrete pier in a city you've never visited.

Every second of every day, somewhere on this planet, a small colored dot is about to move.

You just got to watch one.

Now go back up. Hit play. Turn the sound on. Don't blink.

And if you see it dip, if you catch that tiny shiver in the red tip before everyone else does, drop a single word in the replies.

Slup.

Let's see how many of you caught it.

text:
Wikipedia records confirm that Jobs told Wozniak Atari had paid only $700—resulting in Wozniak receiving $350—when Atari had actually paid approximately $5,000. Reports from Business Insider and Yahoo Finance confirm that Jobs refused to grant Kottke stock options; when another executive offered to match whatever amount Jobs was willing to give, Jobs replied, "Fine, I'll give him zero." Wozniak subsequently gave away about $10 million worth of his own stock to early employees who had been excluded.

The *Breakout* Incident: Verifiable Details
Atari's actual payment. The Wikipedia entry for Steve Jobs explicitly states: "According to Wozniak, Jobs told him Atari had only given them $700 (instead of the actual $5,000 payment), so Wozniak's share was $350. Wozniak did not learn the actual bonus amount until ten years later." Reports from Business Insider and 9to5Google confirm this figure.

Wozniak's reaction. Wozniak said that if Jobs had told him the truth and explained that he needed the money, "I would have given it all to him." A report by Infobae quotes Wozniak: "I cried many times when I found out the truth. But what hurt more was the betrayal by a friend, not the money."

Technical achievement. Working non-stop for four days and nights, Wozniak reduced the chip count from over 100 to between 42 and 46. Atari engineers typically used 150 or more chips. Jobs used his share of the money to buy a farm in Oregon.

The Kottke Incident: Verifiable Details
Jobs's refusal. When another Apple executive confronted Jobs about Kottke’s lack of stock options—offering to match whatever amount Jobs was willing to grant—Jobs replied, "Fine, I’ll give him zero." Kottke, a college friend of Jobs who had traveled to India with him, was Apple’s twelfth employee.

Wozniak’s response. Wozniak created the "Woz Plan," offering up to 2,000 shares from his own holdings to the excluded early employees at $5 per share—at a time when the IPO price was already $22. In total, he gave away personal stock worth approximately $10 million. Wozniak said, "I did it because it was the right thing to do."

Wozniak’s logic. He explained that his motivation stemmed partly from his experience at Hewlett-Packard, where quarterly profit-sharing made employees feel like owners. He said, "It didn't feel right to me. I felt that everyone around us was part of the effort."

Verdict
The core facts of the story—that Jobs cheated Wozniak out of the "Breakout" bonus and refused to grant Kottke stock during the Apple IPO, while Wozniak compensated the excluded employees with his own shares—have been confirmed by multiple independent sources. The tension between Jobs’s business genius and his personal conduct is a recurring theme in the history of Silicon Valley. The description by *Corriere della Sera*—"a genius and a visionary, yet also a tough, ruthless businessman who gave nothing away and always demanded a great deal"—captures this contradiction. Wozniak’s choice, however, points to a different logic: success need not come at the cost of betrayal, even if it means bearing a personal cost.

text:
We Know How to Fix Homelessness. Why Don’t More Cities Do It?

Listen · 10:16 min
13OCT2026
By German Lopez
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/iam4mN83U0
Mr. Lopez is a writer for the editorial board.

Homelessness, all appearances to the contrary, is a long-solved problem. We know both the causes and the cure. You wouldn’t think that’s the case from visiting many U.S. cities. Stymied by political and financial hurdles, progressive bastions including Los Angeles, Seattle and Burlington, Vt., appear to have given up. They have surrendered public spaces to the homeless and their encampments to the point that it’s difficult to describe these spaces as truly for the public anymore.

Denver shows what happens when a city puts into place proven policies with determination and focus. Not only has it dramatically reduced homelessness, it embarrasses every other urban jurisdiction that has failed to deal with its Covid-era surge of homeless encampments. Other cities no longer have an excuse.

Denver has recorded the biggest recent drop in street homelessness among the largest U.S. cities, according to my analysis of local data. The city’s drop was roughly 13 times the national rate in 2025, the most recent year for federal statistics. Since 2023, Denver’s unsheltered population is down 64 percent. “What they’re doing is working,” said Samantha Batko, a senior fellow at the left-leaning Urban Institute, which is independently evaluating the city’s progress.

Since Mayor Mike Johnston of Denver took office in 2023, he has focused on getting unsheltered homelessness to zero. He has done so by using some fairly standard ideas. Police officers break up homeless encampments, warning that repeated violations could lead to arrest. With the help of social workers, the city connects those people to services and shelters. Crucially, it has expanded those services to ensure that officers and social workers have something to connect people to.

By successfully combining enforcement and social services, Denver demonstrates that cities don’t need to choose between those binaries. They should do both.

Politically, none of this is easy. On the policing side, progressives remain skeptical of using law enforcement to deal with what they see as largely an economic issue. On the housing side, the constraint is money. Building housing and shelters requires public and private funds that cities often don’t have and aren’t willing to prioritize over other spending and tax cuts.

Speaking from an office stuffed with Colorado memorabilia, Mr. Johnston said he wanted to go further. He laid out a vision to ensure that all people are housed and that public spaces are actually available to the public. “Our fundamental mantra when we started was our belief that all of our problems are solvable and we’re the ones to solve them,” he told me.

On a Monday afternoon, Mr. Johnston played tour guide. He wanted to show me the city’s new homeless shelters and how they differed from traditional facilities. We walked 10 minutes from City Hall — the mayor stopped to congratulate a wedding party on the way out — to a block of tiny houses known as Elati Village.

Each resident there gets a small house that offers a level of privacy not typical for homeless shelters. Valentino Ortiz, a former Elati Village resident and a transgender man, said privacy was important for his safety. He recalled a previous stay at a more traditional shelter. “The third day, I was already getting sexually assaulted,” he said. At Elati, “you have a beautiful tiny home to call your own. You have hot showers, you can cook your own meals and do laundry.”

Next, Mr. Johnston took me to The Aspen, a city-owned hotel. For residents, it is like an apartment complex. The rooms weren’t too different from places I’ve lived before. Mr. Johnston said he wanted the city’s shelters to feel like real homes — “a room of one’s own.”

As we walked through the building, residents told the mayor they finally had been able to get their lives in order. Staff at The Aspen and other shelters spend much of their time preparing people to leave. They help residents get the documents they need to find a job and permanent housing. They connect them to training, education programs and additional government aid, including housing vouchers and rent subsidies. Residents don’t face hard limits on how long they can stay, but providers are, under their contracts, evaluated on how many people they help get on the right path.

The goal is to keep people off the streets for good. To that end, the city still has to address the high cost of housing. Denver has enacted some reforms, but buying and renting a home remain too expensive for much of the poor and middle class.

Ana Miller, an organizer for the homeless rights group Housekeys Action Network Denver, criticized The Aspen for some of its rules and their enforcement, particularly the staff’s room inspections. She also panned the shelter’s provider, Urban Alchemy, which has faced criticisms in other cities for its unorthodox tactics, including its hiring of ex-convicts as staff members. Ms. Miller said Elati Village offers a better model than typical shelters, but she worried about resistance from neighborhoods to building more such communities. The neighbors living in apartments near Elati “literally point cameras at the community and watch them,” she said.

Still, the numbers speak for themselves. Mr. Johnston said that no one has declined an offer to move into one of the new facilities, and that they are consistently at or near capacity. The city’s biggest problem is how it can buy or build more places like Elati Village and The Aspen to meet demand.

Much of the tens of millions of dollars the city has spent on shelters was paid for through temporary federal funds that have expired. The Trump administration has also moved to cut housing subsidies across the country. The financial constraints have led some local officials to question whether the cost of the city’s efforts is worth the benefit. If that sentiment spreads, it could doom progress.

At 6:30 a.m. on Tuesday, I met with a Denver police squad to see the enforcement side of the city’s strategy. Officer Michael Nierenberg, who led the group, told me his goal was not to arrest people. Tall and imposing, he said the threat he presented was only an incentive to push people to get help. Social workers rode along.

Early in the patrol, we came across a tent. Inside, a couple slept with all their belongings scattered across the floor. Officer Nierenberg waited patiently as they woke up, and then explained the consequences of breaking laws against camping outside: a verbal warning, then a written warning, then a ticket or arrest. He started asking about the couple’s situation. They were from Texas, they said, and still had family there. They would like to go back, but they didn’t have the means to do so.

Officer Nierenberg told them to pack up their tent and that he would go see what he could do. He sat in his car, making calls and looking through his computer. After about 15 minutes, he came back with a bus ticket. The man, who identified himself as Chance, cried tears of joy.

We continued like this for the rest of the morning. Sometimes the encounters were less pleasant. One man told the officers, in colorful language, to go away. Other times, people were cordial. “It has been a typical morning,” the officer told me as we headed back to the police station.

Progressives tend to view the enforcement side of anti-homelessness strategies with disdain because it can involve criminalizing an economic or a mental health issue. At the same time, residents don’t want encampments clogging up parks and sidewalks. Progressive cities have tried to get around the dilemma by flooding the streets with social services, hoping that offers of help would get people on the streets to pack up. The reality, as cities have painfully learned, is that people often need a stronger push to abandon their tents.

The balanced approach has shrunk the number of encampments across Denver, the Urban Institute’s evaluation found. Between 2023 and 2025, the number of active encampments fell by nearly half. The number of large encampments, with 10 or more tents or structures, dropped by 91 percent. “It’s pretty much night and day,” said Anthony Mantelli, whose family runs the West Saloon and Kitchen in the city’s 16th Street Mall. “I close the restaurant four or five nights a week. I don’t deal with many issues at all.”

Mayor Johnston described his strategy through his perspective as a former school principal. “Your job is to keep everyone safe,” he said. “That means I love every single kid in the building. And if there’s one kid who’s making other kids in the building feel unsafe, my job is to either help him change his behavior or hold him accountable for it.”

I asked Mr. Johnston if it’s realistic to think a city as large as Denver can eliminate street homelessness. “I genuinely believe we can do it,” he said.

The next phase will be more difficult. Those who continue to live on the streets are much more likely to suffer from mental illness and addiction. They need more than a roof over their heads.

For this step, Mr. Johnston has begun an initiative that focuses on connecting people to mental health and addiction treatment. That will be hard to execute. Many of the sick and addicted are resistant to treatment, and getting them to accept help can require a kind of coercion and policing of low-level crimes that many progressives are uncomfortable with.

I came away from Denver convinced that the mayor’s focus and determination are the most crucial factors. I’ve seen this happen nationwide: Policies that work in one place fail in another because officials can replicate the law or the money, but not the leadership — the force of will — behind the original success.

But Democrats around the country should figure out how to copy Denver’s program. The party’s failure to tackle homelessness and public disorder more broadly has haunted it nationwide. It’s one reason the party is unpopular, even as President Trump has approval ratings in the 30s, leaving many voters with two options on the ballot they don’t particularly like.

“When you see a problem in front of you every day and nothing happens, your only option is either to blame your neighbor or to blame democracy,” Mr. Johnston said. Mr. Trump “has proved that if things are bad enough, Americans are open to both of those arguments.”

He added: “I think the opposite’s also true. If you can prove that there’s something hard to do and we work it out together and it gets better, you train people’s muscle memory to turn to each other — not to turn on each other.”

More on housing and homelessness

Strengthening Mental Health Support in Wyoming County

On September 23, 2026, WNY R-AHEC had the opportunity to train and certify staff from WCCHS (Wyoming County Community Health System) in Mental Health First Aid!

Mental Health First Aid gives participants the knowledge and skills to recognize signs and symptoms of mental health and substance use challenges, respond with confidence, offer initial support, and connect individuals with appropriate resources and professional help.

Training staff in Mental Health First Aid helps strengthen the support network within our healthcare and community systems. These skills can make an important difference when someone is experiencing a mental health challenge and may not know where to turn. 

We’re proud to partner with WCCHS and support their commitment to the health and well-being of individuals and families throughout Wyoming County. Together, we can continue to increase mental health awareness, reduce stigma, and build communities where people feel supported and know that help is available.

Thank you to the WCCHS staff who took the time to participate and invest in their own knowledge and the well-being of the community they serve!

@wycohealthsys

13:36 SWITZERLAND 🇨🇭 | 06:36 CME / CHICAGO 🇺🇸
NQ / NASDAQ — MORNING REGIME RADAR
13 OCT 2026

MAIN CONCLUSION: NQ begins Tuesday under pressure from a global semiconductor sell-off rather than from the bond market. Nasdaq-100 futures are down roughly 0.5%–0.7%, while the US 10Y has retreated towards 5.19%–5.20%, oil is falling and the dollar has softened. That combination is unusual: the macro denominator is improving, but technology is still weakening. The market is therefore confronting a much more important question — whether concerns about AI competition, capital intensity and future returns are beginning to outweigh the benefit of lower yields.
KEY CONFIRMATION / RISK: Today’s critical signal is whether NQ and SOX can recover while the 10Y remains near 5.2%. If technology fails to respond positively to lower yields, lower oil and a softer dollar, the weakness is increasingly internal to the AI/semiconductor complex rather than simply macro-driven.
MONDAY’S HOLIDAY SESSION LEFT A WEAK TECHNOLOGY HANDOFF
Monday’s US cash session operated without normal Treasury cash-market participation because of the bond-market holiday.
The S&P 500 finished almost flat, the Dow advanced, but Nasdaq fell approximately 0.4%.
That divergence already suggested some rotation away from technology.
Today the Treasury market is fully back, and the initial message is important.
Yields are lower.
Oil is lower.
The dollar is softer.
Yet Nasdaq futures are weaker.
That makes Tuesday fundamentally different from several recent sell-offs.

These reports are free. If you find this analysis useful, please LIKE and REPOST it so it reaches more traders, and leave a comment with your view.

TODAY’S PROBLEM IS COMING FROM INSIDE TECHNOLOGY
For much of the past two weeks, NQ weakness could be explained through the macro denominator.
Yields rose.
Oil rose.
The dollar strengthened.
The discount rate became more restrictive.
Today, those variables are actually providing some relief.
The US 10Y is around 5.19%–5.20%, materially below the recent 5.36% extreme.
Brent has retreated towards approximately $104–$105.
The dollar has eased from recent highs.
And Nasdaq futures are still lower.
That is important information.
THE GLOBAL CHIP SELL-OFF IS THE CENTRAL EVENT
The semiconductor weakness began in Asia and has spread globally.
South Korea’s KOSPI suffered a dramatic decline, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix falling sharply.
Taiwan and Japan also saw technology weakness.
US semiconductor stocks are following that move in pre-market trading, with NVIDIA, AMD and Micron among the names under pressure.
This is not simply another routine NQ pullback.
The market is reassessing competitive positioning across the global semiconductor industry.
CHINESE MEMORY COMPETITION HAS BECOME A REAL VARIABLE
A major catalyst is growing concern around technological progress from China’s memory-chip industry.
The market is beginning to consider the possibility that Chinese manufacturers can narrow the technological gap faster than previously assumed.
That matters particularly for memory producers.
For years, the bullish assumption was that leading-edge semiconductor technology would remain highly concentrated among a relatively small number of companies.
If that competitive moat begins narrowing, investors must reassess future pricing power, margins and returns on capital.
This does not destroy the semiconductor cycle.
But it changes the valuation debate.
MICRON IS PARTICULARLY EXPOSED TO THIS QUESTION
Micron is under meaningful pre-market pressure.
That makes sense.
Memory is one of the semiconductor segments where additional Chinese competition could have a direct impact on pricing and future supply.
The AI cycle has created enormous demand for high-bandwidth memory.
But high demand alone does not guarantee permanently high margins if supply competition increases.
The distinction becomes:
AI DEMAND STRONG
versus
WHO CAPTURES THE ECONOMIC RETURN?
That may become one of the next major questions for the semiconductor trade.
BROADCOM ADDED ANOTHER LAYER OF CAUTION
Comments from Broadcom CEO Hock Tan have also attracted significant attention.
His warning about speculative behaviour around parts of AI investment has reinforced concerns that capital may be flowing into projects without adequate understanding of eventual economic returns.
This does not mean Broadcom is bearish on AI.
That distinction is important.
The concern is not whether AI technology matters.
The concern is whether every investment being made under the AI label will generate sufficient returns.
That is exactly the debate we identified last week.
THE AI STORY IS ENTERING A MORE MATURE PHASE
The first phase of the AI trade asked:
Is the technology real?
The answer increasingly became yes.
The second phase asked:
Will demand create enormous semiconductor and infrastructure revenue?
Again, the answer has largely been yes.
The third phase is more difficult:
Who actually earns an adequate return on the capital being deployed?
That question introduces competition, financing costs, depreciation, power requirements and infrastructure utilisation into the valuation equation.
The market is becoming more discriminating.
That is healthy long term.
It can create substantial volatility short term.
THE 10Y IS ACTUALLY HELPING NQ TODAY
The US 10Y is around 5.19%–5.20%, well below last week’s approximately 5.36% high.
This is exactly the kind of movement that normally supports technology.
The 30Y has also eased from its recent multi-decade extreme.
That gives us an unusually clean analytical test.
If NQ can stabilise and recover while yields remain lower, the macro relief is working.
If NQ continues falling despite lower yields, the market is signalling that the problem has moved from the denominator to the numerator.
That distinction may define today’s session.
THIS IS THE REVERSE OF LAST WEEK’S REGIME
Last week, the question was:
Can strong AI fundamentals overcome rising yields?
Today the question is:
Can falling yields compensate for weakening confidence in parts of the AI trade?
That reversal is extremely important.
A market where NQ rises despite higher yields demonstrates fundamental strength.
A market where NQ falls despite lower yields suggests the earnings or valuation narrative itself is being questioned.
That does not automatically mean the broader bull market is over.
But it changes what traders need to monitor.
OIL IS PROVIDING RELIEF
Brent has fallen roughly 2% and is trading around the $104–$105 region after Monday’s rise above $106.
WTI is near $91–$92.
The decline follows improved expectations for additional fuel supply while geopolitical risks remain elevated.
For NQ, the direction is helpful.
The familiar chain now works in reverse:
OIL ↓ → INFLATION PRESSURE ↓ → TERM PREMIUM ↓ → TREASURY YIELDS ↓ → VALUATION RELIEF.
The fact that technology is still weak despite this support reinforces the significance of the semiconductor story.
THE DOLLAR IS ALSO LESS HOSTILE
DXY has pulled back from recent highs.
That represents another improvement in financial conditions.
A weaker dollar normally benefits multinational technology earnings and global liquidity.
Again, this creates an important asymmetry.
The external macro environment is not worsening this morning.
The technology complex itself is generating the weakness.
That makes semiconductor breadth today's most important equity signal.
THE BANK EARNINGS SEASON HAS STARTED
Major US banks begin reporting today, providing the first substantial earnings evidence of the new quarter.
JPMorgan and Wells Fargo have already reported, with profits improving but investor reactions relatively cautious.
The important information for the broader market extends beyond individual EPS numbers.
Investors need to understand:
loan demand,
credit quality,
consumer resilience,
investment banking,
trading activity,
and how much higher Treasury yields are affecting financial conditions.
Banks provide a broad diagnostic of the economy.
Technology provides the valuation debate.
Together, they begin shifting the market from macro speculation towards earnings evidence.
THE BROADER EARNINGS BAR IS EXTREMELY HIGH
Consensus expectations point to approximately 30% year-on-year S&P 500 earnings growth for the third quarter, with technology and energy expected to be major contributors.
That is extraordinary.
But high expectations create asymmetric risk.
Companies do not merely need to grow.
They need to exceed already demanding assumptions.
This becomes especially important for AI companies where valuations already reflect years of exceptional expansion.
Good results may no longer be enough.
The market may demand exceptional results plus credible return on investment.
THE IMF HAS ADDED A SYSTEMIC WARNING
The latest global financial-stability assessment has highlighted the increasing amount of leverage and complex financing associated with AI investment.
That matters because the numbers involved are enormous.
The concern is not that AI investment is inherently unsustainable.
It is that a significant disappointment in AI profitability could produce a larger financial-market adjustment because the investment cycle increasingly involves debt, private capital and interconnected financing structures.
This reinforces the framework we have been developing:
AI strengthens future earnings.
But AI also consumes extraordinary amounts of capital.
THE NUMERATOR / DENOMINATOR FRAMEWORK HAS EVOLVED AGAIN
The original structure was simple.
NUMERATOR: AI demand, earnings growth, semiconductor revenues, cloud investment.
DENOMINATOR: Treasury yields, oil, inflation, dollar and financing costs.
Today, the denominator is improving.
But the numerator itself is becoming more complicated.
Competition is increasing.
Capital intensity is rising.
Investors are questioning returns.
Therefore the market can no longer assume that every dollar of additional AI spending creates the same amount of shareholder value.
That is a major evolution.
SOX IS TODAY’S MOST IMPORTANT INTERNAL INDICATOR
The broader semiconductor index matters more than NQ itself during the first part of the session.
If SOX absorbs the Asian sell-off and begins recovering after the US open, the market may conclude that the competitive concerns have been exaggerated.
If SOX continues lower despite falling yields, the signal becomes much more serious.
The ideal repair structure would be:
SOX recovery + NVDA stabilisation + MU/AMD improving + 10Y ≤ 5.2% + NQ recovery.
That would indicate the macro relief is eventually overpowering the semiconductor fear.
NVIDIA IS THE SYSTEMIC AI TEST
NVIDIA remains the single most important stock within the AI complex.
Its moat is different from the memory-chip companies directly exposed to Chinese DRAM competition.
That makes its reaction particularly informative.
If NVIDIA stabilises while memory and selected semiconductor names remain weak, the market is differentiating between business models rather than abandoning AI broadly.
If NVIDIA also suffers sustained institutional selling, the interpretation becomes much more serious.
That would suggest the market is reassessing the AI multiple itself.
TODAY COULD BECOME A ROTATION SESSION
Dow futures are firmer while Nasdaq futures are lower.
That creates the possibility of another rotation away from expensive growth and towards financials, healthcare and other sectors.
Rotation is not the same thing as broad risk-off.
That distinction matters.
If S&P 500 breadth remains healthy while technology falls, capital is moving rather than leaving equities.
If the weakness spreads from semiconductors into the entire market, the interpretation becomes more defensive.
Watch breadth carefully after the bell.
THE CASH OPEN WILL TELL US WHETHER THE ASIAN SELL-OFF TRANSMITS
The US cash market opens at:
15:30 SWITZERLAND | 08:30 CME / CHICAGO.
This is particularly important today.
Asian semiconductor markets experienced aggressive selling.
European technology is also weaker.
US investors now decide whether to extend that move or buy the decline.
A strong recovery after the open would indicate that US institutional investors see value in the pullback.
A failed bounce would suggest the global repricing has further to run.
TOMORROW’S CPI IS ALREADY IN THE BACKGROUND
September CPI arrives Wednesday.
That remains the most important macro event of the week.
Consensus expects headline inflation to remain elevated, while core inflation will determine whether underlying price pressure is moderating.
The importance of today's decline in oil and Treasury yields is that it provides NQ with some cushion before CPI.
A hotter-than-expected report could remove that cushion immediately.
A softer core reading could reinforce the current bond rally and provide technology with stronger valuation support.
TODAY’S REACTION MAY TELL US MORE THAN CPI EXPECTATIONS
There is a valuable test before tomorrow’s inflation report.
If technology cannot rally today even though yields, oil and the dollar are moving favourably, the market enters CPI with weakened internal structure.
If NQ and SOX recover despite the global chip sell-off, then the AI bull market has passed another significant stress test.
The market is offering a clean experiment.
Macro conditions are improving.
AI confidence is weakening.
Which one dominates?
BULLISH SCENARIO — ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE: 45%
The bullish case is that the global semiconductor sell-off becomes an overshoot.
US investors buy the weakness.
NVIDIA stabilises.
SOX recovers.
The 10Y remains around or below 5.2%.
Oil continues easing.
DXY remains contained.
The strongest confirmation would be:
SOX recovery + NQ recovery + 10Y stable/down + OIL ↓ + DXY ↓/stable + VIX contained.
That would suggest the market continues to treat AI concerns as company- and segment-specific rather than systemic.
BEARISH SCENARIO — ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE: 55%
The bearish case has the edge this morning because technology is falling despite improving macro conditions.
SOX continues lower.
NVIDIA, AMD and Micron remain under pressure.
The market interprets Chinese competition and capital-return concerns as reasons to reduce AI exposure rather than simply rotate within the sector.
The strongest bearish confirmation would be:
SOX ↓ + NQ ↓ despite 10Y ↓ + VIX ↑ + broader mega-cap weakness.
That would be particularly significant because the denominator is no longer providing the explanation.
ANALYTICAL EDGE
BULLISH: 45%
BEARISH: 55%
EDGE: SLIGHTLY BEARISH — INTERNAL TECHNOLOGY RISK IS CURRENTLY OVERRIDING A MORE SUPPORTIVE MACRO BACKDROP.
This is not a structural call against AI.
It is an assessment of today’s setup.
Lower Treasury yields, lower oil and a softer dollar would ordinarily justify a bullish NQ bias.
The fact that futures remain weaker tells us semiconductor-specific concerns deserve respect.
The opening needs to prove that buyers are willing to absorb them.
CURRENT REGIME
CURRENT REGIME: GLOBAL SEMICONDUCTOR DE-RATING / LOWER-YIELD RELIEF / AI RETURN-ON-CAPITAL SCRUTINY / EQUITY ROTATION RISK.
The market has moved into a different regime from last week.
The macro denominator is no longer the dominant immediate problem.
The debate has shifted inside the AI ecosystem.
Competition, capital requirements and future returns are increasingly important.
That makes semiconductor breadth the central confirmation signal.
FINAL ANALYTICAL VIEW
Today may be one of the most informative NQ sessions in several weeks because the market has inverted the familiar relationship.
For most of the recent period, AI fundamentals were strong while Treasury yields fought the rally.
Today, Treasury yields are helping — and AI stocks are still under pressure.
That means we can isolate the problem much more clearly.
The market is no longer asking whether AI demand exists.
It is asking whether current valuations correctly reflect competition, capital intensity and the distribution of future profits.
Chinese technological progress adds competitive uncertainty.
The enormous infrastructure buildout adds financing uncertainty.
Recent industry comments add return-on-capital uncertainty.
None of these factors implies that AI growth is ending.
But together they demand more discrimination.
The next phase of the AI trade may therefore look very different from the previous one.
Instead of every company connected to AI benefiting equally, capital may increasingly concentrate in businesses with genuine technological moats, strong cash generation and proven returns on investment.
That could create enormous dispersion within NQ itself.
For today, the hierarchy is therefore clear:
Watch SOX first.
Watch NVIDIA second.
Watch the 10Y third.
Then watch whether NQ can respond to the macro relief it is being offered.
If yields fall and technology still cannot recover, the message is important.
If semiconductors absorb the global sell-off and NQ recovers, the market will have passed another major AI stress test.

ethereum:0x5283d291dbcf85356a21ba090e6db59121208b44 Price Crashes 99% From ATH: Is Blur Officially a Dead Coin After the Shutdown News?

#BLUR has crashed nearly 37% since the Blur shutdown announcement and printed a fresh all-time low of $0.011963 today. The token is now 99.14% below its February 2023 ATH of $1.3952, a collapse that took less than four years.

To put it in simple numbers: a $10,000 investment at the top is now worth around $86.

Here is the complete breakdown: what happened, why BLUR dumped so hard, why traders loved it in 2023, and the only level that can save it from the dead coin list.

🔰 What Happened: Blur Announces Its Frontend Shutdown

On October 12, 2026, Blur confirmed in an official thread that it is closing its main platform:
➡️ The https://t.co/0qugGcfTtf frontend will be shut down on November 12, 2026
➡️ Blend, Blur's NFT lending protocol, will stop matching new loans on the same date
➡️ Borrowers must repay their Blend loans before the deadline or allow them to default
➡️ After the deadline, Blur will offer a frontend tool only for withdrawing assets
➡️ The on-chain marketplace protocol stays live, and BLUR continues to control the fee switch

The team framed it as "only the frontend," but the market read it very differently.

🔰 Why the BLUR Price Crashed So Hard in 24 Hours:
1️⃣ No frontend means almost no users. Most NFT traders use the website, not the smart contracts directly. Removing the interface removes the main source of activity.

2️⃣ Blend lending is being wound down. Blend was one of Blur's strongest products. Stopping new loans signals the team is winding down operations, not building.

3️⃣ NFT volume has collapsed. Blur's monthly trading volume fell from about $1.43 billion at its March 2023 peak to under $7 million by March 2026, a drop of more than 99.5%.

4️⃣ Token unlocks continue until February 2027. Even with the platform shutting down, new supply keeps entering the market, adding selling pressure.

5️⃣ The Blast shutdown shook confidence. The announcement came right after the shutdown news for Blast, the Layer 2 launched by the same founder, which hit trust in the wider ecosystem.

6️⃣ The team had gone silent. The Blur team posted only 4 tweets in all of 2025, and its first tweet of 2026 was the shutdown announcement. Nearly 10 months of silence followed by a closure notice is a major red flag for any investor.

🔰 Flashback to 2023: Why Everyone Loved BLUR

During the 2023 FOMO phase, BLUR was one of the most hyped tokens in crypto. Here's why:
✅ The biggest airdrop of the year. BLUR launched on Valentine's Day 2023 with a massive airdrop, and many farmers received life-changing amounts.
✅ Paradigm backing. Support from one of crypto's most respected VCs gave the project instant credibility.
✅ It dethroned OpenSea. Zero trading fees, optional royalties, and professional trading tools helped Blur capture more than 80% of Ethereum NFT volume at its peak.
✅ The points and farming meta. Season 1 and Season 2 rewards turned every trader into a farmer, which drove huge volume.
✅ The NFT-Fi narrative. The launch of Blend lending made Blur the center of the NFT finance story.
✅ Exchange listings and Blast hype. Major listings such as Upbit's KRW pair, plus the Blast L2 launch, fuelled repeated pumps.

It was the trending coin, and almost everyone was bullish. That is exactly the kind of setup where retail buys the top.

🔰 BLUR/USDT Technical Analysis (HTF Chart)

The HTF chart showed four clear exit signals long before today's crash:
👉 Exit Signal 1: A double top formed near the Feb 2024 highs
👉 Exit Signal 2: Price was rejected from a bearish order block
👉 Exit Signal 3: A breakdown below key support in Jan 2025
👉 Exit Signal 4: A second breakdown confirmed the bearish continuation
👉 Today: A fresh new low, with the structure fully bearish and a series of lower highs and lower lows

🔰 BLUR Price Prediction: Key Levels to Watch

Bullish flip level: $0.0228
➡️ BLUR must break and hold above $0.0228
➡️ It needs a confirmed HTF close above this level to signal any real reversal

Bearish scenario:
➡️ As long as BLUR stays below $0.0228, there is no bullish reversal
➡️ With the frontend shutting down and unlocks continuing, BLUR is heading toward the dead coin list

🔰 Final CryptoPatel Verdict: Is BLUR a Dead Coin?
A 99% drawdown, a shutdown announcement, collapsing volume, ongoing unlocks, and a silent team all point the same way. Until BLUR reclaims $0.0228 with an HTF close, the trend says this project is moving from NFT king to dead coin.

🔰 Lessons for CryptoPatel Investors
👉 Hype is not fundamentals
👉 Airdrop farming volume is not real demand
👉 A silent team is a warning sign, not a buying opportunity
👉 Never fall in love with any coin
👉 Always book profit when you're in good profit

What happens to Blend loans?
Borrowers have until November 12, 2026 to repay their loans or allow them to default. After that date, Blur will provide a withdrawal tool.

I got a reply from Arizona State, then never sent another message.

It's still one of the dumbest recruiting mistakes I made.

I was at school when my high school coach pulled me into a room.

Sitting there was the wide receivers coach from Arizona State.

At the time, that felt massive.

It was just the ASU coach, my head coach, and me.

No camp line.

No crowd.

Not a bunch of other quarterbacks trying to get noticed.

Just a real chance to talk to a college coach.

So I walked up, shook his hand, and introduced myself.

The first thing he said was:

“You remind me of a quarterback I coached back at Penn State, Christian Hackenberg.”

That made my day.

I probably thought about that line for the rest of the week.

We ended up talking for around 30 minutes, then I went back to class.

The next day, I sent him an email.

I did not expect much.

But he replied.

That should have been the start of a real recruiting relationship.

Not a guaranteed offer.

Not some fantasy where Arizona State was about to build the offense around me.

But a real relationship.

A coach knew my name, talked to me in person, and responded to my email.

And then I disappeared.

I never sent another email.

Never sent another message.

Never followed up with new film, a season update, or even a simple check-in.

I don't even remember the excuse, but knowing myself back then, I was probably scared.

Scared to bug him.

Scared to get rejected.

Scared to find out the interest was not as strong as I wanted it to be.

So I did nothing.

And doing nothing gave me exactly what it usually gives you.

Nothing.

Would I have gotten a scholarship from Arizona State?

Probably not.

But I would have had a better chance than I gave myself.

That is the part I want you to understand.

Follow-up is not annoying when there is already a real reason to follow up.

If a coach talks to you, replies to you, watches your film, invites you somewhere, or tells you to stay in touch, that is not the time to disappear.

That is the time to keep the door open.

Send the update.

Ask the question.

Share the new film.

Keep the relationship alive until the coach gives you a real answer.

Let the coach tell you no.

Do not tell yourself no because you were scared to send the message.

I learned that one the hard way.

text:
Read “Out of the Shadows” by @jaystratton. The subtitle promises "the truth about non-human intelligent life." Here’s what it delivers…

By my chapter count, about 45% is history we already knew, about 15–20% are newish claims, about 15% is his family's paranormal story, and only about 10–15% is actually about non-human beings or craft.

Labeling new claims takes some generosity: Stratton provides his insights on the CIA-run crash-retrieval "Legacy Program," he specifies 12 craft held by Lockheed (some with occupants), and discusses the filmed 1964 contact at Holloman AFB with some detail. None come with documentation of course, but it offers some teeth for investigators. We must assume Congress already knows - so we’ve seen what’s come of it already; nothing.

What he calls for: restore the Disclosure Act's power to seize recovered tech, amnesty for insiders, and a presidential "we are not alone." What he doesn't ask for: release of the Holloman film, or open scientific access to recovered tech. He wants 'replication efforts' kept protected and the effort led by 'the private sector' (p.288–289). Moving material from one secret program to another isn't disclosure. It's a custody transfer, and the secrecy structure stays the same without significant changes that have yet to be addressed.

The business (private sector) context, which isn't in the book: in 2022 he joined defense contractor Radiance Technologies to grow its intel business. QuantumFrontier LLC, founded by Stratton, Travis Taylor and Lue Elizondo and moved to Virginia in July 2024, says its mission is "to master and reverse engineer the world's most hyper-advanced technologies." A retired Lockheed Skunk Works tech chief was billed as its advisor on a UAP investment panel. So the book says Lockheed holds 12 craft, while its author co-founded a reverse-engineering venture advised by Lockheed's former tech chief. No wrongdoing, but readers deserve to know.

Add the media package: a HarperCollins book, Farah Films rights, and a scripted series from the Sopranos writer with HarperCollins attached. An unproven claim still seems to be worth more as a story than a settled one, and movements from the media/entertainment structures signal continued pursuit rather than expected revelations are even the insiders hedge.

Verdict: a gripping insider memoir. The hunt without the answer. Credible-sounding revelation inside a commercial framework. Watch whether the asks ever go past where the companies begin.

text:
Good morning, dear friends. As the soft light of dawn gently breaks across the sky this October morning, I’m grateful to pause with you and reflect on a beautiful promise from Scripture. Isaiah 41:10 reminds us, “Fear not, I am with you...” These words, spoken by God Himself, offer a steady anchor for whatever this day may bring.

Many of us wake with quiet worries pressing on our hearts. Perhaps you’re thinking about work deadlines or financial pressures that seem to grow heavier each week. Maybe family health concerns or the well-being of loved ones far away keep you up at night. In a world filled with rapid changes, political tensions, and everyday uncertainties, it’s natural to feel a little unsteady as we step into the hours ahead.

Yet God meets us exactly where we are. He does not ask us to pretend the challenges aren’t real. Instead, He simply says, “Fear not, I am with you.” That presence changes everything. It means we don’t face the commute, the difficult conversation, the doctor’s report, or the news headlines alone. His companionship is personal, steady, and available right now.

Think for a moment about the small moments that make up today: the first cup of coffee, the walk to the car, the emails waiting in your inbox. In each of those ordinary places, the same God who spoke to Isaiah walks beside you. When anxiety rises, we can quietly return to His promise and let it settle our breathing and our thoughts.

This hope also moves us outward. As we feel God’s nearness, we become better able to notice others who are carrying burdens. A text of encouragement, a patient word, or simply listening can become ways we share the comfort we’ve received. In a time when so many feel isolated, these small acts of presence reflect the greater Presence that never leaves us.

So let’s carry Isaiah’s words with us through the morning and into the afternoon. Whatever rises up today, remember you are held by the One who promises to be with you. There is strength, peace, and hope in that truth.

text:
After the Ledger Incident, Are Cold Wallets Still Safer Than CEXs?

“A user bought the dip in June, accumulating 80 BTC. Just a week ago, they transferred the entire amount to a Ledger wallet. Now, all of it has been stolen.”

Recent security incidents involving Ledger have once again put cold wallets under the spotlight.

Multiple users in Southeast Asia reportedly lost their assets, with the affected devices all originating from CryptoBilis, an official Ledger reseller. Investigations found that some Nano X devices had been fitted with unauthorized hardware components capable of stealing users’ recovery seed phrases.

In the wake of the incident, OneKey also revoked CryptoBilis’ authorization, suspended the onboarding of new resellers, and began reviewing its existing distribution network.

For years, one of the most common security recommendations in crypto has been straightforward: buy your crypto, withdraw it to a cold wallet, keep your private keys under your own control, and avoid leaving your assets on exchanges whenever possible.

But now, even the cold wallets themselves, their distribution channels, and the supply chains behind them can become potential sources of risk.

So the question is: Where is the safest place to store your crypto assets—a cold wallet or a centralized exchange (CEX)?

🌟 Cold Wallets: Does Holding Your Own Private Keys Guarantee Safety?

Cold wallets have long been considered one of the safest ways to store large amounts of crypto because private keys do not need to remain exposed to internet-connected devices.

However, there is one easily overlooked question: Has the device itself been tampered with?

From manufacturing and shipping to distribution and final delivery, a security failure at any point in the supply chain could directly threaten the safety of users’ private keys.

There are also plenty of crypto events and promotions that give away cold wallets as prizes. This is not to suggest that these wallets are necessarily compromised. However, from a security perspective, it can be difficult to verify the origin and chain of custody of a giveaway device.

Has it been opened before? Was it initialized by someone else? Who handled it along the way? Ordinary users often have no reliable way to verify every step.

Yishi, founder of OneKey, also specifically addressed the question of how users can confirm that a hardware wallet has not been tampered with. Users can check tamper-evident packaging and single-use security seals, inspect the device’s status, and use the official app to verify the device and its security chip.

Supply-chain risks are not merely theoretical. There have been cases in which unusual purchasing channels or suspicious device origins were linked to stolen assets.

In July last year, a user reported that a friend had purchased an imToken cold wallet for RMB 618 from a https://t.co/mazjp4Sln2 store called “ConsenShop Studio.”

The friend subsequently transferred a total of 4.35 BTC from a CEX in several batches. About two hours after the BTC arrived, hackers began draining the funds.

When the user opened the wallet again two days later, the balance had dropped to zero. The store from which the wallet had been purchased had also shut down.

Following the CryptoBilis incident, wallet manufacturers have begun reassessing the security of their resellers and supply chains. OneKey stopped onboarding new resellers and initiated a review of its existing distribution channels. It also offered free device replacements to users who had purchased devices through CryptoBilis.

At this point, another question comes to mind: If a cold wallet fails and the assets are stolen, is there any compensation mechanism?

In most cases, the answer is no.

The hardware wallet industry has no standardized compensation mechanism. The reason is straightforward: a cold wallet may sell for just a few hundred dollars, but the manufacturer has no control over how much money a user chooses to store in it.

The reported losses associated with the CryptoBilis incident have already reached approximately $102 million. Losses attributed to a Coldcard firmware vulnerability this year have also exceeded $100 million.

Since Ledger is a privately held company, its latest reliable financial figures are difficult to obtain from public sources. For comparison, we can look at a larger hardware wallet manufacturer operating in the same market.

Take Tangem, for example. Its revenue in 2025 was approximately $61.3 million. A single major security incident can result in losses that exceed the annual revenue of a large hardware wallet manufacturer.

Therefore, when assets are stored in a cold wallet, if those assets are actually stolen, users will generally have to bear the losses themselves unless the manufacturer explicitly accepts responsibility and voluntarily provides compensation.

That said, it is important to note that such incidents are extremely rare. Hardware wallets have been around for more than a decade, and publicly documented cases of large-scale asset theft directly caused by tampered devices or compromised supply chains remain relatively uncommon.

🌟 CEXs: What Are the Risks of Entrusting Your Assets to an Exchange?

Keeping assets on an exchange may seem much more convenient. You do not need to manage recovery seed phrases yourself or worry about losing a physical device.

But exchanges come with their own risks.

Looking through exchange collapses, hacks, and shutdowns over the past few years, CEX risks can generally be divided into three categories.

1. Account Takeovers

As AI-generated images, videos, and deepfake technology become increasingly sophisticated, account recovery procedures that rely on identity documents and facial recognition are opening up new attack surfaces.

Recently, two similar cases involving stolen user assets have emerged in Chinese-speaking crypto communities.

In these incidents, attackers reportedly obtained extensive personal information about their victims and then exploited identity verification procedures and security-setting changes to take over their accounts.

2. Misappropriation of Customer Assets

FTX was once one of the world's leading cryptocurrency exchanges. However, it had allowed Alameda Research to use customer assets over an extended period while granting Alameda what was effectively unlimited credit.

Large amounts of customer funds were used for trading, investments, and debt repayments, eventually leaving a customer fund shortfall of more than $8 billion.

In November 2022, problems with Alameda's balance sheet came to light. The market began selling FTT, while customers rushed to withdraw their funds from FTX.

The exchange lacked sufficient liquid assets to meet withdrawal requests. It subsequently suspended withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy.

3. Exchange Business and Operational Risks

As market conditions deteriorate, trading volumes and liquidity decline. Major exchanges and on-chain trading platforms put increasing pressure on smaller competitors, while tighter regulatory requirements across jurisdictions continue to raise compliance costs.

This year, shutdowns among smaller and mid-sized CEXs have become increasingly noticeable. BitMart, BitMEX, AscendEX, and CoinEx have all announced the cessation or gradual winding down of trading operations.

Some platforms may simply be exiting the market in an orderly manner, while others have experienced funding shortfalls.

BitMart, for example, was left with a reported reserve shortfall of approximately $319.5 million following an earlier hacking incident. As its business conditions deteriorated this year, users reportedly became unable to withdraw their funds normally in line with their account balances.

Although these three categories of risk are fundamentally different, problems at a CEX do not always mean that assets become inaccessible instantaneously. There may be a brief window in which warning signs emerge and users can take action.

After an account takeover, for instance, an exchange may impose security reviews on changes to account settings and apply withdrawal protection periods. In the FTX case, several days passed between the exposure of Alameda's financial problems, the ensuing bank run, and the eventual suspension of withdrawals.

Of course, none of this guarantees that users will recover their money.

However, compared with a compromised private key that allows assets to be transferred directly on-chain, a CEX at least offers the possibility of intervention through risk controls, account freezes, and manual reviews.

🌟 Final Thoughts

Whether cold wallets or CEXs are safer has always been a contentious debate. It is somewhat like arguing over whether cars or airplanes are safer.

Depending on the metrics used, such as accident rates or passenger miles traveled, airplanes may be significantly safer. Yet many people are still afraid of flying because when a serious aviation accident occurs, the consequences can be catastrophic.

Cold wallets and CEXs operate in a similar way.

From the perspective of asset ownership and control, cold wallets clearly have the advantage. Your private keys remain entirely under your control, and you do not have to worry about an exchange misappropriating your assets.

But if your private keys or device are compromised, your assets could be drained within minutes, with very little opportunity for recovery.

CEXs operate under a different security model. An exchange could be hacked, fail as a business, or misappropriate customer assets internally, as FTX did. However, if the exchange maintains sufficient reserves, effective risk controls, and the financial capacity to compensate users, a security incident does not necessarily have to translate into losses for customers.

Here are two recommendations for ordinary crypto users:

1. Never keep all your assets in one place.

Long-term holdings can be stored in cold wallets, while funds used for active trading can remain on leading CEXs. Diversifying across different storage methods helps reduce concentration risk.

2. If you use a CEX, prioritize platforms with transparent reserves.

Ideally, choose exchanges that provide Proof of Reserves (PoR) and allow users to verify, through a Merkle tree, whether their assets are included in the reported reserves.
